This research focuses on addressing inconsistencies in data tables that contain missing values and functional relationships. Unlike conventional approaches that require adherence to these dependencies, our work aims to explore theories for handling instances that breach certain dependencies, with no preconditions on the presence of missing values. We establish a framework where each data entry can be associated with a truth status: true, false, inconsistent, or undetermined. Furthermore, our framework facilitates examination of pressing problems like data quality assessments, query validation, and data merging. Specifically, we investigate query validation as the central problem of this research, building on the foundation established by recent studies. Key contributions of this research are (a) an innovative strategy for handling inconsistencies, (b) methods for determining the veracity of data tuples, and (c) an examination of our approach's relevance to Four-valued logic and data merging. Additionally, we provide an original solution to query validation and contrast it with existing data repair approaches. Lastly, this research is concluded by outlining potential future extensions and related problems, including data cleaning and data integration. Despite its standalone status, this research paper is an extension of an earlier publication on query validation.

We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel object representation that
replicates both object points and relative poses in relation to a target, using
category-level descriptors. We apply this representation in object manipulation,
with the aim of repeating tasks on new object instances from the same category
after witnessing a single demonstration. To achieve this, we use optimization
to locate the pose whose descriptor corresponds to that in the demonstration. NDFs
are efficiently trained without expert input, using a self-supervised 3D
auto-encoder, and exhibit robust performance across 6-DoF rotations and translations.
In experiments, NDFs master tasks from just a handful (5-10) demonstrations,
in both simulation and with a physical robot. Results show our method excels at
generalizing over different object instances and poses, surpassing a comparison
method relying on 2D descriptors. The NDF project is hosted at https://yilundu.github.io/ndf/.

Alternatively, we have previously found $|z_c|$ to be around 2.03, 1.68 for $N=2, 4$ although these earlier results have a larger systematic uncertainty. These updated results confirm the functional renormalization group predictions made previously and support the idea that the universal exponent $\gamma$ is close to 1.78 for all classic universality classes in three-dimensional QCD. In statistics and machine learning, it is frequently essential to establish whether a basic optimization method on a non-convex function can eventually enter a region where the function becomes locally convex. To address this, we developed an inequality that enables us to analyze the properties of the optimization landscape surrounding the solutions produced by an approximate message passing (AMP) algorithm. Specifically, we applied our inequality to demonstrate the local convexity of a particular TAP free energy function, which is relevant to the Z2 synchronization problem and the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model. Additionally, our inequality led to a confirmation of a previous conjecture regarding the efficiency of a sampling algorithm in the "easy" regime of these models. Furthermore, our results encompass the results of recent studies by M. J. W. and A. S., as well as those of A. A. and M. M. in the "hard" regime. It is worth noting that our results were achieved without relying on the 'BBP' ruggedness assumption that is required in the existing studies. Our results also implicitly demonstrated the stability of the algorithm in the 'easy' regime. In contrast, the results of our previous study for the Z2 synchronization problem were achieved through the application of a different technique that is based on the use of the Sudakov-Fernique concentration inequality within an post-AMP analysis. This previous result led to the discovery of a specific boundary layer where the algorithm is no longer stable. In addition to these results, we established an inequality that led to the discovery of a particular boundary layer where the TAP cost function is not convex. It is essential to note that the width of these boundary layers increases proportionally with the squared root of the underlying dimensionality parameter. We believe that our results have broader implications that are relevant to the stability of the AMP algorithm as well as its potential to be applied in contexts where the ease of convergence is difficult to establish. We also demonstrated the efficiency of a sampling algorithm in the 'easy' regime of the random bond Ising model through the application of our results to this model. We believe that our results have the potential to be applied to a broader class of models that are similar to this model. While using photometry from stars to monitor the atmosphere may seem uncomplicated for optical astrophysics, achieving a precision of 0.01 for measuring the aerosol depth has been challenging. By taking wide-field photometry over a broad altitude range, the aerosol depth can be determined quickly, regardless of the system's absolute calibration, and even provides calibration as a by-product. Our team used extensive data from the FRAM telescope at the Pierre Auger Observatory and a similar telescope at the Cherenkov Telescope Array site to improve the precision of this technique to a precision of possibly 0.01. To accomplish this, we conducted precise laboratory measurements of the system's response to varying light intensities and spectra to counter the limitations of non-linear CCD detectors under observation conditions. These experiments were conducted using a range of light intensities that mimic both daytime and nighttime observation conditions. Furthermore, we conducted observations of the system with a CCD detector similar to those used in telescopes and compared the results with the expected readings to better understand the effects of the detector and possible calibration errors on the accuracy of the measurements. To apply this technique to remote sites, we conducted measurements of the aerosol depth at the Cherenkov Telescope Array site during the construction phase and found that the average aerosol depth at this site is around 0.5. Additionally, we found that the aerosol depth measured by this technique is consistent with measurements made by satellite-based sensors and found that the precision of this technique is around 0.01, which is in line with the expectations of its creators. We believe that this technique has the potential to monitor the aerosol depth continuously and automatically at any location with a photometric telescope and can provide accurate and precise calibration of the system as a by-product. Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through the construction of correspondence constraints utilizing these intermediate cues. This study concentrates on refining two-stage pipelines by combining two distinct concepts: projection grouping on one hand and correspondence learning on the other. We initially employ a patch-based method to forecast projection heatmaps, representing the likelihood distribution of projected corners from 3D bounding boxes. Next, a projection grouping module is proposed to eliminate redundant maxima from heatmaps. Rather than feeding 2D-3D correspondences directly into the Perspective-N-Point (PnP) algorithm, correspondence hypotheses from local maxima and surrounding areas are sampled, ranked by a network that assesses correspondences, and the most credible ones are selected to determine the object pose. We tested the proposed framework on three public datasets and the results demonstrate its superiority over current state-of-the-art approaches. The proposed framework is termed DeepHMap++ and its code has been made publicly available. The proposed project grouping and correspondence learning concepts can also be applied to other object pose estimation tasks. Our new method calculates a variation of eigenvector centrality for multi-layered networks that incorporate node importance across different layers. In these networks, defined by separate interconnected graphs without connections between different layers, the value of a node's centrality is determined by the sum of the values of the connected nodes within each specific layer, similar to traditional eigenvector centrality calculations. Unlike standard approaches, our approach takes into account the relationships between different network layers and their respective impact on the centrality values. Unlike current multi-layer eigenvector centrality frameworks that account for inter-layer connections, our approach uses a separate set of equations that can be solved using a hybrid algorithm. This new algorithm first determines the degree of separation between different layers and then uses a Levenberg-Marquardt solver to adjust the centrality values. We validate our method by applying it to real-world datasets including science collaboration networks and cultural heritage conservation networks. Our results show that the proposed method outperforms existing multi-layer eigenvector centrality approaches in terms of accuracy and reliability. Moreover, our method provides a way to investigate the dependency between network layers and their impact on the distribution of centrality values, offering a new research avenue in the field. Our code is available for public use on GitHub at the URL https://github.com/alihassan-k/MLEVC.

Our calculations using first-principles methods reveal that cubanite exhibits unusual orbital selectivity, with electrons occupying certain molecular orbitals while being localized in other atomic ones. This phenomenon is exceptionally rare in 3d transition metal compounds, providing a theoretical basis for the experimentally observed lack of charge disproportionation, anomalous Mössbauer spectra, and ferromagnetic coupling between adjacent iron ions. Moreover, our results predict that cubanite's orbital selectivity can result in an unusual phase, an antiferromagnetic arrangement of spins aligned c-face to c-face, or an antiferroorbital arrangement beneath a ferromagnetic background, albeit with very low energy costs, so that any of the possible scenarios could be observed depending on the specific conditions. Experimental characterization techniques such as Mössbauer spectroscopy, X-ray absorption, and photoemission, are specifically suggested to provide a comprehensive understanding of this unique orbital selective behavior. Despite its complex chemistry, cubanite is found to be a good candidate for the "120 degree" spin cable geometry, offering valuable insights into how to realize this geometry in other compounds. Alternatively, applying strain or intercalating atoms into the cubanite lattice is proposed to shift its energy costs, allowing any of the possible phases to become the ground state, thereby offering a versatile model compound for experimental and theoretical analysis alike.

Quantum states known as single-photon catalyzed coherent states (SPCCSs) can be generated via quantum-optical catalysis using beam splitters or parametric amplifiers. These states occur when a coherent state and a single-photon state interact in two input ports, and a photon is detected in a specific output channel. We examine the success probabilities associated with detecting these states, as they vary depending on the catalytic device used. Notably, our analysis reveals that states produced by beam splitters and parametric amplifiers exhibit the same characteristics when analyzing the distribution of photons. We thoroughly investigate the unique quantum properties of SPCCSs, including sub-Poisson statistics, anti-bunching effects, and quadrature squeezing. These findings demonstrate that SPCCSs possess abundant non-classical behavior, thereby conferring a quantum advantage for executing various technological tasks. We also explore the durability of these states in noisy environments, discovering that they resist degradation caused by photon loss and optical amplification noise. Nonetheless, mechanical motion turbulence poses a significant threat to these states, suggesting the need for optical isolation in catalytic devices. We conclude by examining the potential of SPCCSs in various applications, including parametric amplification, beam splitting, and coupled systems, and propose a feasible experimental setup for generating these states using fiber optic culprits. Lastly, we outline the fundamental differences between SPCCSs prepared using beam splitters and those prepared using parametric amplifiers, and investigate the unique property of annihilation operator statistics in these states. These states exhibit intricate behavior beneath the surface, necessitating further, in-depth analysis.

Identifying tumors in the esophagus from CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external objects such as feeding tubes. To compensate for these difficulties, doctors often rely on supplementary information from other imaging techniques, medical histories, and endoscopic findings. Acquiring and combining these sources of information is time-consuming and sometimes produces inconclusive results. In this study, we investigate the potential for a more streamlined clinical approach that solely utilizes CT scans for automatically identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus with satisfactory precision. To achieve this, we designed an automatic, start-to-finish method based on deep neural networks called the Dilated Dense Attention Unet. This model leverages spatial and channel attention mechanisms in dense blocks to prioritize specific features and regions. It employs dilated convolutional layers to manage memory requirements and expand its ability to detect distant patterns. We gathered a comprehensive dataset consisting of 792 CT scans from 288 different patients with varied anatomies and included air pockets, feeding tubes, and proximal tumors. To test the robustness of our network, we conducted repeat studies on different training and validation sets. Our model produced a dice similarity coefficient (DSC) of 0.79, a mean surface distance of 5.4 mm, and a Hausdorff distance of 14.7 mm for 287 test scans. These results demonstrate the efficacy of a simplified, CT-only clinical approach for identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus. Our code is available online at this link https://github.com/yousefis/DenseUnet_Esophagus_Segmentation.

Human-generated descriptions are commonly used to train and evaluate image description systems, which are typically ranked based on their similarity to these descriptions. This method's reliability hinges on the quality of these descriptions. Since, as demonstrated in Section 2, current datasets are inadequate, I believe we require more precise guidelines balancing visually impaired users' needs and practical description generation feasibility. High-quality reference data could be ideal for system evaluation, yet we should also consider other alternatives. I discuss feasible routes to evaluating systems using smaller, more manageable description sets, including simple, existing datasets, and more sophisticated options like crowdsourced data. Evaluating system evaluation methods itself can provide a better understanding of how to efficiently develop superior image description systems. I also examine the possibility of varying reference data across different system evaluation tasks. Further investigation into the characteristics of both human providers and the tasks they perform will help us pick the most suitable reference data, thereby ensuring the efficacy of evaluation systems for their intended purposes. Ultimately, a one-size-fits-all solution is unlikely, and we should be prepared to experiment with multiple approaches to determine the best method for a broad, diverse category of image description systems. I conclude by highlighting a related issue, the need to develop rigorous standards for evaluating the clarity of image description systems. Tantalum oxide compounds, with the formula Ta$_2$O$_5$, are distinguished by unique properties including high dielectric values and minimal reflectivity. Recent studies have also considered Ta$_2$O$_5$ nanoparticles as potential enhancers for hadron therapy treatments of cancer. To understand the material's electronic behavior, researchers have used theoretical simulations from first principles. Yet, Ta$_2$O$_5$ has various forms, complicating attempts to identify their individual features. To resolve this issue, researchers used time-dependent density functional methods to study the energy loss function in Ta$_2$O$_5$, specifically in its optical state, and across different polymorphs. These studies have demonstrated that experimental reflection loss signals can be interpreted assuming that Ta$_2$O$_5$'s $\gamma$-phase represents the primary structure of the material. Notably, researchers have also determined that both the effects of local fields and spin-orbit interactions are vital to correctly determining the energy loss of Ta$_2$O$_5$. Lastly, further validating the $\gamma$-Ta$_2$O$_5$ structure, researchers have used a Monte Carlo method to compare calculated reflection loss spectra with the actual results of experiments, achieving a very accurate match. Ultimately, this research has clarified the crystal structure of Ta$_2$O$_5$, and provides a method for predicting its electronic behavior in other situations.

Previous studies attributed online misinformation dissemination to personal factors, such as information literacy, and social media influences, but ignored a third aspect: the impact of the physical separation of Americans in geographical regions. We tested the significance of this phenomenon, known as "The Big Sort," on online misinformation spread. We analyzed more than 8 million Reddit comments from news articles spanning four years and found that misinformation did not spread primarily through the features of the Reddit platform, but rather was linked to user population size in each state, following a supply-and-demand model. Furthermore, variations in misinformation dissemination were explained by local personality traits and cultural characteristics rather than economic, social, or political conditions. In areas where residents are less diligent in nature, and cultures place little emphasis on adherence to norms, we found increased circulation of all news, including credible sources. In contrast, areas with diligent and norm-adherent populations restricted misinformation circulation, but also limited access to news sources, including credible ones. Our study highlights the significant role of geographical isolation in contributing to the circulation of misinformation and suggests that interventions focused on reducing misinformation circulation should take this factor into account. Moreover, our findings have implications for understanding the dissemination of true information, given that areas with diligent populations also limit access to news sources. Finally, our study provides a novel application of life and social science theories in an empirical analysis of online misinformation. We propose further research on the dynamics of misinformation dissemination among subgroups within these populations and the effectiveness of targeted interventions to reduce misinformation circulation based on the findings presented. We also offer a platform for discussing the General Sort's effects on mis- and info-communication, as well as recommendations for future research on the subject. Humans employ spoken language to efficiently teach other people various skills. Although robotic demonstrations are a natural teaching method, learning from solely observed actions does not take full advantage of audio feedback from the instructor. To effectively incorporate auditory cues present during demonstrations, understanding their underlying content and purpose is essential. This study examines audio input from humans instructing a robot using Sawyer via spoken language by analyzing three key features: speech duration, tone variation, and speech content. Evaluating these features across four dimensions, it was discovered that instructors frequently use the same vocabulary to describe specific task elements despite varying situations such as task types, audio instructions, and errors encountered during demonstrations. However, differences in speech patterns including duration and inflection are present across these conditions, showing that human speech carries significant, potentially valuable information for enhancing robotic learning through demonstration-based methods. The results of this research can be utilized to design more effective speech-based interfaces for teaching robots in similar contexts. The current study focuses on demonstration-based learning in a controlled environment but the analysis and findings can also be applicable to other situations involving audio teachings by humans. The data collected during the study in the form of transcripts and waveform graphs of the spoken language is available for further study. The current study may serve as a foundation for future research in areas such as speech recognition and robotic learning. This contributes a universal term to the energy-momentum tensor complexity, which we find to be (c/12)(M^2/dM^2). Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are often hindered by the limitations of requiring at least one well-supplied domain and over-reliance on domain-agnostic preferences, which is impractical given the ubiquitous sparsity in real-world scenarios. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) that tackles multi-target cross-domain recommendation in multiple sparse domains. In contrast to conventional CDR methods, MSDCR considers all participating domains as equally data-poor, thereby simultaneously enhancing the recommendation performance across each domain. We devise a Multi-Domain Separation Network (MDSN) and a Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module to augment a user's specific aspect preferences in each domain by transferring complementary preferences from other domains, while maintaining domain-specific uniqueness through adversarial training and dynamically determining the degree of complementarity using GAPE. Additionally, we introduce a Multi-Domain Adaptation Network (MDAN) to capture a user's general, domain-agnostic aspect preference. By integrating the domain-specific aspect preference and the domain-agnostic aspect preference, MSDCR attains a thorough understanding of user preferences across each data-poor domain. The empirical evaluations on real-world datasets unequivocally demonstrate the superiority of MSDCR over state-of-the-art single-domain and CDR models. The proposed approach also achieves meaningful interpretability results, enabling the physical meaning of model learnable parameters to be deduced, thereby providing valuable insights into the intricate mechanisms of multi-target CDR. The corresponding code is available at: https://github.com/zhoukai1997/MSDCR.

Convex optimization issues often take on a more manageable form when represented with conic formulations that leverage a wide variety of exotic cones. Exotic cones in this context, refer to specialized geometric shapes with properties enabling efficient implementation of computational tools, specifically barrier oracles for their own and dual shapes. This work introduces Hypatia, an interior-point solver designed to handle these complex shapes with ease. Developed using Julia and interfacing with JuMP, Hypatia can utilize a wide assortment of predefined exotic cones. It then generates simplified equivalent formulations for various optimization applications that can provide significant improvements in processing speed and memory consumption. The proposed method demonstrates a marked improvement in problem-solving efficiency when compared to more conventional and complex conic formulations. The proposed method can be applied to a wide range of optimization applications, including multistage robust optimization, dynamic fully convex two-stage robust optimization, and stochastic linear programming. The paper is accompanied by a downloadable code and data available at: https://github.com/HypatiaOpt/Hypatia_Jump. The proposed method is further evaluated using real-world instances from the COUENNE test suite and the National Digital Library of Theses and Dissertations. The results show a marked improvement in problem-solving efficiency when compared to more conventional and complex conic formulations. The proposed method can be applied to a wide range of optimization applications, including multistage robust optimization, dynamic fully convex two-stage robust optimization, and stochastic linear programming. The escalating quantity of MRI data necessitates automated quality control to ensure reliable and efficient analysis, especially for extensive research projects. Several approaches have been explored to develop scalable and dependable quality control pipelines, but effectively generalizing these methods across diverse, previously unseen data remains a significant challenge. This study evaluated the MRIQC pipeline's performance on multiple large datasets, utilizing ABIDE with 1,102 subjects and CATI-derived data with 9,037 participants for both training and assessment purposes. Our investigation concentrated on MRIQC preprocessing steps and assessed the pipeline's efficacy with and without these preprocessing methods. Further analysis examined site-specific and study-specific classification probabilities for models trained on ABIDE and CATI data without preprocessing. Our primary findings showed that using MRIQC features without preprocessing yielded the best results in models trained and evaluated on diverse, multi-center datasets with varying population characteristics. This led to an improvement in ROC-AUC scores on unseen data of 0.10 when using a subset of the CATI dataset. Nonetheless, models trained on diverse, heterogeneous populations showed questionable generalizability, as evident from site-specific and study-specific probability predictions and derived classification thresholds. This research highlights the challenges of generalizing MRIQC models and highlights the importance of future work on developing robust, dependent data analysis techniques to enhance the efficacy of MRIQC pipelines in real-world applications. The development of efficient and controllable quantum communication networks will depend heavily on reliable creation and manipulation of solid-state devices that interface photons with electronic spins effectively. In silicon material, T-type damage centers have shown significant potential for this interface, thanks to their unique optical properties in the O-band region and long-lived electronic and nuclear spin lifetimes. Although research on these defect centers has so far been conducted as part of bulk silicon studies, we demonstrate the consistent creation of high T center densities within the 220nm device layer of Silicon-On-Insulator (SOI) wafers, using a process that combines ion implantation and heat treatment. By developing a method to measure spin-dependent optical transitions, we found that high T center densities located near the interface can exhibit ~1 GHz levels of spectral diffusion without the need for extensive optimization of the fabrication process. Furthermore, we showed that a 300nm thick device layer can exhibit ~10-fold increased T center densities, and that etching the device layer allows for an increase in optical transition rates by ~20-fold. To facilitate the development of quantum integrated devices, we also established a method to characterize the optical and spin properties of T centers in SOI materials. Overall, our findings provide a way to optimize T center densities in SOI materials, offering great potential for the creation of quantum devices that couple photons with electronic spins. Lastly, we discuss possible approaches to enhance T center densities further, including the use of multiple ion implantation layers and passive layer etching to increase the optical transition rates. We examine the concentration behavior of functionals of random vectors whose entries reside in the discrete cube. These vectors must adhere to either the stochastic covering property (SCP) or the strong Rayleigh property (SRP). Our findings concerning SCP measures yield new subgaussian inequalities of a bounded-difference type, surpassing earlier results by Pemantle and Peres and extending analogous outcomes for matrix-valued settings as seen in recent estimates by Aoun, Banna, and Youssef. For functions under SRP we establish stronger inequalities of a Bernstein-type for matrix-valued functions, thereby broadening earlier general bounds for linear combinations of positive definite matrices due to Kyng and Song.

Furthermore, we investigate the unique case where we condition on Bernoulli random variables with independent outcomes for their sum. In doing so, we establish sharpened estimates resulting in specifically tailored log-Sobolev inequalities, as well as Talagrand's convex distance inequality, with concentration inequalities for convex functions, polynomials, and matrix-valued functions as direct consequences. These generalised inequalities encompass results for uniform distributions over discrete slices of the cube, extensively explored in numerous studies. Notably, as n increases, the distribution of conjugacy classes becomes increasingly complex and refined, ultimately mirroring the structure of the classical group Sp_n(K). Despite this complexity, Springer established an algorithm for defining each conjugacy class completely, using only the characteristics and parameters of the group. This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word2vec model, particularly in its implementation with the Skip-gram learning method. We investigate how NLP embeddings, now widely applied, are impacted by the distribution of terms within a given corpus. A mathematical framework is employed to elucidate the implicit structural assumptions of the model, revealing its reliance on Markovian assumptions that provide a clear theoretical understanding of how embeddings are generated and capture the essence of frequentist synonyms. We also develop generative models and conduct explicit analyses of commonly used loss functions. To further illustrate the limitations of these models, we create synthetic corpora with varying levels of complexity, demonstrating the ability (or inability) of word2vec to effectively learn these structures. We also empirically assess the capabilities of these models using a substantial financial news dataset covering 12 years and spanning 42 million articles, relying on the Loughran-McDonald Sentiment Word Lists. Our results show that these models are prone to confusing antonyms as frequentist synonyms and mixing terms with opposing polarities. Notably, our research also uncovers the non-stationarity of financial corpora, revealing time-varying patterns in cosine similarity among polarized words or company names. Our analysis highlights the entangled mixture of semantic and co-occurring word distributions that these models are capturing, posing challenges for their disentanglement. Our work offers a mathematical framework that can be extended to other NLP tasks and models, suggesting possible avenues for exploring the underlying structures of various word embeddings. Our code is available at https://github.com/ali-ghosh/polar-word2vec. This article presents the SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM based IDET systems as alternatives to our previously proposed optimal wideband waveforming strategy in [1].
Fair-throughput and sum-throughput optimisation problems are defined and formulated.
By leveraging an algorithm that utilizes fixed points, we derive the optimal fair-throughput and sum-throughput values for SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM systems. 
A hybrid fast time-diviation multiple access (FTD-MTA) scheme is proposed to implement the optimal fair-throughput and sum-throughput values in practice.
In the FTD-MTA scheme, the base station determines the optimal power allocation, divides time within the optimal boundaries, and combines the data in the carrier domain.
Simulation results confirm the performance gains of SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM systems over SISO and the corresponding OFDM system.
The proposed FTD-MTA scheme achieves the desired performance in practice, with only a small gap to the ideal scenario. 
This article provides the SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM based IDET system design, along with the proposed FTD-MTA scheme, as alternatives to our previous optimal waveforming strategy in [1].

By leveraging the strengths of these approaches, we've developed a numerical strategy utilizing Cartesian grids to efficiently handle complex boundary transformations and high-resolution interface representation. This method enables a second-order conservative numerical scheme and has been effectively applied to solve various problems, including Stefan problems, dendrite growth, and Rayleigh--B\'enard instabilities, even in the presence of melting boundaries. Furthermore, we've compared our results to existing literature, demonstrating close agreement and improving the resolution of certain phenomena. To accommodate dynamic boundary conditions, we've introduced a numerical predictor--corrector technique and implemented a simple algorithm for reducing the occurrence of grid-based artifacts known as 'grid tangling.' This approach has been applied to a moving contact line problem, resulting in the standard fountain profile in both conservative and non-conservative formulations. Additionally, we've modified the method to handle floating objects and moving phase boundaries, demonstrating its capabilities with the injection of a non-round hole and the melting of an ice cube. This numerical model has been incorporated into an open-source code available for public use. In this research, we've focused on adapting the level-set method to solve problems involving changing phase boundaries, with the aim of paving the way for its application to more complex problems, including solidification and flow in the presence of moving boundaries, and even with floating objects. In the process, we've run into issues with grid-based level-set methods that are now well-documented. In the final section, we've outlined some of these challenges and potential solutions, in the hope of contributing to the advancement of level-set methods and related algorithms. In the process of conducting this research, we've also developed a number of related ideas, including the introduction of a moving contact line algorithm, the implementation of the level-set method on irregular boundaries, and even the creation of a hybrid method for solving PDEs on irregular boundaries, all of which could be explored in greater detail in the future. In multiagent learning settings beyond finding equilibria, learning rationalizable behavior that steers clear of dominated actions is another key goal. However, existing algorithms in the general multiplayer games scenario require an exponentially large number of samples relative to the number of players to determine rationalizable equilibria when working under bandit feedback. This research develops an initial suite of efficient algorithms to learn both Coarse Correlated Equilibria (CCE) and Correlated Equilibria (CE) that achieve polynomial sample complexities in line with problem parameters including the number of players. It also includes an enhanced approach for identifying a rationalizable action profile with a significantly improved sample requirement, exceeding the current benchmark established in 2021. Our innovative solutions involve the integration of multiple cutting-edge techniques that concurrently ensure the rationalizability and absence of (swap-)regret through correlated exploration and dynamic learning rate adjustments, offering potential value as standalone contributions. Moreover, our results are complemented by a sample complexity lower bound, underscoring the precision of the devised guarantees. This study is further distinguished by the incorporation of a rationalization-focused proxy CCE, a novel concept introduced here, that provides a broader framework incorporating existing notions of rationalizability. Ultimately, our results are likely to extend to other performance metrics, such as the learning of (swap-)optimal actions, a hypothesis left for future investigation. This research builds on the fundamentals established in recent multiagent learning over finite action spaces, with an emphasis on establishing rigorous results within the general context of large gameplay scenarios. The development of our algorithms has been theoretically motivated with an emphasis on linking theory and practice, offering a potential path for future empirical study. The proposed framework, along with the associated challenges and techniques, provides a starting point for further exploration in a range of applications beyond game theory, including statistics and machine learning. The corresponding code is available at https://github.com/ChenghaoXu94/RationalizableEquilibria.

An analysis of a stochastic Susceptible to Infective to Recovered model is conducted, where the model is based on an Erdős-Rényi random graph that changes dynamically as susceptible individuals connected to infected neighbours form new connections or sever existing ones. As the model is scaled to accommodate large populations, researchers obtained mathematical proofs of key properties of the model, particularly its early stages and the phase where the epidemic spreads rapidly. They also found that under certain conditions, there are sharp thresholds where the model suddenly switches between two completely different behaviours. It has been proven that these transitions are more dramatic if the model is changed to only form new connections to uninfected individuals, where the model suddenly switches from no infections to complete spread. This change affects the way the model scales with population size. Interestingly, it was discovered that increasing the frequency of new connections can actually decrease the rate of infection spread. This model is comparable to other epidemic models such as the susceptible-exposed-infective-recovered model and the SIR model with mutations, and it provides a unique insight into the effect of changing connections between individuals on the spread of an epidemic. Ultimately, this research uncovered key statistics about the model, particularly the average number of infections and the time it takes for the model to reach a steady state. It also established a relationship between the model and a branching process known as the ANCP process. This process is complex and not easily understood, but it is crucial for understanding the model's early stages. The research paper also explored a variation of the model called the super-spreader model, where certain individuals, known as super-spreaders, are more likely to infect multiple people. This model is significant because it provides a mathematical explanation for the sudden and extreme spread of an epidemic due to a small group of individuals. To accelerate policy optimization in complex, dynamic systems with multiple influencing factors, reinforcement learning agents can effectively utilize previously collected historical data. Standard experience replay enables agents to retain information from prior iterations. However, the current approach equally values all collected observations, neglecting their varying significance. A more adaptive method, the variance reduction based experience replay framework, selectively leverages the most informative historical data. This approach prioritizes past observations more likely to represent the current target distribution. Theoretical and practical evaluations demonstrate that this method accelerates optimal policy discovery and boosts the effectiveness of state-of-the-art policy optimization methods. When compared to the conventional experience replay method, our variance reduction based approach on a simple policy optimization method achieves an average return that is 15% higher in a complex simulation environment. Furthermore, our framework enhances the effectiveness of a cutting-edge policy optimization method, obtaining return levels that are 25% higher than conventional experience replay in a more challenging setting. Our approach can be integrated into various policy optimization algorithms and is applicable to a wide range of dynamic systems. Moreover, our findings validate the practical utility of our approach across real-world systems. The variance reduction based experience replay framework is capable of enhancing the efficacy of policy optimization in various contexts, as evident from our simulations and real-world experiments. We introduce MG-GLAM, a computational tool developed to rapidly create comprehensive N-body simulations for various cosmological theories, specifically modified gravity models. This program builds upon the existing GLAM code and incorporates an advanced multigrid method to solve the non-linear equations characteristic of modified gravity theories, resulting in highly efficient simulations. For $f(R)$ gravity, MG-GLAM includes multiple variations that mimic distinct behaviors of these models and offers tailored algorithms to maintain speed and precision. The code excels at producing a broad spectrum of modified gravity simulations and offers significant computational benefits, outperforming existing N-body simulations by a factor of over a hundred while yielding accurate results for key cosmological metrics. MG-GLAM is suited for creating large sets of modified gravity simulations that can be utilized in mock galaxy catalogues and emulators for ongoing and future galaxy surveys. The code is available for download at [www.mgglam.com]. The accompanying catalogue comprises 1450 simulated galaxy distributions for a range of modified gravity models, available for researchers to use. The scale of these simulations allows for the direct comparison of different cosmological parameters derived from galaxy surveys for a range of modified gravity models, thus providing valuable insights into the underlying physics of the cosmos. The most efficient version of the code was capable of producing one galaxy simulation at a mass scale of $10^{14}$ solar masses within approximately 14 hours on 64 processors. The code has the potential to be applied to future large galaxy surveys, such as Euclid and LSST, which are set to observe the cosmos at a greater scale than ever before. The simulations conducted using the MG-GLAM code demonstrate its capability in accurately determining the underlying cosmological parameters of the universe, achieving results that are in close agreement with the fundamental principles of general relativity. The results also highlight the distinct ways in which modified gravity models behave under different observational regimes, with the power spectrum slope changing sign as the mass scale increases from $10.0_{-2.0}^{+5.0}\times 10^{12}$ solar masses. The MG-GLAM code has been applied to a range of gravitational models, including the Einstein gravity theory, $f(R)$ gravity with the bare Einstein and Einstein-Hull form, $f(R)$ gravity with the pure monopole form, and $f(R)$ gravity with the Kennedy-Abbott form. The code has also been used to develop two novel variants of $f(R)$ gravity: the Logarithmic form and the Fractional form.

Miller and Sheffield introduced the concept of an imaginary surface as a pairing of subdomains of the complex plane and associated Gaussian free fields under conformal equivalence. Specifically, they considered the relationship between these pairings and chordal Schramm-Loewner evolution. This paper develops Gaussian free field-valued processes in the upper half-plane and the first orthant of the complex plane, establishing their connection to multiple SLE evolving in time on these domains. We demonstrate that such connections can be made locally by driving multiple SLE with the Dyson model on the real line and the Bru-Wishart process on the positive reals, respectively. Ultimately, these pairings yield domains that evolve in time and associated Gaussian free fields. We observe these domains to be conformally equivalent to the initial upper half-plane and the initial first orthant. This leads to the characterization of the associated Gaussian free fields as harmonic functions in these evolving domains. This characterization further extends to the analysis of multiple SLE on more complicated domains following the idea of Miller and Sheffield. Additionally, this characterization enables us to recover the results of Daneri and Ghislain, as well as to establish the boundary continuity of Gaussian free fields in time-evolving Riemannian metrics. Furthermore, this characterization facilitates the construction of multiple SLE with specified boundary values, thereby extending the domain of defined multiple SLE and revealing the space-filling nature of multiple SLE on the unit disk. Lastly, this characterization also enables us to couple multiple SLE of different sizes on the same domain, demonstrating that the modulus of a domain is a monotone function of the modulus of its subdomains. This further extends to the analysis of multiple SLE on time-evolving domains, demonstrating that the modulus of a domain is a continuous function of its changing subdomains. This latter result can be applied to prove the boundary continuity of Gaussian free fields, as well as to extend the results of Kerber and Miller to multiple SLE on the unit disk. into a sophisticated collaborative platform for developing high-quality manuscripts
and software projects. Originally developed at McMaster University's theoretical
biology lab, WorkingWiki enables multiple users to work together on a range of
tasks by utilizing command-line tools to translate raw'source code' into desired outputs.
Its features cater specifically to programmers and researchers who use languages
like R, Python, and C, and it boasts specialized tools for seamless LaTeX editing.
By integrating features from collaborative editors, development environments,
version control systems, and publishing platforms, WorkingWiki unlocks the
full potential of wiki-based collaboration, and its customizable'makefiles'
and modular architecture enable users to tailor and repurpose its functionality. Though
developed in-house to suit McMaster University's particular needs, WorkingWiki
is now available to the public, awaiting the contributions of a broader community
that can further its development and refine its features for a wider range of applications.

Understanding how genomic elements affect specific traits through genome-wide association studies remains complex due to the sheer number of available annotations. We've developed a statistical approach to pinpoint relevant genomic elements, based on associations across the entire genome, by identifying patterns of influence in trait-associated SNPs. This approach can incorporate multiple annotation types and has been successfully applied to eighteen human traits such as blood, platelet counts, metabolism-related disorders, height, obesity and a bowel disease, by examining 450 distinct genomic features across one hundred plus tissues and cells types. Our results show that protein-coding regions influence traits to a degree of up to twenty percent, in comparison with two percent, in a wide range of cases and demonstrate specific patterns of depleted and enriched regions associated with different traits and SNPs that target repressed or accessible regions specifically within certain cell types. Furthermore, by re-ranking associations based on functional genomics, we have increased confidence in a significant portion of associated SNPs with an estimated 5%. Additionally, we have observed similarities in patterns of depleted and enriched regions at the level of different tissues and cells types that differ significantly more than expected. In conclusion, the pervasive nature of tissue and cells type specific enrichment and depletion in the human genome is evident and this knowledge can be utilized to improve the interpretation of genome-wide association studies across various traits and conditions. Observations of some variable X-ray sources within the Milky Way's center that have shown no outbursts in over a decade have led some researchers to suggest a significant population of stellar mass black holes in the region. A crucial aspect of the theory that these sources are actually black holes is the claim that neutron star binaries with low masses exhibit recurring X-ray bursts within short intervals. This study contradicts that idea by revealing that about half of the known LMXBs, featuring a neutron star as the primary component, exhibit outburst recurrence times exceeding a decade when detected by the MAXI telescope. Moreover, to reconcile the total population of neutron star binaries with observed and radio pulsar populations within the Milky Way, researchers find that a significant majority of these binaries have recurrence times exceeding a century for outbursts visible to the MAXI telescope and most remain undiscovered. This study's findings also examine the likely distribution of recurrence times for newly discovered variables among the known LMXBs with short recurrence times, suggesting that the majority of variables with short recurrence times are actually neutrons rather than black holes, although still constituting a small fraction of the total neutron star population. Ultimately, this study's results imply that the majority of the Milky Way's neutron star binaries remain invisible to the MAXI telescope and suggest that the notion of defined minimum recurrence times for neutron star binaries is incorrect. Improving neural conversational agents' ability to produce diverse, engaging responses in casual conversations is a challenge. To tackle this issue, this paper introduces two significant innovations. Firstly, it proposes a new assessment metric that employs Natural Language Inference to gauge the semantic variety of responses generated by the model in a conversation. Using a previously established framework, this metric was tested and showed a clear connection between Natural Language Inference Diversity and semantic variety. It was discovered that the contradiction relation yields more precise results than the neutral relation in measuring diversity and integrating the NLI model's confidence achieves the highest performance to date. Secondly, this paper demonstrates a way to enhance the semantic variety of responses generated by the model through an iterative procedure called Diversity Threshold Generation, which, in comparison to standard generation methods, results in an average 137% improvement in NLI Diversity. Moreover, this method was integrated into a renowned conversational agent evaluation metric and discovered that Diversity Threshold Generation also leads to a 57% improvement in the Semantic Average Precision score. This paper's discoveries have been applied in a real-world setting, namely in creating chatbots for multiple popular comics and sitcoms. The code and data for this research are available at the website: \url{https://github.com/ParthGhosh/Diversity_in_Dialogue_NLI}.

Bipartite graphs depicting connections between distinct groups of objects have numerous practical applications, and their visualization often takes the form of a 2-tier layout where corresponding entities are aligned horizontally across two parallel lines, connected by lines representing relationships between them. The task of reducing edge crossings within these visualizations can be computationally intensive, yet might not always guarantee sufficiently low crossings levels to maintain the visualization's clarity. In contrast, an approach has been developed to remove edge crossings by splitting specific nodes, targeting the minimum number required to yield an edge-free (planar) drawing. The question of determining if an edge-free representation exists after breaking at most a specified number of nodes remains tractable in relation to that number. The paper presents an iterative bidding algorithm that achieves this tractability in a manner dependent on the number of nodes available for splitting. The approach's effectiveness is further demonstrated through experimental results comparing its performance against a genetic optimization approach for various real-world data sets. The problem of bipartite graph non-planarity can be tackled by an algorithm that has a known parameterized complexity, and by extending the approach, a more complex task of 2-page drawing of bipartite graphs also has a known parameterized complexity. The paper's findings also confirm that a previously known polynomial-time algorithm is tractable when considering a specific, limited type of node splitting, and the results' discussion highlights possible research opportunities for further development. The paper's research has been conducted during the COVID-19 pandemic, with the authors collaborating remotely. The paper presents an FPT algorithm for bipartite graph non-planarity, as well as a 2-page drawing problem, and contributes to the paper's results presented at the COCOA conference. In order to enhance side-channel attacks, this research introduces a new technique, HyperDegrade, which incorporates previous methods and employs simultaneous multithreading architectures.  A novel analysis into the causes of performance degradation through cache eviction was also performed, leading to the discovery of an unknown source of slowdowns.  Compared to existing techniques, HyperDegrade resulted in more significant slowdowns and improvements, which in certain cases achieved an enhanced time granularity of three orders of magnitude for Flush+Reload attacks.  To further evaluate the technique, metrics for side-channel leakage were proposed, which demonstrated that HyperDegrade could be effective in side-channel amplification without compromising data integrity.  A fair comparison between three different performance degradation strategies in combination with Flush+Reload attacks revealed HyperDegrade's efficacy, which enabled the development of an attack on an OpenSSL vulnerability three times more efficient than other methods.  In addition, HyperDegrade's applicability to Raccoon-like attacks was also demonstrated, which can succeed with real-world data and extend the scope of existing attacks to various protocols, filling in the gap left by previous research.  The source code for HyperDegrade has been made available online.

A localized alteration in knot diagrams is referred to as an unknotting operation. It can be demonstrated that any knot diagram can be converted into a trivial unknot through a sequence of unknotting operations, combined with some variations in the diagram configuration, which are referred to as Reidemeister moves. Unknotting operations hold significant value in the field of knot theory; they serve a purpose in analyzing the intricacy of knots and knot-related properties. Moreover, they also have implications in the fields of biology, chemistry, and physics for studying complexly intertwined structures of molecules, substances, and DNA. The purpose of this paper was to introduce a novel type of unknotting operation, which is called the diagonal move, applicable to classical and welded knots. The study shows that the cross-over change, the delta-move, the sharp-move, the gamma-move, the n-gon move, the pass move, and the 4-move can be achieved by applying a sequence of diagonal moves. The study also delves into defining a distance measure that originates from the diagonal move, as well as examining its characteristics. The proposed move has advantages over other moves as it results in a less complicated change at the level of the diagram, which makes it suitable for implementing algorithms and is also an accurate indicator of the complexity of the knot. The research paper introduces an algorithm that generates the delta-move, the sharp-move, the n-gon move, the pass move, and the 4-move via a sequence of diagonal moves, which can be executed through a set of basic rules. The purpose of the delta-move algorithm is to convert any knot diagram into a diagram representing a welded knot that contains exactly two loops, along with proving that the algorithm is valid for all knot diagrams. The study also examines the properties of the distance measure, which includes demonstrating that the distance measure is additive in nature, and feasible to estimate, along with investigating its characteristics. The proposed move and algorithm of the paper were validated by executing tests on a set of sample knots. The results showed that the paper's approach is applicable to a wide range of knots. The paper concluded by discussing some possible improvements and the challenges that need to be addressed in the future, along with presenting some applications of the paper's method in the fields of biology, chemistry, and physics. In this context, we explore a privacy-preserving approach called federated learning that enables several entities to train a robust machine learning model jointly, without exchanging sensitive information about their data. Based on how entities cooperate, FL can be categorized into two primary forms - horizontal and vertical FL. The former involves participants who collaborate using identical data attributes, while in the latter, entities with overlapping sample IDs collaborate using different features. Given its versatility, vertical FL is deemed particularly suitable for collaborative training by major enterprises. Here we concentrate on FL and delve into possible privacy breaches in actual VFL implementations. Two applicable attacks were created by us - one is called a reverse multiplication attack designed to circumvent logistic regression, while the other, known as a reverse sum attack, targets XGBoost protocols. Our empirical study validates that both attacks are successful, effective, evasive, and straightforward - they do not diverge from the predefined protocol, nor do they lower the model's accuracy; even with data encrypted. Additionally, we found out the stolen information can train a new machine learning classifier which is just as accurate as the one trained using actual data, without knowing beforehand much about the target user. Last but not least, we propose a possible answer to the problem of classifier's parameters being different from the information obtained from the stolen information. This research paper examines conformally flat hypersurfaces of n-dimensional space (n is 4 or higher) within a hypersphere of n+2 dimensions. We start by classifying and describing these conformally flat hypersurfaces when they have constant M\"obius curvature under specific transformations. Next, we prove that a compact hypersurface with this constant M\"obius curvature, denoted R, is specifically equal to $(n-1)(n-2)r^2$ for values of r less than 1. Furthermore, if this hypersurface is compact, we establish that it is topologically equivalent to a torus defined by the union of a circle with a radius of $\sqrt{1-r^2}$ and a hypersphere with a radius of r in the space of n+1 dimensions. Additionally, if this hypersurface is compact and has a constant mean curvature, we demonstrate that it is topologically equivalent to a sphere with a radius of r in the space of n+1 dimensions. Finally, if the hypersurface has constant M\"obius curvature and is topologically equivalent to a sphere in the space of n+1 dimensions, we conclude that it is conformally equivalent to a sphere with a radius of r in the space of n+2 dimensions. However, unless it has a vanishing mean curvature, this implies it is not conformally flat. Hence, we establish a specific case of the M\"obius scalar curvature rigidity theorem for hypersurfaces in the space of n+2 dimensions. Lastly, we provide a brief discussion on the extension of our findings to include the case of compact Riemannian manifolds in the space of n+2 dimensions.

Network vulnerability assessment is crucial for creating strategies to prevent the spread of malicious information and diseases in networks. Researchers often study network immunization, but traditional approaches typically focus on broad measures, such as network criticality and component size. In contrast, this paper delves into a micro-level analysis, where the removal of individual nodes during an attack is examined in detail. Based on percolation theory, the authors analyze the effects of removing a single node that causes other nodes to disconnect from the main component. Specifically, this paper investigates the number of nodes that become disconnected from the main component as a result of removing one node. By applying this micro-level approach to a random attack on a Cayley tree network, the distribution of the resulting node removal sizes is derived. Furthermore, a critical threshold exists below which a single node's removal results in the disappearance of the giant component, and an in-depth analysis of this threshold provides valuable insights. By exploring different attack scenarios, this research demonstrates how the distribution of removal sizes remains robust, while the fraction of removed nodes that become disconnected from the main component does change. Additionally, a comparison is made with existing research on random graph attacks, highlighting the differences in distribution shapes. This paper's findings are relevant to various network contexts, including internet, supply chains, and biological networks. The approach used here, with its focus on single-node attacks, provides a precise understanding of network vulnerability, but it also gives rise to computational challenges. To overcome these, the authors used an efficient algorithm to determine the node removal sizes, which can be adapted for other networks. This research offers a micro-level perspective on network vulnerability, and as such, it is distinct from traditional, more general approaches. This approach can be further expanded to investigate the effects of node removal on network properties, as well as to develop more precise immunization strategies. This paper's results can be applied to various settings, including cyber security, epidemiology, and transportation, where the removal of infected nodes corresponds to the application of medical treatments. This research on the attack size distribution of a Cayley tree network provides a foundation for exploring other complex networks. This approach can be extended to static networks by incorporating attributes of individual nodes, as well as to dynamic networks by accounting for changes over time. This paper's findings suggest that the distribution of removal sizes remains robust in response to changes in the beta parameter and the attack type, but it does change in response to changes in the gamma parameter. This resistance to changes in the distribution of removal sizes is unique to the Cayley tree network

By transforming the detector into a system with multiple coupled cavities, this design outperforms the conventional signal-recycled Michelson setup by overcoming optical loss-induced limitations. Lately, researchers have focused intensely on solid electronic theory's strongly correlated systems and graphene, yet the $sp^{2}$-electrons that form Dirac bands in graphene lack strong interactions. Consequently, novel, interaction-induced phenomena tied to Dirac points are underutilized. We propose GaCu$_{3}$(OH)$_{6}$Cl$_{2}$ as a new material where Dirac electrons are paired with strong interactions and frustrated magnetism. Calculations indicate its crystallographic and electronic properties harbor symmetry-protected Dirac points at the Fermi level, allowing for multifaceted physics encompassing possible instabilities of charge, magnetism, or superconductivity. By merging various methods to assess its many-body behavior, researchers have observed potential transitions to Mott-Hubbard, magnetic or charge ordering states, along with $f$-wave unconventional superconductivity in this unique compound. Despite its complexity, researchers believe GaCu$_{3}$(OH)$_{6}$Cl$_{2}$ can be synthesized, and its study holds significant potential for advancing understanding of interplay between different interactions in solid state physics. References: S. Kadambi et al., arXiv: 2106.03803; J. Phys. Chem. C, 123, 25, 2023; J. Phys. Cond. Mat., 35, 2023.

Researchers explored the capabilities of the NA62 experiment at CERN to enhance restrictions on a specific parameter in the Standard Model, specifically related to the interaction between a particular lepton and heavy neutral particles. By analyzing the process of $K^+ \to \pi^0 e^+ N$, they determined the present limit can be set at $2\times 10^{-6}$ for a particular lepton interaction with masses ranging from 125 to 144 MeV, a region that current production searches lack in depth. Combining existing data with optimized detection tools or improved photon rejection techniques can significantly narrow this limit. For example, incorporating into the analysis the study of $K^+ \to \gamma e^+ N$ decays or utilizing a more effective photon filter can achieve this goal. Ultimately, this research found the NA62 facility has the potential to expand the restriction on this parameter by a factor of 100 over its current level, and with a 50 times increase in data, can reach the level of interest for future production searches. Furthermore, this research identified opportunities to enhance the understanding of the $K^+ \to \pi^0 e^+ N$ decay process, including deriving a more precise estimate of the hadronic form factor, and determining the relative branching fraction with higher precision. This can be achieved either by employing a different detection approach or optimizing the analysis tools, which would also contribute to a deeper comprehension of the underlying physics. This research was previously published in the journal "Physics Letters B", volume 817. This article is a summary of the paper titled: Improved sensitivity to the effective number of neutrino species from the $K^+
  \to \pi^0 e^+ N$ decay at the NA62 experiment at CERN, which can be found at this URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.physletb.2022.137044.

Neural language models have largely surpassed $N$-gram models due to better performance, but our findings suggest that $n$-gram models still excel in many situations with low computational costs, demonstrating a strong foundation of language understanding. Building upon this discovery, we developed a neural model that learns from the remaining knowledge between $n$-gram models and the true language distribution, allowing for both a deeper grasp of language and the flexibility to adjust models through the $n$-gram base without altering the neural model. Through extensive experiments on tasks including language modeling, machine translation, and summarization, our hybrid approach consistently delivers enhanced performance over standard neural models and facilitates seamless domain adaptation by simply swapping the $n$-gram base, eliminating the need for additional training. This challenging problem is compounded by the extensive variability of head poses, which significantly expands the potential solution space and complicates modeling efforts. To break down this complex task into more manageable components, our approach focuses on modeling both pose and occlusion. In this regard, we introduce an end-to-end framework called SADRNet, which produces a face that varies based on the orientation and another face that remains invariant, then fuses these faces via a self-alignment mechanism informed by occlusion. Exhaustive testing of our proposed technique on the widely used AFLW2000-3D and Florence datasets shows substantial performance enhancements over existing top-ranking methods. Moreover, our approach achieves simple and precise code, with a limited 230,000 parameters, enabling efficient face reconstruction on a range of platforms. The proposed technique has also been applied to real-world datasets, demonstrating promising results and opening possible avenues for future research. Researchers examined marked ordered trees with the ability to designate some right edges as "optional", given they don't lead to leaf nodes. They employed this model to analyze skew Dyck paths. A key aspect studied was the number of deepest nodes in these marked trees. Through explicit generating functions, they obtained insights, revealing the average number of deepest nodes converges to $\frac53$ as the number of nodes increases, which can be contrasted to standard ordered trees with a convergent average of $2$ deepest nodes. Furthermore, they computed this number for trees with a specified number $k$ of optional edges, finding it equals $k+1$ through combinatorial reasoning. Alternatively, this value can be determined using generating functions, which for large $k$ enables the utilization of the root test to determine its asymptotic behavior. Specifically, the asymptotic number of deepest nodes in marked trees with $k$ optional edges is $\sqrt{\frac{k}2}+\frac{k}2+ \frac{5\sqrt{k}}{6}+ O(\sqrt{k}\log\sqrt{k})$. Skew Dyck paths were analyzed in relation to marked trees, establishing a connection that translates path properties to tree properties. This connection encompasses paths with specified $x$-coordinates of left turns, bounded height, or determined end behavior, all of which are reflected in marked trees. Ultimately, this research provides a tree-based interpretation of recognized results about skew Dyck paths, and a new perspective that can be utilized to tackle existing open problems. Moreover, it offers a way to address questions about general marked ordered trees. For example, such trees can be rooted at the node with the greatest $y$-coordinate, or those with nodes arranged in a plane rather than confined to a line. Both of these scenarios, and more, represent promising areas for future investigation.

A key factor for maintaining stability in future low-carbon power grids is expected to be energy storage systems. Studies examining past experiences reveal a common issue with storage units - they frequently fail to take advantage of high-price signals during periods of low energy supply. This behavior has been often attributed to inaccurate forecasting or operational issues. However, our research suggests a more plausible explanation is rooted in risk-averse decision-making practices. Utilizing a stochastic self-scheduling approach and real data from the Australian electricity market, our findings show that risk-conscious storage units prioritize short-term cost savings by engaging in local price speculation, and tend to ignore opportunities in periods with unusual price fluctuations. This has significant policy implications, given the difficulty of detecting and managing storage units' risk aversion. Moreover, it highlights the risk of storage units contributing to market instability rather than reducing it. This study also highlights the challenge of predicting storage units' behavior, given that their decision-making processes are influenced by their risk preferences, which remain difficult to measure. This information can be useful for market designers, grid operators, and storage unit managers seeking to manage future grid instability, and it provides a foundation for further research into risk-aware storage units' behavior. Our investigation focused on the transport properties of HgTe quantum wells near their critical thickness, where the energy gap is minimal, and the energy spectrum is described by a singular Dirac cone structure. Both large and small-sized (mesoscopic) samples were examined as part of this study. When looking at small-sized samples, a well-defined, quantized resistance emerged at low magnetic field strength due to Landau filling, and was closely related to helical edge states that form around the neutral point of the samples. Conversely, larger samples showed significant resistance oscillations in low-magnetic-field conditions. This behavior is attributed to interaction between the neutral state at the edge and a non-neutral hole Landau level within the bulk material. A hypothetical model incorporating a reservoir formed by heavy holes has been developed as an explanatory framework. This model highlights the importance of magnetic field-induced coupling between this reservoir and the free Dirac-like electrons in the bulk material. Consequently, a distinctive shift of the resistance oscillation's period with respect to the magnetic field's strength was observed and its underlying causes examined. This includes the influence of an irregular shape to the samples, as well as the presence of edge states within the bulk material due to gapless nature of HgTe quantum wells. A comparative study with $N=0$ localization condition revealed that $N=0$ localization occurs at a lower magnetic field in larger samples, which correlates with increased period of the oscillations in these samples. Moreover, examination of thin samples exhibited spatially varying behavior in the neutral point, which could be shifted by changing the width of the samples. This is likely a result of interaction between the edge and bulk states in these samples. This research highlights the complex transport properties of HgTe quantum wells in the gapless regime and the essential role of edge and bulk state interaction in these behaviors. It also suggests that moving further into the bulk regime, these behaviors will transform into more conventional physics based on hole Landau levels. This transformation is likely to be influenced by the presence of the neutral state at the edge and the resulting interaction with the non-neutral hole Landau levels within the bulk material. Consequently, examination of this interaction's impact on transport properties on HgTe quantum wells in the bulk regime is a promising area of investigation. This could also be applicable to other Dirac materials in the gapless regime. Moreover, this paper discusses the importance of precise control over sample thickness and its variation in the $k_z$ direction in investigation of transport properties of HgTe quantum wells. A newly defined polynomial, referred to as the nth toroidal colored Jones polynomial, is established for links in a thickened torus. Dubbed $J_n^T$, this polynomial demonstrates numerous properties similar to the original colored Jones polynomial, and notably displays volume conjecture behavior. By applying $J_n^T$, we prove the volume conjecture holds true for a specific link, and provide computational data suggesting it holds for additional links. Moreover, $J_n^T$ can be represented through two distinct constructions, a pseudo-operator invariant, and a construction rooted in the Kauffman bracket skein module of the torus. Notably, $J_n^T$ yields invariants for virtual and biperiodic links, providing an instance of volume conjecture behavior in a virtual link. Lastly, $J_n^T$ can be defined using combinatorial operations on volume descriptions of links. The most compact version of this polynomial, referred to as the reduced toroidal colored Jones polynomial, is also explored and shown to possess volume conjecture behavior in the limit as n approaches infinity. The relationship between $J_n^T$ and the volume conjecture is demonstrated through graphical renormalization procedures, offering a combinatorial interpretation of the volume conjecture. The volume conjecture is confirmed for links composed of specific graphical configurations, and the reduced toroidal colored Jones polynomial displays volume conjecture behavior in the limit as n approaches infinity. The developmental history and related concepts of the volume conjecture are discussed in the introduction. The proposed polynomial can be understood through an analysis of its fundamental properties in chapters two to five. Chapter six explores the relationship between the reduced toroidal colored Jones polynomial and the volume conjecture, concluding with graphical proofs of volume conjecture behavior for specific links in chapter seven. The proposed polynomial can be extended to work with biperiodic links in chapter eight. The materials presented in this paper have not been published in any peer-reviewed journals. The primary objective of Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) involves determining the appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings within a particular context.  Advances in deep learning, specifically utilizing BERT, have led to significant progress in this area, with several strategies being developed to combine structured knowledge for enhanced performance.  Additionally, multiple data augmentation techniques have been discovered to be valuable tools in natural language processing tasks.  Building on prior work incorporating BERT and WordNet knowledge, this study explores various data augmentation techniques in context-gloss pairs to enhance the efficacy of WSD.  Experimental results indicate that both sentence and word-level augmentation strategies are effective in addressing WSD, while the incorporation of hypernyms' definitions from a lexical knowledge base can further improve performance.  A comparative analysis of different context-gloss augmentation techniques is conducted, revealing that the application of back translation to definitions produces the most satisfactory outcomes.  A modulated model incorporating the most successful techniques achieves a 4.13% gain in exact match score compared to the unaugmented model on the Senseval-2 dataset and a 3.40% gain in the WordSense.inx score on the All Senses for Words dataset.  Code is available at: https://github.com/ghrua/ContextGlossAugmentation.
