The CMS experiment at the CERN LHC detected the production of top quarks for the first time using proton-lead data at an 8.16 TeV nucleon-nucleon center-of-mass energy. Top quark production was identified in events featuring one isolated electron or muon and four or more jets, from a data set totaling 174 inverse nanobarns of luminosity. The measured signal exceeded the five-standard-deviation threshold expected for a background-only hypothesis, and the cross-sectional measurement for top quark pairs was found to be 45 nanobarns with an 8-nanobarn uncertainty, consistent with theoretical predictions from quantum chromodynamics. This finding was further confirmed by analyzing data sets totaling 100 inverse nanobarns of luminosity at a 5.02 TeV nucleon-nucleon center-of-mass energy, with the cross section for top quark pairs narrowing to a 4-nanobarn uncertainty. Both measurements indicated that the production rate of top quark pairs is a linear function of the heavy ion nucleus's mass number, and depended little on the centrality of the collision. Additionally, the degree of longitudinal polarization for top quark pairs was constrained to be less than 0.03, consistent with theoretical expectations. This observation paves the way for further studies of high-transverse-momentum quark production in proton-lead collisions, and provides a crucial test of perturbative quantum chromodynamics in heavy ion collisions.

This study focuses on key elements in cross-domain text-to-SQL parsing, specifically schema linking and value filling. To enhance encoding abilities, a column selection auxiliary task is proposed, leveraging explicit targets for relevance matching. Additionally, two value filling approaches are presented to bridge the gap between current zero-shot parsers and practical applications, considering that many existing parsers overlook value filling in synthesized SQL. Experiments on the Spider dataset demonstrate the superiority of our proposed framework over baseline models in terms of execution and exact set match accuracy when database contents are inaccessible, with further analysis pointing to areas for future improvement. Moreover, our proposed framework shows promising performance when database contents are accessible, outperforming baseline models in almost every category of evaluation metrics. Code is available at GitHub repository: https://github.com/ghrua/End-to-End-Text-to-SQL.

Building upon this description, we derived a linearized stochastic hydrodynamic model that simulates long-lasting non-equilibrium situations while sacrificing a more precise quantum fluctuation treatment, and found it to be directly connected with the established Bogoliubov approach. We define a new concept of relative 1-homotopy type for mappings between a surface and a metric space that contains a specified set of Jordan curves, and investigate its properties. This enables us to prove the existence and local smoothness of the surfaces with minimal area within a particular relative 1-homotopy class in certain types of metric spaces. Furthermore, we establish that when the ambient space has a certain topological characteristic, maps that are relatively 1-homotopic are also relatively homotopic. These findings also hold for closed surfaces and improve previous results of several mathematicians. Additionally, we provide a specific instance of a space where relative 1-homotopy type is distinct from relative homotopy type. Finally, we discuss how these results tie into the existing literature and T. R. Rockingham's previous work on the subject.

Recent studies on the 64Ni nucleus with a low-spin structure have provided significant insights: combining data from four experiments allowed researchers to identify several 0+ and 2+ excited states below 4.5 MeV, and characterize their properties. Using a Monte Carlo shell model, scientists were able to explain the findings and uncover a surprisingly intricate pattern of shapes existing together, where a high-energy prolate 0+ state at 3463 keV, and a collective 2+ state just above it, 286 keV, marked a first in Ni isotopes. This discovery in Ni isotopes, combined with previous findings in 48Ca and 70Zn, supports the idea that shape coexistence is driven by the monopole-tensor interaction in the mean-field level, and also highlights the unique position of 64Ni as an occurrence of low-spin structure in an odd-numbered nucleon count. One-proton and one-neutron removal experiments revealed that 64Ni's collective 0+ and 2+ states are dominated by 0+ and 2+ configurations made from the nuclides 52Ni and 56Ni, which added further understanding of this shape coexistence phenomenon. Machine learning models often undergo performance assessment through k-fold cross-validation to facilitate model selection and parameter adjustment. Yet, due to the random partitioning inherent in CV, estimated model performance exhibits significant variability. This unpredictability makes effective parameter tuning challenging, as it introduces substantial uncertainty into the choice of parameters. Moreover, our study reveals that the optimal parameters obtained are excessively sensitive to the manner in which the data is divided, often resulting in suboptimal solutions and significant difficulties in achieving reproducibility. In contrast, our research suggests employing the reduced variance j-k fold CV method, which involves conducting multiple independent assessments across K subgroups within the training set J times. We introduce a new efficient framework for representing functions in graphical models, which serves as a foundation for a variety of computational tasks. Our concise model then leverages this framework, specifically using deterministic finite state automata within a variable elimination approach known as Bucket Elimination. We dub this variant FABE, which we found significantly enhances Bucket Elimination by substantially reducing the computational time and memory usage. Our FABE approach compares favourably to the current state of the art methods, particularly recursive best-first and structured message passing for the most probable explanation, as well as CPLEX, GUROBI and toulbar2 for constrained optimisation, by achieving a 5 orders of magnitude improvement in our experiments following a widely established evaluation procedure. Our FABE source code is now available as a public contribution.

We investigated the absorption of a single, monochromatic light beam at 689 nm as it passes through a cloud of ultracold $^{88}$Sr atoms. Due to the interaction, the absorption pattern deviates significantly, taking on an asymmetric shape as a result of a shift in frequency that is equivalent in magnitude to the natural width of a specific atomic transition in strontium. This effect becomes more pronounced under conditions of high saturation. Our research incorporated momentum transfers resulting from the absorption and emission of photons, as described by a modified version of the optical Bloch equations. We demonstrated that even a single-beam setup can illustrate photon recoil effects that have substantial implications for fields like saturation spectroscopy, Ramsey interferometry, and absorption imaging. Furthermore, we provided a method for correcting frequency shifts resulting from photon recoil in homodyne detection schemes. Given the precise control over light and matter in ultracold gas experiments, our findings highlight the importance of considering photon recoil effects, especially in situations characterized by high saturation or precise frequency measurements. This is particularly relevant for certain applications in quantum computing and metrology that rely on robust frequency shifts or multiple atomic levels. Given the similarity in atomic mass between strontium and other systems like lithium, bosonic chromium, and lead, our research is also applicable to these systems. This is also true for atomic ions, where the influence of photon recoil is minimized due to the use of closed transitions with long wavelengths. Nevertheless, in cases involving open transitions or with spatial extension, photon recoil effects will dominate, resulting in shifted widths and frequencies, as well as asymmetrical shapes in absorption spectra, combined with shifted mean occupations or influenced stochastic dynamics. This is true for both homodyne and single-beam absorption schemes, and it highlights the significance of properly accounting for light-matter interactions in a way that incorporates the influence of frequency and momentum transfers resulting from the absorption and emission of photons. When subjected to high stresses, the vast majority of dense mixtures undergo a sudden and extreme thickening, characterized by a transition from fluid-like behavior to rigidity. Researchers propose that abrupt shear thickening serves as an initial indicator of a state transition, developing a comprehensive framework for interpreting viscosity through a universal function that bridges the frictionless point of jamming and a state of rigidity influenced by friction, anisotropy, and shear. Studies involving cornstarch in glycerol and silica spheres in glycerol found that for these two systems, viscosity can be condensed into a singular, stress- and volume fraction-independent curve, revealing distinct scaling regimes that reflect different universality classes and implying that isotropic and anisotropic shear jamming have unique characteristics. Furthermore, by integrating the effects of microscale interactions into a dimensionless variable that gauges the distance from shear jamming, scientists have paved the way for applying theories developed for equilibrium phenomena to better understand the physics governing the shear thickening transition. The universality of these findings is demonstrated across two separate systems: dense silica spheres in glycerol, which exhibit no anisotropy, and cornstarch in glycerol, which contains anisotropic particles and exhibits microscopically localized shear jamming. The progression of the function for these two systems converges at the point of shear jamming, offering valuable insights into the unique characteristics of each system. The work presented here contributes to a deeper understanding of the physics governing the shear thickening transition, and the developed framework has the potential to extend to other non-equilibrium state transitions and complex systems. The dimensionless variable that gauges the distance from shear jamming also provides a way to interpret the results of simulations or other measurements of the shear thickening transition, offering a universal perspective that bridges different universality classes. Additionally, the series known as the Hilbert-Poincar\'e series of the centralizer $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ can be computed explicitly. The research discussed also extends towards the special Askey-Wilson algebra as well as more complex, higher rank variants of the same, allowing further exploration of its underlying principles. The connection to the Askey-Wilson algebra specifically arises from considering a particular composition multiplication, which leads to the recovery of the Serre relations through application of certain properties known as exchange and unitarity. The series known as the Hilbert-Poincar\'on series is then defined and computed for these higher rank variants, offering a characteristic that distinguishes them from other, related algebras. The research discussed also explores the relationship between the centralizer $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ and the Racah algebra $R(n)$ at an operational level, presenting an explicit procedure for constructing the operators belonging to the centralizer through application of a specific embedding of the Lie algebra $U(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ within a tensor product. The paired-permutation test in NLP systems has long relied on testing the statistical significance of differences in performance. This test aims to verify that observed discrepancies aren't simply coincidental. Despite the importance of accurate results, a lack of suitable exact algorithms forces practitioners to use time-consuming Monte Carlo approximations to achieve this goal. In contrast, we've developed an efficient method for calculating paired-permutation test results exactly. This exact algorithm takes significantly less time to compute than Monte Carlo methods. In particular, we observed a 10 times speedup when using our exact algorithm versus the commonly employed Monte Carlo approximation on a representative dataset of 20000 samples. Furthermore, our method maintains the statistical integrity of the paired-permutation test. We've made our code available to the public as an open-source project. This code can be used to implement the exact paired-permutation testing method within the GPyRanker system, a previously developed tool for ranking multiple options. In addition to PaPer, we've also developed a standalone Python module called exact_permutation that can be used independently of GPyRanker. This module is compatible with both Python 2 and Python 3. In evaluating our exact paired-permutation testing method, we compared its performance to that of the commonly used Monte Carlo approximation on multiple datasets. Our results showed that the Monte Carlo approximation often overestimates the p-value significantly. In contrast, the exact algorithm is accurate, reliable, and efficient. In particular, we found that the p-value estimated by the Monte Carlo method was more than 10 times greater than the actual p-value in at least 20% of the cases we tested. In contrast, the exact algorithm yielded results that were precise and consistent with the expected outcomes. In evaluating our method further, we analyzed the effect of the number of samples on the computing time required by the exact algorithm. Our results showed that the time needed to compute the p-value by the exact algorithm increases roughly in proportion to the square of the number of samples. In particular, we found that the time required to compute the p-value on a dataset of 20000 samples was approximately 400 times greater than the time needed to compute the p-value on a dataset of 100 samples. In addition to evaluating our method on random datasets, we also analyzed the effect of the number of samples on the computing time required by the exact algorithm in a setting with real-data. The switch complex encompasses the loom space's invariants, with these invariants being derived from the underlying surface and a collection of curves, rather than a graph. In particular cases, such as when the underlying surface is a sphere, it is demonstrated that the loom space's reduction can be determined directly from the switch complex, without needing reference to the underlying graph. Contrary to elliptical flow's dependence on centrality, we discovered minimal variation in triangular flow centrality. However, once the influence of initial geometry was removed, we observed an increase in $v_3/\epsilon_3$ in proportion to transverse particle density, mirroring $v_2/\epsilon_2$'s behavior. Additionally, we found triangular and elliptical flow to exhibit analogous transverse momentum dependencies for identified particles. Our findings were further validated by analyzing $v_3$ coated around $p_T$ and centrality, yielding results consistent with general trends. In conclusion, our analysis demonstrated that $v_3$ behaves in a similar manner to $v_2$ across various facets, suggesting that $v_2/v_3$ remains constant, with an average value of 0.67 determined from our data. This ratio's constancy is expected to hold true across different colliding systems and energies. Lastly, we proposed $v_3$ to be directly proportional to the number of flow angles divided by average flow angle, which may facilitate better understanding of particle polarization. Our research was presented at the 21st Particles and Nuclei Conference.

A critical aspect in devising numerical methods for time-dependent partial differential equations involves preserving inherent properties of the original solution. Researchers have a rich history of developing and analyzing preservation-based discretization techniques, including validating existing schemes' preservation properties and proposing innovative methods achieving both high accuracy and property preservation. Although such schemes, when paired with implicit time-stepping methods, ensure preservation of certain properties, they are generally limited by requiring an exact solution to the nonlinear system of equations for each time-step. However, this requirement is manageable for small systems but becomes infeasible for large systems resulting from the spatial and temporal discretization of typical PDEs. To address this limitation, this study proposes modifying the flexible generalised minimum residual iteration to enforce constraints on numerical approximations, and demonstrates its applicability to both conservative and dissipative systems. Additionally, this method's effectiveness is illustrated through specific PDE examples. By taking a flexible Krylov preservation approach, this study aims to provide a more accessible and easier-to-implement option for researchers and practitioners seeking to preserve properties in numerical solutions. Soft-tissue navigation is highly dependent on non-rigid registration. For laparoscopic liver surgery, we integrate an organ model derived from preoperative CT scans with a partially reconstructed intraoperative surface from laparoscopic video footage. The complexity of this task arises from insufficient and inaccurate intraoperative data, real-time processing needs, and unknown variables, such as organ properties and boundary conditions. The liver's featureless surface and varied image modality noises also pose significant challenges. We addressed this challenge by training a single convolutional neural network to simultaneously identify surface correspondences and perform non-rigid registration. The network's training dataset includes realistic biomechanical simulations of randomly generated organ models undergoing deformation. This allows it to efficiently apply to novel patient organs without retraining, also enabling robust performance against noisy intraoperative surface inputs during testing. The trained network provides an optimal displacement field to map preoperative volume to the intraoperative surface, demonstrated by multiple experiments showing its applicability and efficiency with real-world data. The developed code is now openly accessible online. The proposed method has numerous applications in laparoscopic liver surgery, as well as in radiotherapy and soft-tissue trauma analysis. The challenges faced during development also motivate future research opportunities in organ property estimation and boundary condition inference from intraoperative data. The proposed method has been evaluated using a previously published dataset in addition to the newly collected liver dataset, showing its generalizability. Determining scene flow involves calculating the three-dimensional motion trajectories for specific points within an animated three-dimensional environment. Motion trajectory data has been found beneficial for downstream tasks like activity classification and obstacle detection. Nonetheless, obtaining precise data through LiDAR sensors and stereo cameras is laborious due to its computationally intensive annotation process. We address this issue by presenting a 3D scene flow benchmark alongside a novel self-supervised training framework for estimating scene flow. The benchmark comprises progressively complex datasets to study the estimation process, beginning from a singular object in motion to complex real-world environments. We introduce a unique method, Adversarial Metric Learning, for self-supervised flow estimation where two models work in tandem: one performs flow estimation and another derives a latent metric to differentiate the altered points from the target point cloud, achieved through a Multi-Scale Triplet loss calculation using intermediate feature vectors. We leverage our benchmark to gain insight into various models and our proposed framework, finding that our method successfully preserves spatial coherence and detailed geometric structures, whereas many self-supervised baselines fail in this aspect. Nonetheless, overcoming occlusions remains a significant challenge. Nonetheless, our proposed framework is beneficial for various downstream tasks, as verified through various evaluation metrics in various evaluation setups. We make our benchmark, models, and data available to the public.

In recent years, AI networks, specifically those based on artificial neural systems, have significantly outperformed competitors in a wide range of tasks including image recognition, sound analysis, and language interpretation. However, widespread use of such models was previously hindered due to their massive computational requirements for both initial training and operational deployment. Neuromorphic computing technology, which allows bio-realistic neural networks to operate at high speeds while minimizing energy consumption, has now become an appealing substitute. We present a proposal to utilize a Random Neural Network as a versatile classifying model that combines the efficiency of spiking neural networks with the high classification accuracy achieved by traditional neural networks, showcasing this concept's effectiveness across real-world classification datasets. We believe this model has vast potential applications in the development of efficient artificial intelligence.

A Perfect-Matching-Hamiltonian property in a graph implies that each perfect matching can be combined with another to create a Hamiltonian cycle. This concept was first introduced by Las Vergnas and Haggkvist in the 1970s. Our research aims to explore the relationship between cubic graphs and 3-edge-colourings to identify those whose every perfect matching corresponds to a colour of the graph's edge-colouring. This property is equivalent to even-2-factorability (E2F), which means all the graph's 2-factors are even cycles. We can disregard bipartite cubic graphs, as they automatically satisfy the E2F condition, thus our focus shifts to non-bipartite cubic graphs. A non-bipartite cubic graph with the PMH-property will satisfy the E2F condition, even though it is not a necessary condition. Our work involves introducing the papillon graph, an infinite family of E2F non-bipartite cubic graphs parameterized by two values. We then determine the parameters under which the papillon graph exhibits the PMH-property or E2F condition, as well as proving no two distinct papillon graphs have identical structure. Finally, our research demonstrates that a 3-edge-colouring of a papillon graph is equivalent to a 3-edge-colouring of a specific subgraph, allowing us to determine the coloured vertices and edges of the papillon graph. This in turn enables us to identify the perfect matchings corresponding to each colour and determine the Hamiltonian cycles that can be created from the perfect matchings. This leads to our main finding: a papillon graph's 3-edge-colouring forms a decomposition of its edges into three Hamiltonian cycles. This decomposition is unique up to cyclic reordering, which is a novel contribution to the study of 3-edge-colourings of cubic graphs. This paper introduces a new method called Timeloops for automating system call filtering policies in containerized applications. During operation, Timeloops can automatically determine the system calls a program should be permitted to make and prevent unauthorized system calls from being made. In addition, Timeloops rectifies various shortcomings of static analysis-based techniques, such as the creation of highly precise filters for programs in languages like JavaScript, PHP, and Python. Developed using standard, reliable technologies, Timeloops features a simple and efficient design comprising less than 500 lines of code. Our research showcases the capabilities of Timeloops by implementing system call learning for individual services and a couple of benchmark applications employing Python Flask, Apache Thrift, and Memcached, among other technologies. Furthermore, we show that Timeloops' performance, despite generating a more limited system call filter, is comparable to that of an unsecured system. Finally, we explore timely possibilities of integrating Timeloops with orchestration tools. The source code for Timeloops is currently available under the permissive BSD 2-Clause License at https://github.com/utk/csafe_timeloops.

The dynamics of soccer games mean even small moments can greatly impact the outcome, making players, coaches, and scouts intensely curious about how to act effectively in pivotal situations. In such moments, teams may lose possession of the ball or score, leading to a desire for an optimal course of action. To address this need, we propose a novel way to describe the game's state and a batch reinforcement learning method to train a strategic policy network. By analyzing the contextual aspects of situations, the network can provide the best action to increase the team's chances of scoring, drawing on real soccer data from InStat. In a large-scale experiment with 104 European soccer matches, we found our optimized strategy consistently outperformed the standard policy, and it even mimicked the behavior observed in real games. Notably, we observed situations where actions like committing a foul or kicking the ball out of bounds might be preferable to shooting, showcasing the importance of nuanced decision-making. By leveraging our model's insights, coaches can gain a deeper understanding of these situations and make more informed tactical decisions, such as deploying specific players in certain contexts. Furthermore, our methodology provides a framework for researching other team sports, like American football, where similar analyses can be conducted using video feeds. High-resolution subsurface modeling via seismic imaging has the potential to be greatly improved with Full Waveform Inversion (FWI).  However, FWI can become trapped in local minima due to its nonlinear optimization nature. Two alternatives, Wavefield Reconstruction Inversion (WRI) and Extended Source Waveform Inversion (ESI), have been proposed as methods to improve seismic imaging. Both of these methods relax the strict adherence to wave equation accuracy found in FWI and instead, WRI and ESI introduce non-physical source concepts that match observed data with synthetic data generated using extended sources. Formulations for WRI and ESI are developed within a Lagrangian-based mathematical framework, and both can be viewed as weighted versions of the classical FWI. Conjugate gradient methods are also explored to solve the normal equation for an efficient solution, and both time and frequency domain formulations of the wave equation solver are feasible. Despite these developments, the challenge of the large storage requirement for time-domain wavefields through iterations remains, and two possible workaround strategies for reducing this demand are proposed, including extracting sparse frequency-domain wavefields or utilizing time-domain data rather than wavefields. The theoretical aspects of these methods are supported by numerical examples using synthetic data, including 2D data sets with increasingly complex geological structures and 3D data sets of reasonable size. The results demonstrate that both WRI and ESI can converge and improve seismic imaging, and the easy implementation of time-domain formulations makes them accessible for a wide range of real-world data sets. The storage issue challenge is also addressed by demonstrating a notable decrease in the storage demand when transitioning from time to frequency domain. The paper concludes by outlining potential directions for further development, including the application of time-domain wavefields and the investigation of suitable preconditioning techniques. To analyze the interplay of species competition and dispersal, an asymmetrical noisy voter model was developed for a regular lattice structure. The model allows one species to colonize nearest-neighbor sites, while another species can settle at any distance but is less successful in doing so. The model includes external noise, which can lead to random species swaps in the lattice. The combination of these dynamics results in various species competition outcomes, including the exclusion of one species, distinct population coexistence, or bistable coexistence dependent on the starting population ratio. The model shows that an abrupt transition occurs as immigration intensity surpasses a critical point, causing the irreversible decline of the species with shorter dispersal range due to a cusp catastrophe leading to half loop dynamics. The model further reveals that this catastrophe results in the inclusion of the shorter ranged species in noise induced SWM state, enhancing its survival over the longer ranged species. The model also demonstrates how this scenario is altered when the population competition ratio is changed, leading to repeated cusp catastrophes and the alternation of survival species in bistable coexistence state. The model's findings are independent of the noise level in the noise intensive regime. The model includes an alternative representation where the species competition and dispersal ranges follow a tradeoff relationship, resulting in the description of a disaster landscape. The model's analysis shows that the model's fundamental dynamics are determined by noise and competition dispersal interactions, rather than their precise values. The effectiveness of programmable electrostatic phase plates is subject to debate 
given their varying suitability for particular applications. Our study delves into 
alternative designs of phase plates specifically tailored to mitigate spherical 
aberration in Transmission Electron Microscopes (TEMs). Through numerical analysis, 
we investigate the potential for a phase plate to attain down to 1 Angstrom 
resolution on an uncorrected TEM. By examining various design features 
(fill-factor, pixel pattern, symmetry), we identify how they influence the electron 
probe size and current density. Our proposed designs exhibit probe sizes ($d_{50}$) 
as low as 0.66 Angstrom, indicating that a programmable phase plate with 
electrostatic elements can successfully rectify spherical aberration well beyond the 
1 Angstrom threshold. Furthermore, we discover that plate designs featuring a 
'dot-pattern' exhibit $d_{50}$ values 5% lower than those with a 'line-pattern'. 
The minimal space required and ease of fabrication make programmable phase plates 
attractive alternatives to fixed mechanical designs, offering considerable 
versatility in various TEM applications.

We derive new conclusions regarding the additive Galois module properties of specific wildly ramified finite non-abelian extensions of Q. Notably, in cases where K/Q is a Galois extension with a Galois group isomorphic to A4, S4 or A5, we determine essential and sufficient criteria for the ring of integers in K to be freely generated over its associated order within the rational group algebra constructed from the Galois group G. Our analysis also explores the relationship between certain subgroups of G and the additive Galois module properties of rings of integers in K. Moreover, our findings include specific cases of non-Galois extensions with similar characteristics, enabling us to establish connections between specific ideal class groups and the rational group algebra constructed from G. Our work extends and expands upon previous results of the same nature, specifically those of the second author, enabling a broader examination of the underlying principles. A distinctive feature of neural development is the rhythmic shifting of cell nuclei
between the upper and lower layers of the neuroepithelial tissue as interkinetic nuclear
migration (IKNM) unfolds. In this study, we utilize extended, high-speed lightsheet and two-photon imaging
techniques in live zebrafish retinas during initial development to gain insights into the underlying mechanisms governing
the behavior of cell nuclei during IKNM. Our high-resolution images permit us to accurately map the migration
patterns of multiple densely packed nuclei across the retina. By analyzing these migration tracks, we develop and test
a hypothesis that retinal IKNM is driven by a diffusive process fueled by the accumulation of new nuclei at the upper
retinal surface. Our results demonstrate how the tight packing of nuclei at the upper surface influences their movement
patterns, provide a reliable, quantifiable explanation for the uneven distribution of nuclei across the retina, and may
have implications for random cell fate selection within this system. Furthermore, our findings are applicable to other
neuroepithelial tissues exhibiting IKNM, and we show that a diffusive model can effectively capture the core aspects of
this process. Our research involves collaborative work with the retinal field theory group, whose expertise in analytical
methods complements the primarily experimental approach employed in this study. Our combined efforts involve the
retinal field theory group in the initial stages of the research, during which they proposed the diffusive model idea. 
Our initial findings for a simple, uniform system are consistent with the results obtained by the theory group. However, 
the system we studied is complex and diverse, and our research focuses on the inherent difficulties of translating this 
complexity into a viable model. Ultimately, our research yields insights into fundamental processes governing the 
spatial organization and random cell fate selection within developing neuroepithelial tissues.

Experimental results demonstrate the advantages of optimized codes over random codes in both video compressed sensing and color image demosaicing. In addition to its applicability to compressed sensing, this research's findings can also contribute to other image processing tasks that involve code patterns, such as super resolution and blind deconvolution. This facilitates easier data entry for service operators.  To enhance accuracy, the extracted text was further corrected using Natural Language Processing.  When tested using 50 Indonesian ID card images, the F-score achieved was 0.78, and the extraction process for each ID card took approximately 4510 milliseconds.  The proposed system can be used for both verification and service delivery websites by converting ID card information from text to format for validation purposes.  This may have implications for reducing account-related fraud in Indonesia.  The proposed system consists of Optical Character Recognition and NLP technologies, with the following components:  an Indonesian ID card image uploader, an OCR module, a spell checker, a grammar checker, and a verification module. The proposed system has been made available online at https://indonesianktpextractor.000webhost.com/.  All that is required to use it is to upload an Indonesian ID card image. However, even when restricted to single passes through the input, some functions in these models can still be undecidable by Turing machines with infinite input, despite being defined by finite-state machines. To address this issue, a new decision-making approach is proposed for determining whether a specific function is computable and if so, to create a corresponding Turing machine. 

For the type of functions in question, being computable is equivalent to having a specific property called continuity, effectively simplifying the original problem to deciding if a given function is continuous. To accomplish this, a more general rule is established to characterize continuous functions that preserve regular languages under a specific operation, and this is applied to demonstrate that continuity can be reliably determined for rational and regular functions. Furthermore, this decision-making approach is efficient and takes only $\mathsf{NLogSpace}$, a previously known but higher $\mathsf{PTime}$ requirement. 

Additionally, a more nuanced concept related to continuous functions is explored and related to its computable counterpart. In a recent experiment involving a highly complex system with distinct time scales and multiple coexisting patterns of behavior, a reservoir computer of the new design demonstrated several advantages over its traditional counterpart. This technique and its performance are important areas of study for a wide range of complex systems that exhibit multiple coexisting patterns of behavior, such as chaotic systems in physics, biology, medicine, climate science, and finance, among others. We have adapted the quantum relational Hoare logic originally proposed in (Unruh, POPL 2019) to incorporate "expectations" into preconditions and postconditions, thereby enabling the quantification of pre-/postconditions that reflect the relationship between programs' inputs and outputs when comparing pairs of programs. This modified logic, which we call QREL, enables the quantification of preconditions and postconditions using the expectation operator, and allows for the comparison of programs based on the similarity of their inputs and outputs, as measured by the absolute value of the expectation of the difference between the output of one program and the input to the other. Furthermore, QREL can express assertions that describe the equality of programs' inputs and outputs, as well as the expectation of the difference between them. By applying this logic to two programs, we can certify that the programs behave in the same way with respect to a particular property, as well as validate that two programs are equivalent, as defined by the logic. Moreover, we have demonstrated the applicability of QREL to various programs, including those that incorporate randomness and those that consist of sequences of operations. Additionally, we have demonstrated that QREL enables the verification of programs that, when executed multiple times, behave in the same way as a single execution. Lastly, we have discussed the challenges associated with extending QREL to a quantified version of the logic. The modified logic, as well as the guidelines for its application to specific programs, are thoroughly illustrated in the accompanying supplementary material. The original quantum relational Hoare logic was based on the relational Hoare logic proposed in (Broberg, JLP 2009). The development of QREL was facilitated by the quantum relational Hoare logic proof assistant tool, QuProVer, which is described in detail in (Dremon--Preignat, Giamppergher, Unruh, POPL 2021). The rapid transmission of contagious diseases is frequently intensified by a single high-transmission event, a super-spreader occurrence. This effect should be given considerable consideration in traditional epidemiological modeling, which requires reliable estimates of critical parameters such as $R_0$. We illustrate in this report that the effective $R_0$ value in scenarios featuring a super-spreader event is significantly elevated, with an order of magnitude equivalent to several hundred, which is indicative of a very brief period of rapid transmission during such events. A simulation involving a well-mixed space aligns with these findings and contributes valuable insights to modeling infectious transmission dynamics within enclosed environments. These environments diverge significantly from the parameters typically modeled in a standard SIR scenario. The proposed model also yields expressions that relate $R_0$ values to physical and operational variables of these closed spaces. The influence of a super-spreader event on public health is highly variable and ultimately depends on factors such as the epidemic's overall severity and how the virus transmitted through that single event continues to spread among community members. The appendices include a detailed mathematical explanation of a specific simulation where a single transmission occurrence led to a large number of new cases, which is referred to as a beta-distributed model. This model illustrates how a single high-transmission event can result in a substantial number of additional infections, which may seem paradoxical at first glance. The spread of the virus among community members that stems from that single event is then analyzed by combining the model with a Susceptible-Infected-Recovered model. The resulting statistics, such as the basic reproduction number $R_0$ and the ultimate recovery rate $\rho$, are then calculated through complex integration and algebraic manipulation. The complex integration involves the solution to a beta distribution integral, which is derived in the appendices. The paper addresses the problem of bias in vector magnetic field maps, particularly in estimating the component perpendicular to the line-of-sight, Bperp. This issue has been identified previously; however, the current study aims to provide a more in-depth analysis of its sources, quantification, and possible solutions. Initially, the authors establish precise metrics to assess Bperp bias, accounting for both local and native components. Secondly, various inversion techniques and data sources are tested and compared, incorporating a crucial factor called magnetic fill fraction (ff). A simple model is employed to evaluate the effects of noise and bias models. The results reveal that the bias primarily affects under-resolved structures but also manifests in areas with strong magnetic fields. Noise in magnetograms exacerbates the problem, but it's not the main contributor. The research indicates that fitting ff explicitly can significantly mitigate the issue; however, other factors like choosing appropriate chi^2 weights and optimization algorithms also play a crucial role. Finally, the authors propose a straightforward, post-processing correction that can be applied before resolving the 180deg ambiguity in Bperp. This approach is valuable for using global-scale structures as model boundary inputs. The study's findings advocate for employing inversion codes that fit ff directly or utilize data pre-processed in a similar manner, such as SyntHIA. The research was conducted using the Optimization Code (OC) and the Regularized Gradient-Based Inversion Algorithm (RGIA), and the effects are observable in various inversion codes and data sources, including the Rapid Inversion Algorithm (RIA) and the Vector Spectral Synthesis Code (VSSS), and data from the Interface Section of the Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO) titled Integrated Photosphere and Low Atmosphere (ILM). The paper's results highlight the importance of carefully selecting inversion and post-processing techniques to avoid bias in vector magnetic field maps, particularly in estimating the component perpendicular to the line-of-sight. A sign problem encountered in Monte Carlo simulations beyond half-filling can be mitigated by transforming the integration path. However, this transformation introduces an additional computational cost associated with the Jacobian determinant in the Boltzmann weight, posing a significant barrier for large-scale simulations. Our proposed architecture, based on a novel application of complex-valued affine coupling layers in neural networks, efficiently circumvents this challenge by achieving linear scaling of the determinant cost. As a result, this method allows us to tackle intractably large systems plagued by a severe sign problem. Our complex neural network's precision has been thoroughly assessed across multiple benchmarks, including the hubbard model, Ising spin glass, and complex-edited Edwards-Anderson model. Our findings demonstrate not only a linear scaling of the determinant cost but also a signs' growth problem's strong inverse correlation with the network's depth. Furthermore, determining the optimal network depth across different benchmarks has shown that the ideal depth depends on the specific problem being solved and is influenced by the problem's difficulty as defined by the signs' growth rate. Our analysis has been complemented by a discussion on the determinants' scaling behavior and a related open mathematical question. Lastly, this research introduces a novel application of complex-valued neural networks in statistical physics, specifically in resolving the sign problem encountered in Monte Carlo simulations. Our code is available at https://github.com/ComplexNetworks/SignProblem.

By leveraging previously acquired skills and adapting them to unfamiliar tasks without explicit guidance, humans demonstrate impressive cross-task capabilities.
This study aims to enhance the cross-task generalization ability of massive language models in unsupervised settings, with a focus on models like T0 and FLAN.
We introduce a novel, unsupervised retrieval-augmentation method known as ReCross, which employs unlabeled samples to selectively draw from existing data, fine-tune the model for better performance.
The proposed method seamlessly integrates both high-efficiency dense retrieval and a more effective pair-wise re-ranking process to produce outstanding results, surpassing non-retrieval methods and alternative baselines in our experiments. ReCross delivers remarkable improvements in both dense retrieval-based models and composite methods, demonstrating versatility in various cross-task generalization scenarios. The code for ReCross is available at https://github.com/ChenXuEconom/ReCross.

Optimizing hyperparameters in the private version of the stochastic gradient descent algorithm is a critical issue due to limited access to private datasets for hyperparameter tuning. The development of algorithms that efficiently find optimal hyperparameters for a favorable balance between privacy and performance within a predetermined search space is, therefore, crucial. In this paper, a generalized framework is established to determine an optimal balance between privacy and performance, and three cost-effective algorithms are systematically examined within this framework: evolutionary optimization, Bayesian methods, and reinforcement learning. The results of our experiments, conducted using MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets for hyperparameter tuning in private deep learning, show significant improvements over the conventional grid search method. The paper addresses existing challenges and potential research directions in the field, and provides an open-source code for hyperparameter tuning in private deep learning. The code is available at https://github.com/HappyMerit/HDDP. For a Coxeter system denoted by (W,S), we develop the concept of a boolean complex consisting of involutions within W, mirroring Ragnarsson and Tenner's previous work. By applying discrete Morse theory, we identify the homotopy type of this boolean complex for a significant subset of Coxeter groups, including finite groups, revealing that its homotopy type is equivalent to that of a collection of spheres with dimension |S|-1. Moreover, we derive straightforward, recursive formulas to compute the number of spheres within this collection. Additionally, we derive connections between these boolean complexes and the combinatorial properties of reduced words, namely through the means of word posets. Specifically, we show that the boolean complex of a Coxeter group is isomorphic to the poset of reduced words, denoted by W_S, structured by the Coxeter length. Furthermore, we determine the homotopy type of this boolean complex, revealing it is equivalent to a sphere with dimension equal to the number of generators within the group. Finally, we conclude by examining specific examples, including finite groups, permutations, and reflections within a sphere.

A novel approach to measuring the distance to galaxies has been discovered by examining extragalactic planetary nebulae, specifically due to their nearly universal brightness pattern. Determining the precise distances to galaxies through planetary nebulae analysis depends on collecting comprehensive data sets, and the observed frequency of these nebulae directly correlates with the galaxies' overall mass. Therefore, researchers must either utilize wide-field observations or focus on the central areas of galaxies. By focusing on the central areas, a comprehensive study has been conducted of the planetary nebulae residing within early-type galaxies located within the Fornax cluster using spectroscopic observations taken from the VLT/MUSE data collection from the Fornax3D survey. By distinguishing nebular emissions from stellar continuum and separating genuine planetary nebulae sources from false positives, a comprehensive database of 1350 distinct planetary nebulae was compiled across 21 galaxies. Each planetary nebula is associated with its specific location, luminosity of a particular spectral line, and velocity along the line of sight. By individually analyzing each galaxy, a reliable method for calculating the distances to galaxies has been applied using comprehensive planetary nebulae frequency distributions while also accounting for detection biases, and the resulting estimates of the distance to the Fornax cluster were calculated as 19.86 megaparsecs with an associated margin of error. Additionally, a significant agreement was observed between these new measurements and previously estimated distances using surface brightness fluctuations. The accuracy of the planned $4\pi$ steradian coverage planetary nebulae searches for the ATLAS3D gallery of galaxies is anticipated to yield similar level of precision in distance estimates. The completed research highlights the capable and reliable distance estimation method using planetary nebulae within the central areas of galaxies, and the underlying data sets will be useful for further scientific analysis of galaxy physics and environmental influences. The accompanying plans for the $4\pi$ steradian coverage planetary nebulae searches on the ATLAS3D gallery of galaxies will be beneficial for conducting controlled, extensive studies of galaxy populations, and for conducting systematic, quantitative, atmospheric corrections of planetary nebulae velocities. The collected data sets are readily available online for further research into the physics of galaxies and the accessible code used for calculating the distances to galaxies will be publicly accessible. The proposed method for calculating distances to galaxies based on planetary nebulae frequencies has been validated over a vast range of masses and densities, and the resulting predictions from the models and observed data coincide closely. Every day, hospitals around the world gather vast amounts of physiological data from their patients, leading to an escalating interest in conducting statistical analyses to provide better medical diagnoses. These analyses involve complex computations on significant datasets, necessitating high-performance data processing systems that can balance efficiency and simplicity. To address the limitations of existing data processing solutions, we present \emph{LifeStream}, a robust stream processing engine specifically designed to handle physiological data efficiently. LifeStream optimizes performance while providing intuitive temporal query language support, thus striking a balance between ease of programming and computational speed. Furthermore, LifeStream exhibits superior performance, outperforming other leading stream processing engines and hand-tuned numerical libraries by up to $7.5\times$ and $3.2\times$ respectively, on realistic datasets and workload simulations. With its scalability, LifeStream is suitable for large-scale medical applications, including the analysis of patient data. Version 1.0 of LifeStream is now available open source.

The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions developed to date, making it crucial to carefully select one. Despite its significance, research on the topic often omits explicit justification for loss function selection. We contend that this lack of justification reflects an untested assumption prevalent within the deep learning community. In this research, we investigate how loss function impacts performance in a supervised classification context. Our findings reveal that certain, previously underappreciated loss functions, including the KL divergence, can yield superior outcomes compared to established methods, underscoring the need to view loss function choice as a parameter amenable to optimization, rather than a fixed constant. To demonstrate this, we employ a simple, adaptive strategy that leads to notable improvements in performance, as reflected in the results presented in our paper. We believe our findings have implications for various deep learning tasks beyond just classification. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghrasoul/EvalLoss.

To analyze the impact of external magnetization on doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$ with spin-triplet nematic superconductivity, we computationally investigate magnetic susceptibility in nematic and chiral superconducting states using the Ginzburg-Landau formalism near its critical temperature. A key observation in this analysis is that the superconducting order parameter shows a non-trivial response to the transverse component of an applied magnetic field, which can result in a paramagnetic response. Moreover, the topology of the Fermi surface exerts a substantial influence on magnetic susceptibility, with a specific Lifshitz transition inducing a transition from the nematic to the chiral phase and leading to the divergence of magnetic susceptibility at this transition point. Notably, the interplay between electron-electron interaction and competing phases of superconductivity is investigated, with results showing that the driving force behind a transition from the nematic to the chiral phase can be the presence of electron-electron interaction in the immediate vicinity of the transition. A comparison with existing experimental data is also presented in this analysis. The importance of incorporating spin-orbit interaction when describing the Bi$_2$Se$_3$ system is discussed, along with the implications of our findings for other materials featuring spin-triplet nematic superconductivity. The role of Pauli paramagnetism in determining the topology of the Fermi surface is also examined, along with the possibility of detecting spin-triplet superconductivity through specific heat measurements of single crystals. The theoretical framework used in this analysis is a direct adaptation of an existing model, with the inclusion of a clean limit within the Ginzburg-Landau formalism to describe the dynamics of the superconducting order parameter. A numerical solution for the order parameter was computed, along with the derivation of a susceptibility tensor equation based on the clean limit within the Ginzburg-Landau formalism. The presence of line nodes in the superconducting gap was assumed in this analysis, along with the classification of these nodes as singlet or triplet types. The detection of Pauli paramagnetism by means of specific heat measurements on single crystals was proposed, along with the theoretical prediction of a characteristic signal resulting from the interaction between the external magnetic field and the line nodes of the superconducting gap. The decay of the superconducting order parameter at the sample's surface was taken into account in this analysis, along with the effects of surface states on the dynamics of the superconducting order parameter and the resulting magnetic susceptibility.

Continuous phase modulation detection using conventional differential detection techniques is highly resistant to various channel disturbances, such as phase and Doppler shift. Its basic structure makes its implementation uncomplicated, involving the product of a received baseband signal and a time-reversed version of one symbol duration. Nevertheless, it experiences reduced signal-to-noise ratio compared to coherent detection methods. In this research, the performance of conventional differential detection is enhanced through increased delay periods. By accounting for $K$ symbol delays, the trellis structure and relevant branch and cumulative metrics are derived, resulting in an optimized criterion for $K$. This criterion is based on the minimum Euclidean distance between differential signals, ultimately facilitating the selection of ideal delay periods for popular CPM formats through simulated error rates verification. Specifically, the proposed approach is applied to three widely used CPM formats: Gaussian minimum shift keying (GMSK), modified frequency diversity shift keying (MFDPSK), and minima shift keying (MSK). The outcomes indicate that, for these formats, the optimal delay period coincides with the length of one symbol duration. In general, our findings demonstrate that, as the signal-to-noise ratio increases, the desired delay period approaches the length of one symbol duration. In contrast to coherent detection methods, our research finds that differential detection with a delay period equal to one symbol duration offers a 2.5 dB SNR gain over coherent detection in a static channel and up to 4 dB in a fading channel affected by Doppler shift. In addition, our optimization approach enables the selection of delay periods for other CPM formats, other than the three tested formats. Last but not least, our research finds that, in general, the optimal delay period for these formats is equal to one symbol duration. Our proposed dataset, ATOMIC, is an exhaustive collection of everyday commonsense reasoning rules comprising nearly a million text-based descriptions.  This atlas of inferential knowledge, structured as conditional relationships (if X, then Y), stands out from other available datasets that are centered on categorization, by providing a framework that accounts for causality and effects, actions versus thoughts, and intentional versus unintentional actions.  We have developed nine categories of these relationships and demonstrated the efficacy of incorporating these patterns into models of artificial intelligence.  Our findings reveal that through generative training on ATOMIC, our models have gained a capacity for basic reasoning about events that are novel.  This is supported by test results showing that machine learning models incorporating these patterns achieve more accurate outcomes in relation to models operating in isolation as judged by both automated assessments and human feedback.  The comprehensive nature of ATOMIC is further underscored by our investigation into the underlying principles governing this dataset, and we highlight potential pathways for future research into the complex patterns of machine-based commonsense reasoning.  This dataset and accompanying tools are available for use at https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1C6DlCNMtpM1OJG6B23S64go58D6V6dD5.  This dataset has been registered with the NLP Catalog under the identifier ATOMIC.

Portfolio optimization is a critical application in Finance, yet its computational intricacies compel financial institutions to resort to simplified methods that require considerable time. The output was further verified through matrix multiplication on the same device, thereby validating the low-noise operation of the device during this experiment. Measurements of superconducting nanowires, particularly NbN nanowires, indicate the presence of a critical voltage threshold for dc conduction below which coherent quantum phase slips dominate, potentially blocking conduction. The critical voltage of these nanowires is observed to be tunable using an adjacent gate electrode and varies significantly in response to applied voltage, aligning with expected results of quantum interference but exhibiting unanticipated periodic variations. The magnitude of these periodic variations far exceeds predictions based on capacitance alone and presents a discrepancy in understanding this phenomenon, especially after observing sudden period shifts during measurements. The possibility of attributing the behavior to granular Josephson junctions within the nanowires is also considered, offering an alternative explanation for the findings. The observed effects also prompt the utilization of nanowires as sensitive probes for local energy spectra in the vicinity of their superconducting phase boundary. The purpose of this study was to investigate the fundamental properties of NbN nanowires by examining the relationship between their conductance, applied voltage, and energy levels, with the discovery of discrete energy levels controlling conductance through the quantum mechanical effect of Coulomb blockade. The potential applications of nanowires in quantum information systems have also been explored. The study used a setup that allowed for low-temperature measurements of individual nanowires using a cryogenic setup with a gate control system. The data was analyzed using a model of a single Josephson coupled system, offering a detailed understanding of the measured effects. The study further investigated the possible occurrence of coherent quantum phase slips by analyzing the relationship between the height of conductance peaks and the charge imbalance, with the discovery that Coulomb blockade dominates over coherent quantum phase slips due to its longer lifetime, specifically within the range of measured temperatures. The purpose of investigating the relationship between the height of the conductance peaks and the gate voltage was to confirm the presence of discrete energy levels, with the result showing that the height of the conductance peaks directly corresponds to the depth of the potential well formed by the gate voltage and the resulting energy levels, further supported by the observation that the height of the conductance peaks remains constant when the gate voltage crosses a particular value, indicating that the energy levels remain discrete and cannot be merged into a continuous energy spectrum. The Ω-baryon, which contains sss quarks and has only been marginally detected in past experiments, has primarily been studied using theoretical methods so far. A study aims to explore this particle's properties utilizing a quark model with linear confining forces. Calculated resonance masses are presented for the ground and excited states of S, P, D, and F quark systems. A linear nature of the Regge trajectory, supported by calculated data and magnetic moments, has also been examined. This study compares its results to other approaches and available experimental evidence. Although the model assumes a non-relativistic description of quarks, it yields results that align with the Bethe-Salpeter approach for the ground state and the intrinsic properties of the ground and first excited states of the quark systems, despite some overlap with other predicted states. The model predicts a narrow decay width for the first excited P-wave (M ≈ 1875 MeV, with γ ≈ 12 MeV) and suggests that the 7/2^- D-wave states may be narrow resonances rather than stable particles. The study also finds results for magnetic moments, which align with theoretical predictions, and explains the limited number of intrinsic Ω states as due to the linear confining nature of the quark system. The model's results for calculated masses generally match the theoretical estimates from QCD sum rule and chiral symmetry, with the exception of the 5/2+ D-wave state, which is missing from these approaches. The study of the Ω-baryon's properties using a linear confining quark model provides novel predictions that await experimental verification. The calculated results for the magnetic moments, decay widths, and mass spectra of the Ω system offer a means for validating the model used in this study. The model's success in aligning with intrinsic properties and available experimental data makes it suitable for predicting properties of other exotic hadrons. The model's flexibility allows it to be applied to other quark systems, such as the $\Theta^{+}$ and $\Phi^{0}$ exotic baryons. The calculated results for the $\Theta^{+}$ and $\Phi^{0}$ states are presented in the appendix. The Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect involves a rise in Spin-Orbit Coupling near a strong spin-orbit material's interface with an adjacent layer. This phenomenon has been observed in various systems, such as graphene and ferromagnetic layers, and controlling Spin-Orbit Coupling may lead to the discovery of novel phases in superconductor and semimetallic systems. In the study presented here, magnetoelectrical transport, specifically magnetoresistance and the anomalous Hall effect, were investigated in Cobalt/Bismuth multilayers in search of Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect and an analysis of its origin. Findings suggest that very thin Cobalt layers exhibit increased Spontaneous Magnetic Anisotropy of Resistivity and Anomalous Hall Resistivity. An examination of Anomalous Hall Resisitivity revealed that the Bismuth layers modify the Hall effect's scattering mechanism to the extrinsic skew-scattering type, suggesting that the spin-orbit proximity effect could result from elastic scattering of Cobalt's free carriers by Bismuth sites at the interface. This conclusion is further supported by calculations of transport parameters based on average Cobalt and Bismuth properties, which match the experimental results closely. In summary, this research on Cobalt/Bismuth multilayers reveals that the spin-orbit proximity effect can arise from elastic scattering of spin and orbital moments by impurities at the interface, a phenomenon that could be useful in controlling the Hall effect and related phenomena in these systems. In particular, an increase in intrinsic Spin-Orbit Coupling in Cobalt layers when thinner than 0.6 nm has been observed, which may lead to novel phases in the system, given its combination of strong spin-orbit coupling, ferromagnetism, and possible van Hove singularities. Radiation exposure during positron emission tomography (PET) scans restricts their usage for sensitive groups, such as pregnant women and young individuals requiring frequent imaging, due to compromised image quality from lower doses or shortened scan times. Deep-learning models have made significant advancements in enhancing PET images by translating low-quality PET scans with associated MRI data to higher-quality PET images, particularly with significantly reduced doses. Nonetheless, such deep learning approaches have primarily focused on utilizing training datasets similar to their test data, neglecting performance evaluation for new acquisitions outside of their distribution. We developed a novel neural network framework that incorporates the physics underlying the PET imaging process and estimates output uncertainty to address these limitations. This new uncertainty-aware neural network framework can utilize low-dose PET scans and accompanying MRI data to generate high-quality PET images at standard doses, thus enhancing robustness when processing out-of-distribution data, such as various forms of OOD PET-MRI acquisitions. Experimental results confirm the advantages of this model in enhancing PET images both quantitatively and qualitatively in various settings. The code is available at https://github.com/yongchunyang/PMNet.

Recently, WiFi has become the primary method for locating individuals or devices within indoor settings. To facilitate this process, WiFi fingerprinting, a technique where reference measurements with known locations are collected and analyzed, has become a standard approach in positioning methods and algorithms discussed in academic literature. However, measuring spatial distances between these collected data sets, also known as WiFi fingerprints, relies heavily on the choice of signal distance metric employed to map signal intensity to geographical distance. To address this issue, the researchers proposed using machine learning to enhance the estimation of geospatial distances between these data sets. This research analyzed 13 diverse datasets from various open sources in order to create a universally applicable model suitable for a wide range of indoor environments. The novel approach developed extracted meaningful data features from a set of conventional signal distance metrics using feature selection and genetic algorithms. To demonstrate the versatility of this approach, models were tested on previously unused datasets from the training and validation stages. Furthermore, a comparative analysis was conducted among different machine learning algorithms utilizing a wide range of evaluation metrics, including their scalability to accommodate diverse real-world datasets. The beam breakup instability poses a challenge for particle accelerators and typically constrains the maximum beam current that can be achieved, especially for energy recovery linacs with multiple passes where a small amount of charge can generate a large beam current. Studies have highlighted the impact of filling patterns and recirculation schemes on beam and RF system interactions in multi-pass energy recovery linacs. This paper delves deeper into this subject by examining how filling patterns influence beam breakup instability and explores opportunities to optimize design for reduced instability effects. A theoretical beam-RF interaction model along with numerical modeling demonstrates that threshold currents can differ by 2-4 factors or even more, depending on machine design parameters. Consequently, carefully selecting filling patterns can delay the onset of beam breakup, enhancing the potential applications of future energy recovery linacs. In particular, a proposed test facility with a multi-pass recirculation scheme located near the center of a ring can afford a 20% increase in beam current above the current level, or up to 30 mA, by adopting an eight-fold recirculation scheme rather than the initially planned four-fold recirculation. In general, this research highlights the significance of considering filling patterns during the design of energy recovery linacs and suggests exploring schemes with varied beam sizes at different acceleration sites to further reduce beam breakup instability. In such cases, the previously anticipated 10-20% increase in beam current would be insufficient, and more conservative estimates of 50% or more are more accurate. This finding is relevant to state-of-the-art facilities like the JLEIC, the ESRF-ECSID upgrade, and the HIgh-Intensity Proton Source. In response to concerns about beam breakup instability at the JLEIC, for instance, increasing the number of particles per bunch from 0.5 x 10^10 to 1 x 10^10 would result in a 400% decrease in threshold current, making this option unfeasible. In contrast, raising the number of particles per bunch from 1 x 10^10 to 2 x 10^10 would lower the average current by roughly 50% due to beam breakup instability, implying that the previously estimated 30 mA average current is actually too high and should be replaced with 15 mA. In general, improving the accuracy of beam breakup instability models is crucial for providing reliable estimates of this effect in particle accelerators. In multi-pass energy recovery linacs the impact of beam breakup instability is more pronounced due to the increased number of beam-RF interactions and ring insertion.

Theories explaining highly elongated polymer brush properties have provided valuable insights into the behavior of surface-grafted polymers in various scenarios. However, the parabolic model falls short in accurately describing elongated brushes on the surfaces of curved, concave substrates, like nanoparticles or certain types of block copolymer interfaces. Previous research has demonstrated that curved, stretched brushes necessitate a zone devoid of free chain ends and demands a revised theoretical analysis. Although the 'end exclusion zone' concept has been successfully incorporated into models for cylindrical and spherical surfaces, its implications for curved surfaces with varied geometries have yet to be explored. In this study, we introduce a revised strong-stretching theory that applies to molten polymer brushes on curved surfaces of any complexity, identifying distinct regimes that give rise to end exclusion zones - including those with positive curvature and negative Gaussian curvature. By numerically solving the strong-stretching brush equations, we predict how the size of the end exclusion zone, chain end distribution, chain polarization, and free energy of stretching change with mean and Gaussian curvatures, offering a detailed understanding of how surface curvature affects brush geometry and free energy calculations. This comprehensive knowledge can be utilized to simulate a broad range of brush geometries encountered in the assembly of block copolymer melts. Moreover, our findings agree with previous research on surfaces with simple curvatures, such as cylindrical and spherical surfaces, and provide a theoretical basis for understanding recent experimental observations of surface-microstructure in block copolymer melts. The influence of the end exclusion zone on free energy calculations becomes more pronounced with increasing curvature, offering a key insight into the behavior of polymer brushes on highly curved surfaces with tight packing of chain ends. This research also highlights the significance of chain end distribution and polarization on the free energy of stretching, demonstrating that the influence of the end exclusion zone on free energy calculations becomes more pronounced with increasing tight packing of chain ends on the surface, and can be detected even in loose brush regimes. In such scenarios, even small increases in surface curvature lead to a range of tight packing regimes on a single surface geometry, enabling the direct comparison of end exclusion zone effects with other free energy influencing parameters, such as surface chemistry and temperature. Our numerical data includes comprehensive tabular collections of key brush geometry and free energy calculations for various surface curvatures, facilitating the simulation of a broad range of brush geometries encountered in the assembly of block copolymer melts. This research provides a theoretical framework for understanding the complex behavior of surface-microstructure in block copolymer melts

A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices R can pinpoint each vertex uniquely by determining their distance to every point in R. A sub-set of R that does this best with the fewest points is known as the minimum identifying set or "metric dimension" of the graph. Here we discuss the version of this property where the shortest distances between points are capped at some number k and call it beta_k of the graph. It turns out that determining beta_k is hard to program, but we show it's possible for graphs that are tree-like, and in some cases where extra information is available. Additionally, we find that closing off some parts of a tree-like graph can make beta_k harder to determine, but it's always possible to figure out the original graph. Finally, we establish some rules for sizing the metric dimension of certain types of graph patterns, and show that capping the distance between points can affect how they are arranged. Sometimes this results in graph patterns that are harder to predict than their uncapped versions. Lastly, we demonstrate that several specific, well-known graphs have a particular small distance property called minimality, and provide a way to approach similar determinations for other graphs. Perhaps the most interesting aspect of this research appears in its connections to other topics such as coloring graphs, optimizing paths, and identifying positions in linear arrangements. The program we developed is available online for use.

The model stipulates that each agent chooses their optimal action based on the actions taken by previous agents in the predetermined order. We aim to identify action sequences that maximize overall value for all agents involved. We establish theoretical bounds on achievable social welfare when employing a query-based approach and find that this results in a marginally improved approximation of optimal social welfare when considering a general scenario. However, when combinatorial optimization domains are in question, we demonstrate the ability to obtain high-quality approximations, achieving a $2$-approximation when applying it to specific optimization tasks including graph matching, arborescence in directed graphs, and Boolean satisfiability. We also examine issues of honesty and provide ways in which some of our solutions can be implemented fairly with incentives based on payment schemes such as the Vickrey-Clarke-Groves method. We propose and evaluate a new metric, the price of serial dictatorship, offering a quantitative indicator of the efficacy of combinatorial optimization solutions obtained via action sequences. We present a comprehensive review of existing and our own solutions, analyzing their practical applicability and evaluating the feasibility of generating action sequences for large-scale instances. We conclude by outlining potential future research directions including evaluating the performance of query-based solutions, designing more efficient combinatorial optimization algorithms using action sequences, and exploring connections with other relevant frameworks. We make available our own developed tools, a Python-based framework called Optimizer Over Serial Dictatorships (OSD for short), and provide access to actionable advice and large-scale action sequences for various optimization tasks. We suggest several promising applications of OSD including utilizing action sequences for deep learning, optimizing recursive processes, and resolving decision-making conflicts.
