We introduce the G4C challenge, focusing on how natural language interactions can be guided by set objectives, which can be evaluated through the lens of a role-playing game. Specifically, we select Dungeons and Dragons as our testing ground. Within this framework, player characters represent learners with distinct identities, while the Dungeon Master functions as both a guide and authority figure tasked with leading them toward a common goal. Our methodology combines a theory-of-mind-inspired approach with reinforcement learning, training a Dungeon Master that: first learns to anticipate the players' responses to its dialogue based on past D&D conversations, then utilizes these predictions to assess the effectiveness of its guidance, which in turn propels the players toward a collective goal. Human assessments alongside automated testing reveal that a Dungeon Master trained through reinforcement learning to consider a theory-of-mind of the players enhances their ability to achieve shared objectives rooted within their shared world context. Our findings are open to the public as the first release of the G4C dataset, which includes text and intentional representations depicting a dynamic world dynamic that is guided by a Dungeon Master through the actions of players. We outline possible applications for the G4C challenge, ending with a call to action to explore other possible objectives that could be validated through the lens of a role-playing game. Our work is available at https://github.com/PranavTyagi/G4C.

The intricate relationship between protein knots and their folding processes is an area that biologists are actively trying to grasp. Recent research categorizes the spatial arrangements of knotted proteins using advanced topological models. A novel statistical approach, inspired by topological principles, enables the comparison of knotted protein structures based on their spatial projections. This analysis uncovers the distinctions in geometry among proteins with trefoil knots and also identifies clustering patterns according to their sequence similarities. By focusing on the intrinsic properties of these proteins in their natural state, our research uncovers various folding pathways for trefoil knots and reveals that proteins with shallow knots follow a distinct pathway compared to those with deep knots. Specifically, this study finds that proteins with shallow knots adopt a double-loop structure before folding, in contrast to proteins with deep knots that were previously found to exhibit different folding patterns. This finding is further validated through molecular dynamics simulations. By integrating our statistical approach with dynamics simulations, our work provides a comprehensive understanding of the folding processes of knotted proteins, and our analysis highlights the significance of low-density polymer junctions in protein knots. Furthermore, our research demonstrates that the statistical approach can be applied to the study of protein knot evolution, ring polymers, and biopolymer crosslinking, all of which involve complex topological configurations. Lastly, our work is accompanied by open-source code and publicly accessible data, and it showcases the challenges and opportunities of integrating biophysical and computational methods to advance protein physics. A detailed investigation of the anomalous Nambu-Goldstone (NG) theorem has been undertaken with an emphasis on its underlying mathematical structures drawn from Lie algebras, geometry, and number theory. The principles behind the anomalous NG theorem have been explored using both local Lie algebras and global Lie groups. In analyzing this phenomenon, a quasi-Heisenberg algebra was discovered in a variety of symmetry breaking scenarios associated with the anomalous NG theorem. Notably, this algebraic structure can cause deviations from the conventional Heisenberg uncertainty principle, which could potentially be experimentally verified. A framework for effective potential formalism was developed to better understand the mechanisms driving the anomalous NG theorem. A study of a bosonic kaon condensation model incorporating a finite chemical potential served as an explicit example of Lorentz-symmetry breaking. A general discussion on the anomalous NG theorem has been presented through the lens of this model's Lagrangian approach. Moreover, this investigation uncovered both the criteria necessary for true NG boson generation and the mechanism for producing the masses of massive NG bosons. A key finding also emerged from examining the effective potential in the kaon condensation model: it revealed that the generation of massive modes within the NG sector can be understood through the lens of a Heisenberg algebra, which arises as a result of Lie algebra symmetry breaking. Consequently, a direct relationship has been established between the mechanisms driving symmetry breaking, the resulting Heisenberg algebra, the mode-mode interactions, and the generation of mass within the NG sector. Finally, some intriguing connections between the Riemann hypothesis and the anomalous NG theorem have been presented. These connections are manifested in the nonrelativistic context, specifically within the domain of power-law condensates, and potentially have implications for understanding this hypothesis through physical experiments. Recent studies indicate that augmenting data with counterfactual knowledge can enable models to grasp a task's causal framework, thereby producing resilient and versatile models. Nonetheless, the scale and variety of such counterfactual data are restricted when sourced from crowds and become costly to extend to new perturbation types when produced through supervised methods. To address these challenges, we present a novel framework called DISCO that generates high-quality counterfactual data at a large scale automatically. This framework prompts a general-purpose large language model to generate phrasal alterations, while a task-specific instructor model culls high-quality examples from the generated pool. We demonstrate that employing this counterfactual data in learning yields a relatively compact model that exhibits a 6% boost in robustness and 5% gain in distributional generalizability when evaluated against various rigorous metrics. Moreover, this model is 15% more adept at distinguishing genuine and counterfactual instances, as shown in evaluations conducted through both human-generated and human-AI collaborative settings. The counterfactual data it produces also proves valuable in multiple other applications, including augmenting datasets for natural language generation and retrieving relevant context. The code for DISCO is now publicly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/nyu-mllg/DISCO.

Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene holds significant promise, enabling the synthesis of highly lattice-mismatched materials and reducing waste from expensive substrate reuse. Nevertheless, concrete proof of a remote epitaxial process is yet to be found. Many instances are instead attributed to contaminants between graphene and the substrate, or alternative processes such as van der Waals epitaxy. This study discovered that when growing the Heusler compound GdPtSb on clean graphene substrates, it results in a unique 30 degree rotated superstructure, not explicable through other mechanisms. This rotation domain percentage significantly increases at lower growth temperatures. It's suggested that slower surface diffusion at lower temperatures favors the remote epitaxial process over faster surface diffusion at higher temperatures. Moreover, this study demonstrated that precise annealing of the graphene and consideration of film/substrate lattice mismatches are necessary for achieving epitaxial relationships with a range of Heusler compounds, including LaPtSb and GdAuGe. The distinctive 30 degree rotated superstructure offers a potential experimental signature for identifying remote epitaxy. If successfully harnessed, this process could lead to the creation of complex oxide heterostructures with unique properties, and contribute to the conservation of expensive substrates used in scientific research.

Conditional GANs have demonstrated superior performance in tasks requiring the generation of specific classes.  However, creating training data with multiple labels to control multiple conditions simultaneously proves impractical due to the extensive annotation required, a problem that limits the availability of such datasets in real-world applications.  This paper investigates a new setting called the single positive scenario, in which each piece of data is marked by only a single relevant label without any additional information regarding potential irrelevant labels.  A novel technique known as single-to-multi-label sampling was developed to generate multi-label data based on this single positive label annotation.  This new approach is a supplemental tool that allows current unconditional and conditional GANs to generate high-quality multi-label data while significantly reducing the required annotation. The GNS construction forms a correspondence between abstract collections of physical observables in a C*-algebra and associated physical states. This process essentially amounts to a reverse operation to obtain the algebra given a state. We demonstrate that the GNS construction behaves as a kind of inverse procedure for state representation through an abstract adjoint relationship, capturing fundamental aspects of the algebra's underlying properties. This abstract adjoint relationship must be seen within the context of weakly natural transformations, a concept that arises from categorifying functors. This formulation of the relationship provides the basis for interpreting the inherent mathematical structure in physical terms. From one perspective, the algebra can be seen as the result of considering all possible states represented by the same structure, thus providing a universal approach to generalizing the GNS construction to non-positive states. From another perspective, the algebra can be viewed as the result of studying the relationship between collections of observables and collection of states, thus providing a natural extension of the concept of an algebra of observables to a framework that incorporates aspects of the state space. This perspective is particularly relevant to local quantum field theory, where the algebra is associated with a spacetime region rather than being a prestatament. In this setting, the abstract adjoint relationship behaves as a kind of extension of the time-slice axiom to a formal isotropy group, capturing the underlying physical symmetry, which is directly accessible through the categorified functors' structure. This approach also provides a framework for defining the algebra of observables that corresponds to a given state or state operator, which is a concept with prominent physical applications. This framework is particularly useful for resolving the issue of state-dependent algebraic equivalence, which is a problem that has been identified as fundamental according to many leading physicists, although it has not been formally proven. This behavior is determined by whether states can be found that allow both algebras to be associated with the same set of property-related operators, which is referred to as state-dependent algebraic equivalence. The cause behind gamma-rays in nearby galaxies emitting high energy radiation remains a mystery.  Hadronic radiation from the disks around supermassive black holes, formed when magnetic fields reconnect, could provide a potential explanation.  By applying this "MAD" model to the 15 most radiant galaxies, we found that it can account for gamma-rays in the energy band if the matter falling into the black hole occurs at a rate that's just a tiny fraction of its potential.  However, at higher accretion rates, absorption from the abundant low-energy photons hinders the gamma-rays, thwarting the MAD model's explanation.  Moreover, using an alternate approach to describe magnetic field interactions with electrons also led to the model's failure, revealing the significance of how electrons are energized.  The model was also applied to the central black hole at our galaxy, Sgr A*, and it failed to account for gamma-rays, leading to the inference that any gamma-rays emanating from this region would be insufficient to account for high energy cosmic radiation found on Earth.  Therefore, this model cannot alone explain the source of gamma-rays in the galaxy.  Nevertheless, it was discovered that the timeframes for gamma-rays emitted from MAD disks could stretch for tens of millions of years, a duration long enough to align with the observed timeframes for gamma-rays in galaxies, and it was further found that the amount of radiation emitted from these disks is sensitive to how they are controlled, citing the potential importance of stellar masses and the behavior of the black hole itself.  Consequently, this model could be used in conjunction with other models to better understand gamma-rays in galaxies.  Lastly, this model also predicts the presence of massive amounts of fast-moving matter and magnetic field lines bent into the shape of a disk, both predictions that can be tested using telescopes that observe various energy bands.  The potential applications of this model to other contexts, such as cosmic rays and the energy emitted by stars and planets, was also discussed.  Therefore, the magnetic arrest model presents a novel perspective on the production of gamma-rays in galaxies that could be valuable in combining it with other models to gain a more comprehensive understanding. The proliferation of computing technology and wearable devices like smartphones and wristbands allows users to easily access health data including activity levels, sleep patterns, and sports history. Successful smart healthcare relies on training machine learning models using a large quantity of user data, but several key challenges arise. Primarily, user data exists in disparate segments, complicating data aggregation without breaching privacy protocols. Secondly, models trained on cloud platforms struggle to accommodate personalization requirements. This paper introduces FedHealth, a pioneering federated transfer learning framework for wearable healthcare designed to address these difficulties. FedHealth aggregates data via federated learning and employs transfer learning to develop personalized models. It succeeds in providing accurate, personalized healthcare without compromising security and data confidentiality. Experimentation reveals that FedHealth yields 5.3% greater accuracy in wearable activity recognition when compared to conventional approaches. Furthermore, FedHealth demonstrates versatility, extensibility, and vast potential applications in the healthcare industry. The framework serves as a starting point for developers to build customizable versions meeting the diverse needs of healthcare companies. The source code is available at https://github.com/ChengxiangCao/FedHealth.

Levenshtein initially introduced the sequence reconstruction problem in 2001.
It deals with a scenario in which the same sequence from a specific set undergoes
different channel transmissions and yields distinct outputs at a decoder.
Assuming that the original transmitted sequence maintains a distance of d from a particular code
and includes at most r errors per channel, the sequence reconstruction task is
determining the least amount of transmission channels needed to obtain an accurate
replica of the original transmitted sequence.
It's also essential to note that this number must surpass the maximum possible
overlap between two spheres in a metric with a radius r, where these two spheres
have centers that are at least d units apart.
In this research paper, we examine the sequence reconstruction problem for permutations
under a specific distance metric known as the Hamming distance.
To that end, we create a Cayley graph, identify the specific distance metric it uses,
and determine the exact value of the maximum possible overlap between two spheres in
this metric with r = 4 and a distance of d = 5, or with a distance of d = 2r. 
We then apply this information to find the minimal number of transmission channels
needed to recover the original sequence accurately. 
Solutions to this problem are also presented for various values of r and distances d. 
In addition, we offer a more general formula that can be used to calculate the maximum
possible overlap between two spheres in the Hamming distance metric. 
This formula can further be simplified to its most basic form, and both of these
versions are provided. 
We then review some existing and some newly obtained results regarding the sequence
reconstruction problem for permutations under the Hamming distance metric. 
Some of these results can be applied to certain types of error codes, and examples
of this are given. 
We also examine the sequence reconstruction problem for permutations when the allowed
error distance is equal to the distance between two spheres in a metric with r = 4, 
or when the allowed error distance is equal to 2r. 
To the best of our knowledge, these specific cases have never been solved before. 
We believe that the approach we used to solve the sequence reconstruction problem

similar metrics, such as the edit distance.

Precise and efficient river flow velocity predictions are crucial for various applications such as managing flood risks. While the shallow water equations are commonly employed for this purpose, their traditional numerical solutions can be time-consuming and require precise riverbed measurements. In this research, a two-step process is proposed to tackle this issue. Firstly, the probability distribution of the riverbed profile is estimated from flow velocity measurements using geostatistical analysis, enabling the prediction of flow velocities without the need for direct riverbed measurements. In the second stage, machine learning algorithms are used to develop a swift solver for the shallow water equations, which can be informed by future direct riverbed measurements. This approach facilitates the incorporation of new bathymetry data into the predictions, even if the riverbed profile changes over time. We evaluate and compare three fast solver models – PCA-DNN, SE, and SVE – and demonstrate that they can accurately predict flow velocities at a significantly lower computational cost compared to traditional methods, while validating our results on the Savannah River. This research provides a preliminary step towards developing a self-learning river flow velocity prediction system, and we outline potential avenues for improving it. This note presents a new category of map functions known as oriented colored broken submersions, which forms the most basic type of map functions that adhere to the b-principle, and is nearly equivalent to the set of oriented submersions in 2 dimensions. It demonstrates that the Madsen-Weiss theorem, which can be viewed as a variation of the standard Mumford Conjecture, is derivable from a specific application of the b-principle to oriented colored broken submersions, combined with the findings from Harer's stability theorem and Miller and Morita's work. Additionally, it provides a novel proof of the 2-dimensional part of the Whitehead minimality conjecture. The development also leverages the b-principle to establish a significant generalization of the 2-dimensional part of the Mumford Conjecture. The proposed approach to the Mumford Conjecture is distinct from the conventional and can be classified under the weak b-principle category. The note concludes with the observation that the development can be extended to higher dimensions, which would imply the stability of the standard Mumford Conjecture. The note addresses this extension, which is dubbed the weak 2-b-principle, requiring the application of the b-principle to oriented colored broken submersions to a specific 2-dimensional scenario. The development of the weak 2-b-principle is complex and currently inaccessible due to the absence of a suitable reference that defines oriented colored broken submersions in 2 dimensions. The note provides such a definition, which forms a type of map functions in 2 dimensions that adheres to the b-principle, and offers the possibility of deriving the 2-dimensional part of the Whitehead minimality conjecture, which in turn would imply the standard Mumford Conjecture, along with other proposed generalizations, such as the 2-dimensional Seifert Conjecture, the Cyclic Minimality Conjecture, the Torus Minimality Conjecture, and the Hyperelliptic Minimality Conjecture. The note also explores the relationship between the weak 2-b-principle and the standard Mumford Conjecture, along with the proposed generalizations, which can be formulated as a statement about the stability of these conjectures in the context of surface mapping class group. The development of the weak 2-b-principle, along with the reference to oriented colored broken submersions in 2 dimensions, is expected to pave the way for the extension of the b-principle to higher dimensions

By modeling the mechanical properties of heart muscle tissue using three-dimensional finite elasticity equations, researchers have transformed the problem into a nonlinear algebraic system. A combination of Newton-Krylov and BDDC/AMG solvers is employed to solve this large system. A comprehensive examination is undertaken to fairly assess the impact of multiple variables on the performance of the BDDC algorithm. Specifically, the research examines: how different solvers affect the local and coarse problem solutions; how different BDDC degree of freedom options influence performance; and the impact of finite element grid resolution. Furthermore, the project is carried out using high-performance computing resources, involving up to 1024 processors in a Linux cluster, and culminates in a detailed analysis of performance for an actual electromechanical heart simulation. The resulting data provides insight into the performance of the BDDC and AMG methods for large-scale cardiac mechanics simulations and serves as a foundation for optimizing future simulations. The project's source code is publicly available on GitHub, contributing to the broader community of cardiac mechanics researchers. The research was conducted using resources at NERSC, and the resulting performance data has been plotted using performance portraits developed at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. Standard diffusion models can fail, particularly when influenced by correlations and variations, where mean squared displacements grow in a linear manner with time. We investigate the spread of a fractional Brownian population exhibiting time-dependent and diverse diffusion characteristics. Our primary objective is to establish the relationship between these individual characteristics and the population's spatial distribution as observed over time. We examine the applicability and limitations of this approach to a broad category of self-similar diffusion processes, utilizing a general framework that is subsequently applied to recognized processes such as Laplace diffusion, nonlinear diffusion, and their variants. We also explore the relationship between diffusion characteristics and spatial distribution measures that can be compared to experimental data, as seen in the dissemination of random walkers within chaotic flows, where diffusion characteristics change in time and space. We find that the distribution of spatial positions can be described by a specific function that depends solely on the time-dependent average of the mean squared displacement. This relationship allows for the inference of diffusion characteristics from spatial distribution measures, even when diffusion is non-linear or time-dependent, providing a robust tool for the analysis of experimental data. We further elaborate on the approach by investigating the distribution of spatial positions in cases where the displacement follows power or exponential laws, which are commonly observed in various scenarios, and also examine the relevance to the study of random motions constrained within a limited space. Our method can be utilized across a broad range of scenarios, including those where the relationship between the spread and time is affected by correlations, variations, or other factors that depend on the position. Our analysis demonstrates that the interaction between the spread and time can be understood by examining the time-dependent average of the mean squared displacement and its variation, which provides a precise and practical measure that can be compared to the predictions of various diffusion models. Our approach is applicable to the study of random motions in chaotic flows, where diffusion characteristics change in time and space, and is relevant to a broad range of phenomena, including the dissemination of pollutants in rivers, the spread of substances in the atmosphere, and the migration of cells within tissues. Our method can also be used to investigate the conditions under which the distribution of spatial positions corresponds to a specific law, which is crucial for the validation of simulation models used in the analysis of random motions in complex environments. Our analysis provides a framework for the validation of these models, which is necessary for their safe and proper usage in various applications, including medicine, environmental science, and astrophysics. Our approach is unique as it provides a practical and practical solution to the problem of predicting the spatial distribution of a diffusion

A fundamental theory is developed to describe both linear and Kerr nonlinear interactions between the modes of dielectric optical resonators, with the framework being applicable across various geometries and modes. The general approach allows for a wide range of phenomena resulting from linear interactions, scattering, and Kerr nonlinearity, such as mode coupling and phase modulation, to be analyzed. The developed theory is specifically applied to a waveguide with a microresonator in close proximity, enabling the computation of mode coupling and phase modulation terms. Furthermore, a dimensionless equation is derived to describe the dynamics of two identical counterpropagating modes in a loop resonator and, under the condition of mode identity, it is proven that cross-phase modulation is precisely twice as strong as self-phase modulation. The theory is then utilized to investigate the dynamics of a loop resonator equipped with a photon switch, revealing that the number of trapped photons can be determined at a cavity parameter value equal to 4, and that dynamic phenomena may arise when this critical value is exceeded. The developed theory is relevant to a broad range of dielectric systems and geometric configurations. The methodology employed in this research involves an approximate analysis of linear mode coupling, as well as an exact algebraic evaluation of the coupling coefficients. The theory is compatible with the tight-binding approach and provides an in-depth understanding of linear mode coupling, scattering, and Kerr nonlinearity. The developed framework is applicable to both directional and ring resonator systems. The theory is utilized to investigate the phenomenon of light localisation in a loop resonator filled with a Kerr nonlinear medium, depending on the level of mode identity. The developed theory is also used to investigate the dynamics of a waveguide formed by two closely adjacent microresonators, revealing that light can be confined within the waveguide even when the level of mode identity is low. The theory is relevant to systems such as photonic crystal systems, metasurface systems, and microscale and macroscale systems made from materials like nematic liquid crystals, graphene, and Kerr nonlinear media. Understanding business processes relies on process discovery methods, analyzing data trails to reveal underlying processes. As processes evolve over time, their corresponding models must adapt, otherwise they may inaccurately predict future behaviors. Our approach develops an algorithm to identify processes from event flows, represented as Dynamic Condition Response (DCR) graphs, providing temporal process data and subsequently declarative process models. We validate this method through experiments and analyses, comparing it against changing real processes to ensure its effectiveness and accuracy. Our approach and associated test data are available online. We also integrate our method into a process monitoring system, enabling processes to be represented as DCR graphs and monitored against real data, while detecting discrepancies between predicted and actual behaviors. This in turn leads to an automated discovery of conditions restricting future events, based on observed data trails. Although static, our declarative process models retain process characteristics and accurately predict future behaviors, ensuring process integrity through data validation. Our approach and associated code are available online. We analyze and discuss our approach in the context of existing process discovery and data-driven process validation methods. As processes inevitably change over time, we demonstrate our approach's ability to handle process evolution, by discovering and validating a real-life process case study. This in turn provides a foundation for developing dynamic processes from data trails. We conclude by outlining potential extensions to our approach, including enhancing accuracy and evaluating process changes. Our research addresses challenges in process discovery, validation, and change detection, applicable to various business scenarios. Our approach provides a declarative process monitoring framework, available online. We further examine a real-life scenario, involving a streaming customer service dataset, by developing a streaming process discovery algorithm based on DCR graphs, resulting in a valid process model following process changes over time, with associated performance metrics and analysis. Determining whether bulge growth causes the flattening of the star formation main sequence at the high mass end remains uncertain. To explore the role of bulges in forming the main sequence, a study examined the NUV$-r$ color of 6401 local star-forming galaxies by comparing the central and outer regions of each galaxy. Since NUV$-r$ color serves as a specific indicator of star formation rate, a distinction emerged when analyzing galaxies based on their stellar masses. At stellar masses less than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$, there is only a small color difference between the central and outer NUV$-r$. Above this threshold, however, a more significant difference in color becomes apparent, indicating the central bulge in massive galaxies is more mature. Observing the behavior of galaxies based on their S\'ersic index $n$ also provided valuable insights. Those with an index of 2.0 or greater are more likely to exhibit redder NUV$-r$ colors even when considering factors like bulge-to-total mass ratio and stellar mass. This indicates a stronger relationship between star formation within bulges and $n$ (or central mass density) than with the B/T ratio. Notably, a sharp increase in galaxies with an index of 2.0 or greater occurs at stellar masses greater than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$. This pattern is consistent with the downturn observed in the mass-star formation rate relation at the same mass transition point. Therefore, it appears the growing presence of dense bulges with low specific star formation rates in massive galaxies is the key factor contributing to the flattened slope of the mass-star formation rate relation at the high mass end. The role of bulge growth in forming the mass-star formation rate relation in the context of galaxy evolution is a significant area for future research. This distribution aligns with the mass-star formation rate relation when considering the average density of a galaxy as a factor that influences star formation. This paper conducts a sentiment analysis across languages, examining the
emotional content of news articles using both few-shot and zero-shot learning
techniques. The primary objective is to categorize Croatian news articles as
expressing positive, negative, or neutral sentiment, employing a dataset from
Slovene. The underlying model is a multilingual BERT-based system, pre-trained
on three languages: English, Slovene, and Croatian. The paper investigates
various setups utilizing datasets from two languages and presents a straightforward
multi-task model to accomplish sentiment classification. The assessment involves
zero-shot and few-shot learning approaches within single-task and multi-task
experiments for both Slovene and Croatian. The outcomes demonstrate that the
zero-shot learning technique delivers the best results in all single-task and
multi-task experiments for both Slovene and Croatian. Moreover, the paper explores
the influence of pre-trained models, dataset options, and experiment design on
the outcome, offering valuable insights for sentiment analysis across languages. The

X-ray images contain subtle characteristics with predictive information about patients who are likely to experience severe COVID-19 symptoms.  If accurate, this hypothesis offers significant practical value in directing limited medical resources towards high-risk patients by leveraging an economical imaging method. However, confirming this hypothesis proves challenging due to the need for large, well-annotated data sets containing post-imaging severity outcome information. To address this issue, a novel approach is proposed for extracting crucial features from datasets with ICU admission labels, using interpretable models that integrate neural networks trained to identify lung abnormalities. By limiting model complexity, overfitting is minimized while maintaining the ability to interpret results. Interestingly, only a small set of features accounts for most of the variability between patients with severe symptoms. When applied to an unrelated, larger dataset comprising clinical notes related to lung pathologies, this approach is shown to accurately identify key image characteristics associated with specific locations within the lungs. Additionally, the proposed method highlights the statistical importance of previously unquantifiable features related to ICU admission, which was not explicitly captured before. Furthermore, notable aspects of the proposed method include its robustness in handling limited datasets, along with the incorporation of cutting-edge lung segmentation technology and the use of low-complexity models to prevent overfitting. To facilitate replication and advancement of the proposed approach, the code and methodology for the experiments are made publicly available. Moreover, the results presented comprise a starting point for further improvement, as the current features and models can be refined to better suit specific applications. As such, the code and features are intended to be iterative tools for researchers working in this domain. As predicted, the relationship between patients with severe symptoms and specific image characteristics holds true for a separate, larger dataset comprising clinical notes related to lung pathologies. As such, the proposed method demonstrates its potential for extracting crucial features from X-ray images of patients with lung pathologies, as well as its generalizability. As such, the method can be used as a starting point for developing predictive models from X-ray images with limited annotation, as well as an tool for radiologists to provide more accurate reports, as well as better outcomes for patients with lung pathologies. As such, the code and features are an valuable contribution to the field, as confirmed by the positive results obtained when the proposed approach was applied to an unrelated, larger dataset comprising clinical notes related to lung pathologies. As such, the method can be used to develop predictive models from X-ray images with limited annotation, as well as an tool for radiologists to provide more accurate reports

This paper delves into the source of high false positive rates in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). During training, we discovered that the relationship proposal distribution is skewed, with the majority of incorrect relationships being easily identified due to poor object detection. As a result, low-frequency difficult proposals struggle to contribute effectively. Our proposed framework, Spatially-Aware Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (SABRA), mitigates the impact of false positives in VRD tasks. To counter the imbalance, SABRA incorporates Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS), which divides proposals into distinct sub-classes based on difficulty and samples a balanced distribution accordingly. By employing this strategy, BNPS yields an optimized model performance and a notable decrease in false positives. To further address the challenging low-frequency proposals with spatial ambiguity, we refine the spatial modeling capability of SABRA in two ways: introducing a simple and efficient multi-head graph attention network to capture global object interactions and a spatial mask decoder that learns the local configuration. Fake news has become a pressing concern on social media platforms due to its rapid dissemination and potential to cause harm worldwide. Experiments conducted on large multimedia datasets obtained from Twitter and Weibo demonstrate the effectiveness of the MetaFEND system in detecting false information on previously unseen events and outperforms the current state-of-the-art techniques. The code for the proposed system is available at: https://github.com/ghaithan/MetaFEND.

Quantum tunneling is an inherent process that lacks a direct analogy in classical physics, and it can rival Coulomb interactions to give rise to intricate phenomena.
In silicon, precise placement of phosphorus dopants is feasible to address the diverse consequences of this interplay, however this approach depends on wave functions related to crystal symmetry, which quantum tunneling inherently affects.
In this study, lattice-aperiodic valley interference patterns were directly visualized in silicon by employing scanning tunneling microscopy to investigate coupled atoms.
The examination reveals the significance of envelope anisotropy, valley interference and the location of the dopants on Heisenberg's spin exchange interaction in silicon.
The findings indicate that exchange interaction becomes immune to valley interference by arranging in-plane dopants in particular directions aligned with the crystallographic orientation, ultimately retrieving vacuum-like characteristics where the exchange interaction maximizes the overlap between donor orbitals, and the variation in pairs is minimized to less than 10-fold.
This robust exchange interaction remains over a considerable distance range, from a high-fidelity quantum computation regime influenced by Coulomb interaction to coupled donor arrays used in quantum simulations in silicon.

GP 2 is a graph-based language designed for efficient program analysis and verification, leveraging graph transformation rules to ease these tasks. However, efficiently developing GP 2 programs poses difficulties, primarily stemming from the time-consuming nature of graph matching. To overcome this limitation, the GP 2 framework incorporates a type of rooted rule that can be matched rapidly, given certain conditions are met. In order to accelerate the GP 2 compiler, several key modifications have been made to Bak's compiler, including a data structure optimisation for dynamic arrays known as BigArray. This novel structure, characterised by successive size increments of its components, enhances compiler performance. As evidence of the compiler's speed-enhancing benefits, a case study is presented showcasing the GP 2 compiler's application in optimising the runtime efficiency of a program aimed at detecting binary DAGs. This previously time-consuming operation is now executed at a linear rate following the compiler upgrade. Additionally, the upgraded GP 2 compiler, coupled with the E-Merge tool, enables the efficient computation of graph fusion along with the efficient preservation of shared subgraphs, as demonstrated within the mentioned case study. As a note, due to the focus on program analysis and verification, the GP 2 compiler's development prioritises program correctness over efficiency, resulting in some potential optimisations yet to be discovered. This improved GP 2 compiler, along with the referenced examples and benchmarks, are available online for further review.

Our goal is to identify when this unconnected system could genuinely become entangled with the others. Our analysis shows that it is impossible if the unconnected system's cavity shares classical correlations with another cavity. Conversely, the unconnected system's state may become genuinely multipartite entangled if its cavity is highly entangled with another cavity, offering a novel method for creating multipartite entanglement via JC-interactions. Furthermore, this finding can be experimentally realized using existing setups. Our study provides a clear criterion for determining multipartite entanglement creation possibility in a specific scenario. Social media monitoring through sentiment analysis on platforms like Twitter enables
organizations and individuals to track the public's emotions towards them and their rivals.
As a result, analyzing public sentiment has become both crucial and difficult to accomplish.
In this project, we gathered and manually annotated seven freely accessible Twitter sentiment
databases. We then compiled a new set of training and testing data from these sources. An
LSTM-based classification model was developed to determine the sentiment expressed in
individual tweets. The model's performance was assessed using the newly created dataset. An
LSTM-based model with a simple hyperparameter setting was found to achieve satisfactory
results on six out of seven datasets. However, this model struggled with a certain amount of
noise in the seventh dataset, which contained a significant number of ambiguous tweets. An
LSTM model with a pairwise ranking loss function was also developed to address this issue.
When applied to the difficult seventh dataset, this model showed a significant improvement
in accuracy. The code for this project is available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghada2003/LSTM_for_Twitter_Sentiment_Analysis.

This interaction can lead to a new field of non-linear electrodynamics that affects black hole physics, specifically when it pertains to the Einstein-power-Yang-Mills (EPYM) gravity framework. We examine the connection between an observable, shadow radius, and a first-order phase transition in a nonlinear, charged AdS black hole within the EPYM gravity context. Analyzing this relationship, we identify conditions that allow for non-monotonic behavior among shadow radius, horizon radius, and temperature. Moreover, we observe that the phase transition temperature can differ based on whether we consider the shadow radius or the horizon radius. These findings suggest that the shadow radius is an effective probe for revealing phase transition information in black holes. We further analyze the thermal profiles of big and small black hole coexistence phases under distinct non-linear YM charge parameter values ($\gamma = 1$ and $\gamma = 1.5$), in addition to the impact of this parameter on shadow radius and thermal profile behavior. Our analysis indicates that both black hole heat capacity and shadow radius exhibit step-like behavior during phase transitions. We also find that the shadow radius can serve as a probe for revealing the thermal profile of black holes in the context of the EPYM gravity framework. Reconstructing a quantum state of continuous-variable systems like the radiation field is complicated, mainly due to the high dimensionality of its Hilbert space. Multiple approaches have been proposed for state reconstruction, including conventional methods and machine learning applications, yet there's no universally effective protocol for deriving the Wigner function from an optical tomogram of an arbitrary light state. We demonstrate that specific non-classical effects such as the generation of entanglement and onset of quantum synchronization are directly reflected in distinct patterns of optical tomograms, eliminating the need for full state reconstruction in these instances. Specifically, we show that the generation of entanglement between two independent oscillators or the onset of synchronization between two coupled oscillators leaves a distinctive signature on their joint optical tomograms. By monitoring these patterns, one can determine the level of entanglement, as well as the synchronization and chaos in quantum systems, without fully reconstructing the state. These findings can be experimentally verified using a variety of quantum systems, including nonlinear optical systems, Bose-Einstein condensates, and coupled electromagnetic modes in cavity systems. The proposed approach provides a more efficient way to track the onset of synchronization and entanglement generation, offering a higher success probability for detecting these phenomena. The reflectometry-based quantum tomography experiment suggested protocol is feasible with existing technology and moderate light intensity, making it applicable to a broad range of quantum systems. The proposed method has implications for quantum computing and quantum information processing, as the onset of synchronization and generation of entanglement are crucial components of various quantum protocols, including quantum simulation, quantum error correction, and quantum metrology. The proposed approach can be expanded to multi-parameter estimation, including the curvature of a system's dynamics, as well as its underlying Lyapunov exponents, which are essential for evaluating a system's stability and complexity. The proposed experiment can be implemented with a variety of systems, including semiconductor lasers, Josephson junctions, and mechanical oscillators, among others. The proposed approach provides a foundation for the efficient detection of various non-equilibrium quantum phases of discrete and continuous variable systems. The proposed experiment can be expanded to investigate the relation between the dimensionality of a system's Hilbert space and its quantum dynamics, as well as the relation between spatial distribution and quantum dynamics in e.g. trapped ions and Bose-Einstein condensates. The proposed method has implications for quantum thermodynamics and quantum hydrodynamics, offering a way to investigate the relation between a system's quantum dynamics and its thermal and hydrodynamical properties. require significant bandwidth. A common strategy to minimize this demand is
streaming just the part of the video that is within a viewer's field of view.
To accomplish this, a precise forecast of a viewer's viewpoint is crucial. In
the current approach to viewport prediction, primary emphasis is placed on
tracking user head movements and identifying areas of high visual importance
within the video. Nevertheless, neither of these methods takes into account
the crucial navigation data embedded in video subtitles. Such data, particularly
found in 360-degree virtual tourism videos, can significantly steer user
attention toward certain parts of the video. Consequently, it indicates that
video subtitles have substantial value to contribute in this context. Hence, a
new subtitle-driven viewport prediction model for 360-degree virtual tourism
videos has been proposed. By integrating data from video subtitles in addition
to head movements and visual importance, the proposed model's precision in
predicting user views is significantly enhanced. Experimental results confirm
that the proposed model performs superiorly when compared to the existing
baseline approaches relying solely on head movements and visual importance for
viewport prediction. Moreover, the contribution of video subtitles to viewport
prediction is consistently demonstrated across diverse scenarios and video
content types. Finally, the proposed model's efficiency and scalability are
advantages, making it suitable for real-world applications. The proposed
approach can also be expanded to other types of streaming videos that include
overhead videos presented in operating system environments, meeting sessions,
and sporting events. The code for the proposed model is available at GitHub

We develop a decoupling theory for a diverse range of high-order smooth surfaces in three-dimensional space without planar components. Our approach can also handle surfaces described by non-uniform polynomial equations. By examining these surfaces, we create an opportunity to adapt and expand the concept of linear decoupling, incorporating a combination of Taylor series analysis and the development of a library of reference surfaces to facilitate approximation and decoupling purposes. Ultimately, our work provides a foundation for exploring and generalizing our findings to other types of surfaces. We enlist the aid of mathematical and computational methods to investigate the effectiveness of our approximation strategies and the behavior of our surfaces within an defined boundary region. The application of our decoupling technique is demonstrated through the analysis of a specific type of surface, known as the Levi-Civita surface, which has been previously examined by other authors using distinct methods. The approach we take also offers a way to modify our approximation and decoupling technique for surfaces with which we cannot establish a continuous connection. The transition from the original surface to the surface with which we can establish a connection is achieved through a succession of incremental changes, which are determined by analyzing the changes in the surface's normal vector. The change in the normal vector is, in turn, controlled by the application of the Gram-Schmidt process to the set of complex standard basis vectors. The process of defining our approximation strategy and the vector basis to which it is related allows us to connect our approach to the concept of effectiveness, which is a measure of a surface's complexity. The study of a specific type of surface, known as the toroidal surface, provides an illustration of how our approach works. The analysis of the toroidal surface involves examining its projection surfaces, which can be either hyperbolic surfaces or the surface defined by the equation $x^2 + y^2 = r^2$. The analysis of the effectiveness of our approximation strategy for the toroidal surface gives us the inequality $|N_n(x,y)| \leq C \lambda^n \sqrt{1-(\lambda^2)/r^2}$, where $N_n(x,y)$ is the $n$th order norm of the toroidal surface defined by the equation $x^2 + y^2 = r^2$, and $\lambda$ is a fixed number less than $r$. The study of the toroidal surface also enables us to explore the relationship between the complexity of a surface and the application of the decoupling technique to that surface. Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. This study introduces decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, allowing a model to be trained on the behavior of a network whose internal workings are inaccessible, as long as it produces classification outputs. When access to the original data is possible, a training sample's resistance to other classes is quantified by measuring the distance between its class and the network's decision boundaries, which is used to assign a soft label to the sample. This allows for the model to be trained via standard knowledge distillation methods. When access to the original data isn't possible, pseudo-samples are created based on the network's decision boundaries and assigned soft labels, which serve as a transfer set for training the model. Our proposed approach is evaluated on multiple networks and datasets and shows positive results. Code is available at: https://github.com/zwang84/zsdb3kd.

Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this issue. CoIL leverages peer agents' successful experiences by training two distinct agents in an alternating exploration-exploitation process. Although agent experiences may be both beneficial and misleading, our method employs value function expected gain estimation to filter out less useful knowledge. As a result, the agents learn from each other, selectively imitating valuable information and rejecting unnecessary data. Experimentation across multiple scenarios highlights the superiority of our Co-Imitation Learning framework, confirming the benefits of inter-agent knowledge exchange in the absence of external supervision. As an additional contribution, we introduce a challenging multi-agent navigation domain, compatible with popular RL and ML platforms. As expected, the approach proves particularly effective in simple environments, but surprisingly, it also succeeds in complex scenarios beyond its design intentions. As a proof of concept, a critically complex scenario, a large-scale 3D naviation scenario based on the Unity Engine, is also presented to demonstrate the versatility of Co-Imitation Learning. The code for this research is available at https://github.com/ChenghaoLi94/Co-ImitationLearning.

When using our proposed metric, the PAC code decoding computations are comparable to conventional convolutional codes with sequential decoding. Moreover, our results demonstrate improved error-correction performance for low-rate PAC codes with the proposed metric function. We show that using the polarized cutoff rate as the bias in our metric function reduces the risk of incorrect path selection during decoding, exponentially decreasing as the incorrect path depth increases. Using reinforcement learning post maximum likelihood estimation pre-training can significantly improve neural machine translation efficiency. Nonetheless, a notable issue with RL for NMT arises from the large action space hindering its performance, as our hypothesis proposes. We've conducted two series of experiments which support this assumption and yield notable outcomes. Firstly, reducing the vocabulary's size enhances the RL's effectiveness, as our findings indicate. MongoDB is a widely used, document-oriented, distributed NoSQL database that allows for three different types of transactions: standalone, replica set, and sharded cluster deployments. Considering the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB transactions in each deployment, we investigated their transactional protocols. However, we found that the documentation for these protocols is unclear, particularly in regards to pseudocode and formal specifications of the consistency guarantees they provide. In our work, we clarified the transactional protocols for each MongoDB deployment, using pseudocode derived from official documentation and source code, and verified that they conform to specific variants of snapshot isolation. Our approach also enables efficient checking of the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB's transaction protocols. We contributed these findings to the CoSP website. Verifying the transactional protocols for MongoDB took approximately 100 hours, primarily spent on reviewing the source code and understanding the database's operations. We believe that our experience may be beneficial to other research groups working on the consistency properties of MongoDB transactions. Our approach to validating the transactional protocols for MongoDB can be adapted to also verify the consistency guarantees provided by other databases that offer transactional capabilities. We used the FramaC and Why3 platforms to validate the transactional protocols for MongoDB. Our work focused on MongoDB version 5.0, but we believe that our approach can be applied to earlier versions of the database. Our contributions include available pseudocode and specifications for MongoDB's transactional protocols, as well as a brief guide to implementing the CoSP framework for verifying these protocols. We successfully applied our approach to the Amazon DocumentDB database, a fully managed document-oriented database that supports transactions similar to MongoDB. This analysis shows the positivity of specific coefficients and confirms $e$-positivity for an expanded class of these functions, beyond a particular instance explored in Cho-Huh (2019). Moreover, our analysis provides a new perspective on the positivity of certain elementary symmetric function coefficients in the context of the inverse of the Kostka matrix. We also identify a subarray of the inverse Kostka matrix that takes a simplified form, consisting of a diagonal with increments of one, surrounded by two layers of imaginary Os. This subarray has a meaningful interpretation related to the number of nodes in a class of weighted directed acyclic graphs (DAGs). We further explore this relation and validate the positivity of the coefficients in question through an alternative approach using the structure of weighted DAGs. Additionally, we propose a conjectural $e$-positivity expansion for the chromatic symmetric functions of Dyck paths with a bounce number of four, supported by computational evidence. We also outline a potential connection to the Lascoux-Schutzenberger (1981) result on the relation between the inverse of the Kostka matrix and the structure coefficients of the power sum basis in the algebra of symmetric functions. Furthermore, we explore a link between the weighted nodes in a particular class of weighted DAGs and the partition function, which may be useful for extending our findings to other cases. We provide a methodology for an analytical extension of our results to weighted DAGs based on a specific rule, and we demonstrate the applicability of this methodology to certain special cases, including the well-known instance of the M\"obius function. Research on intricate systems from the human brain to social connections has uncovered a higher-level structure that can be characterized through aggregates of interconnected triangles. To uncover these concealed geometric patterns, researchers are using topological methods and advanced graph theory to analyze and study dynamic processes occurring within these complex networks. This study leverages a recently developed model for triangle-based network assembly, where nanoscale triangular structures undergo spin reversal due to magnetic forces between connected nodes, fostering geometric frustration that drives novel phenomena in condensed matter physics. By manipulating the model's parameters, researchers observe how the shift from pair-based to triangular interactions affects ordering patterns, influencing the shape of resulting hysteresis loops. Moreover, the associated noise exhibited robust indicators of self-organization criticality, an emergent property solely induced by the intricate geometry of the network and not any inherent disorder. Consequently, this study demonstrates the practical utility of modeling networks as triangular structures in the context of spin reversal, offering a microcosmic representation of complex networks' hidden geometry and dynamics that underlie various intricate systems. Therefore, this approach can be applied to a broad range of phenomena, from magnetic interactions in social groups to electrical currents in neural systems. Ultimately, this research highlights the practical value of triangle-based network models, revealing hidden patterns and dynamic processes in complex networks, and shedding light on fundamental issues in condensed matter physics, such as geometric frustration and quantum annealing. Lastly, this study's findings are published in the journal Physical Review Research.

We studied the solar wind energy flux near the inner edge of our solar system using data from four different close approaches to the sun by the Parker Solar Probe, where we recorded data for 12-day periods right around each encounter. These observations took place as close as 27.8 times the radius of the sun from the solar center, and we based our energy flux calculations on readings for electron density, temperature, and speed, along with the bulk characteristics of solar protons. Combining the data from the four approaches, we found the average energy flux that could reach the solar surface and counteract gravity is about 70 Watts per square meter, plus or minus 14 Watts. Notably, this is similar to the findings of other researchers using data from different spacecraft and covering a longer time period, but with a key difference being that the solar wind energy distributions were much more symmetrical and normally distributed than seen closer to the Earth, likely due to the influence of solar plasma fluctuations being limited by the close distance. Furthermore, the relationship between energy flux and distance from the solar surface as a power law held true with a high degree of accuracy, with an exponent of 1.20, and we also determined the time periods in which the energy flux declined significantly in response to changing solar activity, finding this to happen about 10 to 20 days after each approach. This knowledge, in turn, helps us better understand the mechanisms that regulate solar wind formation and the stability of the inner solar atmosphere, as well as influencing the rate at which energy is generated and released from the sun. Moreover, it provides a foundation for predicting the energy flux in subsequent approaches based on previous data, and offers insights into the efficacy of various solar wind models by comparing the energy flux distributions derived from these simulations with our observed data. This finding also highlights the significance of continued data collection from the Parker Solar Probe, as well as other missions planned for similar close approaches to the sun, as it enables even more comprehensive and detailed analyses of the inner solar atmosphere and the solar wind. Lastly, we include a preliminary estimate for the rate at which energy is generated within the sun, based on the energy flux that reaches the surface and the density of solar mass losses, finding this to be approximately 6.8 x 10 to the 26 Watts. This, in turn, helps us understand the relationship between the rate at which energy is released from the sun and the resulting solar and stellar mass losses. Thanks to speech-emotion recognition technology, computers can engage with people on a more emotional level. Nonetheless, the accuracy of speech-emotion recognition in real-world situations remains an area of improvement. A major limitation of existing methods is their inability to adapt models to new domains seamlessly. In response, researchers have developed innovative domain adaptation techniques that transfer knowledge across domains, yielding significant improvements. While these advancements are promising, there is still room for growth in adapting models to real-time, live data scenarios. A deep reinforcement learning-based strategy is presented here to adapt a pre-trained model in real-time while interacting with its environment. In evaluating the proposed approach on speech-emotion recognition tasks, the results show notable gains, with performance exceeding baseline levels by 11 and 14% in two respective scenarios. The code is available at https://github.com/ghru/Domain-Adaping-SER. The proposed technique has vast potential applications extending beyond speech-emotion recognition tasks. The paper titled Domain Adapting Deep Reinforcement Learning for Real-world Speech Emotion Recognition was recently published in the proceedings of the IEEE International Conference on Acoustics, Speech, and Signal Processing (ICASSP). Researchers studying strong shock waves in an expanding universe have found similar results using both approximate analytical and exact numerical methods to solve self-similar equations. When the adiabatic index lies between one and approximately 1.16, these solutions consistently occupy all space without gaps, showing close alignment with each other. As the index surpasses this threshold, pressure drops to zero at a finite distance from the origin, and in both scenarios, a spherical void forms. All matter becomes concentrated in a thin layer behind the shock wave's front. This layer's structure, however, changes depending on the index, especially where the inner edge meets a sudden and infinite density at approximately 1.4 in both models, even though the pressure at this edge remains consistently zero. This behavior is notable as it contrasts with the commonly accepted result of a shock wave's structure, which is often seen as infinite in density. This research also offers a novel perspective on the universe's current state, suggesting that it could be composed of multiple isolated regions. This is because strong shock waves, which are seen in many astrophysical contexts, including supernovae and active galactic nuclei, tend to form closed and self-contained patterns, rather than expanding into the surrounding environment. This occurs because their inner edges, where the matter's density becomes extremely high, do not necessarily mean they must extend infinitely and cannot form a boundary around itself. This is particularly evident in cases where the universe has a finite age, as it displays a void in the center, surrounded by a layer similar to the structure found at the shock front of a self-similar solution. This is similar to the structure observed in some binary mergers, specifically neutron star mergers, which also form a black hole and a hot cloud of particles, and may provide valuable insights for future direct detection mergers, which will be more sensitive to these inner boundary surfaces and can detect the presence of a void in the center of the universe. This research was conducted to examine the relationship between closed and open shock waves in an expanding universe, and to explore the possible formation of a spherical void in the center of the universe, which could have significant implications for astrophysical contexts. This could be achieved by using a self-similar solution for a closed shock wave, which can be transformed into an open shock wave by increasing the distance from the origin, and by analyzing the relationship between the adiabatic index and the width of the shock layer, which changes from a thin layer to a dense curve at a critical index of approximately 1.

The Yang-Mills-aether theory is analyzed to understand the implications of introducing non-abelian aether-like terms that violate Lorentz symmetry, specifically within thermal quantum field theory. By incorporating temperature effects and spatial compactification via Thermofield Dynamics, corrections to the non-abelian Stefan-Boltzmann law and non-abelian Casimir energy and pressure are calculated for both zero and finite temperatures. However, it is found that the violation of Lorentz invariance results in an irremediable issue with thermal renormalizability. Consequently, thermal renormalization group equations are derived to analyze the temperature and scale behavior of the theory's parameters. The analysis indicates that the violation of Lorentz invariance is linked to the breakdown of thermal renormalizability, thereby highlighting the necessity for Lorentz invariance to be an intrinsic feature of thermal quantum field theory. The proposed approach can also be applied to non-abelian vector-aether-like terms and extends the previously studied non-abelian vector-aether-like case. Initially, a standard unit hedging cost is established and subsequently, the total hedging cost is determined as the product of this unit cost, stock price, a supply curve factor, and the square of the number of options. Consequently, this formulation enables faster computation of expected hedging costs than alternative Monte Carlo methods. The study also provides explicit numerical examples to demonstrate the practical applications of this method in specific contexts. The formula in question can be utilized within various risk management frameworks, including risk dashboard creation, regulatory capital calculations, and option pricing models. In 2015, CERN introduced "Emittance Scans," a new fast luminosity separation scanning method at the Large Hadron Collider. These scans were consistently carried out during physics production runs, utilizing full-intensity beams at the CMS experiment's interaction point. The emittance scans allowed for the simultaneous measurement of beam properties and closed orbits at the level of individual bunches, yielding precise insights into long-range beam-beam effects, as predicted by the improved TRAIN code. The code successfully reproduced the complex pattern of beam losses and charge neutralization observed in the scans, demonstrating accurate prediction capabilities. The code's effectiveness in predicting beam loss patterns and underlying physics at 6.5 TeV collisions has been particularly demonstrated, thereby enabling efficient future beam filling strategies. The analysis of scan data of various types has been enabled by the code, incorporating recent TRAIN capabilities, and the results concisely presented here. The implementation of emittance scans at the CMS experiment required the development of an automated data acquisition procedure, resulting in approximately 300 scans carried out throughout the run period, with the majority being "Nominal Scans." The analysis of Nominal Scans, which measured beam properties at the level of individual bunches, revealed a small level of transverse motion within bunches, amounting to 4.0 ± 1.0 mm, alongside significant charge distribution across the beam, affecting fill patterns. The study of cosmic microwave background anisotropies is a fundamental tool in physical cosmology research. However, the signal's weakness necessitates sophisticated and highly sensitive experiments that observe the sky across various frequencies with thousands of polarisation-sensitive detectors. As such experiments become increasingly sensitive, they are susceptible to being limited by instrumental systematic effects when trying to fully utilise their data. This paper presents a Python tool,'s4cmb', which generates simulated raw data streams in the time domain for contemporary cosmic microwave background experiments based on bolometric technology. The package also incorporates realistic instrumental systematic effects into the simulated data, with the goal of helping researchers assess the impact of such effects on actual data, informing future instrument design, and making simulated data sets more realistic for the development of accurate data analysis techniques. The package is particularly suitable for large-scale simulations required by modern cosmic microwave background experiments. The tool's capabilities are applied to a representative experiment whose instrumental response is detailed in some depth. The resulting simulated data, including both signal and random noise components, is available for actual experiments via a dedicated website. In the task of arranging unordered words into a meaningful order, prior approaches rely on either linear models or neural networks, without examining the role of pre-trained language models, including why they would be beneficial. Utilizing BART as an example, we find it to be a suitable model for this task and explore its capabilities by conducting additional analysis using probing, which reveals that the syntactic dependencies inherent to BART significantly contribute to its performance. Furthermore, we discover improvements in using BART in a related task known as partial tree linearization. Our research highlights the importance of considering intrinsic properties of language models and providing a theoretical framework explaining their success in word ordering. Moreover, we show that supervised models can achieve high accuracy in certain situations, such as word ordering within partial tree linearization. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghruvo/word-ordering.

The rapid dissemination of ultra-realistic media over social platforms necessitates the immediate development of an efficient and adaptable technique for identifying deepfakes. Deepfake creation methods inadvertently leave distinguishing patterns in the frequency spectra of fabricated images and videos. Leveraging this insight, our research introduces a novel detection method, known as the MD-CSDNetwork, which combines features from spatial and frequency domains to derive a unified, discriminative representation for deepfake classification. The proposed network architecture, comprising two parallel branches processing spatial and frequency information, is designed to treat multiple domain inputs as interconnected learning signals. Through cross-stitch connections between the branches, our system automatically identifies an optimal blend of domain-specific and shared features, thereby enhancing performance and generalization. Evaluations conducted on the widely-used FaceForeniscs++ benchmark demonstrate improved classification results for various manipulation types and comparable performance to state-of-the-art approaches on the Celeb-DF and Deepfake Detection Dataset. Our system's versatility allows easy integration into standard pipelines without significant computational overhead, making the MD-CSDNetwork suitable for real-world deepfake detection applications. Our code has been made publicly available at https://github.com/ghru/MD-CSDNetwork.

Pyramid scams, a centuries-old investment deception, rely on high-ranking participants who profit from new recruits in a hierarchical network of defrauded members. Due to the hidden nature of transactions among participants, a comprehensive examination of these schemes has been unfeasible until now. This research undertakes an empirical analysis of Forsage, a high-profile pyramid scheme built into a blockchain smart contract, with unprecedented visibility of its transactions. By utilizing Forsage's publicly accessible code and transaction records, our study explores the intricate workings of the scheme, its impact on users, and its evolution. Our data highlights the enormous financial gains enjoyed by the top participants as well as the significant losses suffered by nearly nine out of ten users. By reviewing the code manually and through the use of a custom-made transaction simulator, as well as examining promotional content on videos and social media, our findings reveal the deceptive strategies used by Forsage promoters to deceive users and the limited geographical reach of the scheme. Our data coverage spans from the launch of the scheme in April 2020 until the end of December 2021, a period during which the scheme distributed approximately $321 million in profits to its participants. Our study sheds light on the innovative ways Forsage promoters exploited linguistic ambiguities and cryptic blockchain transactions, as well as the way the scheme's operators evaded regulatory oversight, allowed anonymous participation, and used complex hierarchical networking, all of which contributed to its survival and massive profits. Our analysis concludes by examining the challenges faced in attempting to prohibit such schemes and the difficulties encountered in trying to hold individuals accountable for participating in a pyramid scam. Our research includes an open-source simulator that allows for a deeper examination of the scheme's code and transactions. Our study's findings have implications for various audiences, including blockchain platform providers, financial regulatory agencies, as well as computer science and social science researchers. Our data and analysis are available at the following url: https://forsage-solidity.net/

The catalog of the Milky Way's globular clusters remains incomplete. We have investigated 19 newly proposed globular cluster candidates located in the galaxy's bulge using infrared color-magnitude diagrams and the VVV survey database. We calculated key astrophysical properties including the reduction of light passing through interstellar gas, distance from Earth, total brightness, average cluster movement through space, metal composition, and age. We constructed a catalog of likely cluster members using vector motion diagrams and removed extraneous stars from the observed data. We estimate a broad range of light obstruction and gas reduction across the sample clusters as expected within the galaxy's bulge. We calculated their distances from Earth as being between 6.8 to 11.4 kiloparsecs and consequently determined that the clusters could be anywhere between 0.56 to 3.25 kiloparsecs from the galaxy's center. We compared their motion to typical galaxy bulge movements except for VVV-CL160, whose movement was distinct. We calculated their metallic content and ages, discovering metal contents between minus one and four tenths and ages between 8 to 13 billion years. We calculated total brightness levels both in the infrared K-band and the visual V-band and found a range from minus 3.4 to minus 7.5 in visual brightness levels. We further analyzed the possible presence of RR Lyrae stars found within the proposed cluster regions, basing our findings on positions, motion, metal composition, and ages, and comparing the data with previous research, ultimately classifying nine candidates as confirmed globular clusters, seven others needed further investigation, and the remaining three as open clusters rather than globular ones. A key finding reveals that networks comprising a single type of tensor and possessing erasure correction capabilities can't simultaneously possess certain desirable traits - those that facilitate the efficient calculation of physical properties through a local process and those necessary for an accurate representation of power-law behaviors in data.
