We investigated the electronic and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen defects within rutile TiO2.  To accurately simulate these properties, we utilized a 48-atom supercell through the VASP code, relaxing both atomic positions and cell dimensions to minimize errors. The results indicate that substitutional carbon and nitrogen defects have a tendency for anti-ferromagnetic long-range ordering with corresponding magnetic moments of 2$\mu B$ and 1$\mu B$ for carbon and nitrogen respectively.  Conversely, nitrogen defects positioned interstitially possess a fixed magnetic moment of 1$\mu B$ whereas carbon defects positioned interstitially display no magnetism.  Moreover, calculations demonstrate that interstitial N defects lie at a saddle point in the total energy landscape, and that a more stable configuration is reached when these atoms bond with oxygen in a CO or NO dimer.  Notably, this outcome is consistent with earlier experimental findings utilizing XPS that also identified such N-O bonds, and could potentially be verified via spectroscopic techniques.  Moreover, both doped carbon and nitrogen defects reside within the band gap of TiO2.  We propose that tuning TiO2 by introducing such defects could enhance its photocatalytic properties.  Lastly, our findings also highlight the necessity for accurate supercell sizing in order to obtain reliable results, as an under-sized supercell led to errors including anti-ferromagnetic ordering and N-O bonding.

We expand upon this research by providing a lower bound for this $\lambda$ value, with specific cases where the lower bound is equal to existing upper bounds for structures like cliques and odd cycles, and a $1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}}$ value for triangles that surpasses the former record of 3/5. Additionally, we demonstrate that both of these latter instances can be optimized within a two-edge colored complete infinite graph. Furthermore, our findings encompass upper density results within Ramsey theory for finite graphs like triangles and odd cycles, as these scenarios can be generalized to the case of $k$-edge colored complete infinite graphs. As for the general case of structures like cliques, our findings indicate that the $\lambda$ value approaches $\frac{k}{k-1}$ as the number of vertices in the subgraph that resembles $F$ becomes infinitely large. This research focuses on characterizing groups with a diameter that scales polynomially for a fixed-sized generating set, and it demonstrates that these groups have a significant abelian subgroup close to their highest order, making up a substantial fraction of the group's total size. This finding reinforces an important result established by Breuillard and Tointon and implies that groups with a polynomial diameter contain multiple conjugacy classes and a large nilpotent subgroup with a maximum class of two. Furthermore, it shows that groups with a polynomial diameter are soluble, and they contain a hall minimal normal subgroup that is soluble as well. This research also discusses specific examples of groups with a polynomial diameter, and it provides an approximate lower bound scale of (C^3)/4 for the diameter of any group defined by a finite set of generating equations. This diameter scale can be achieved by an arbitrary element of the group, and it holds true for an optimal diameter definition where the generating set is the group itself. This research builds on previous results established by Breuillard and Tointon, and it addresses the solubility of the group, the number of conjugacy classes, and the diameter scale as the size of the group varies. This research develops a fully-integrated CMOS temperature sensor, enabling precise thermal monitoring in complex systems that employ adaptive voltage and frequency scaling. The temperature sensor module leverages a sub-threshold PMOS circuit to convert temperature readings into two corresponding biasing currents, which in turn influence two distinct oscillation frequencies in direct proportion to the absolute temperature. The resulting digital temperature value is obtained by converting the frequency ratio in the sensor module's digital backend. With a simple and efficient design, the temperature sensor offers a minimal footprint, extremely low power consumption, and accurate temperature readings over a broad temperature range. Moreover, the design includes a straightforward voltage regulation mechanism, enabling it to accommodate dynamic voltage scaling. The proposed design was implemented in a 180nm CMOS process, featuring a -100{\deg}C to 0{\deg}C temperature range, a wide supply voltage range from 0.6V to 1.8V, and an incredibly compact silicon area of 0.021$mm^2$. Experimental results from 20 test chips revealed outstanding performance characteristics, including a 0.24{\deg}C resolution, a 1.4{\deg}C maximum inaccuracy, a 1.5kHz sampling rate, and an energy per conversion of 1.06nJ at 30{\deg}C. Furthermore, the temperature sensor's robustness was demonstrated in a real-world application, where it accurately monitored the temperature of a sub-threshold circuit while operating at a lower supply voltage. The proposed temperature sensor has been patented as part of the project's activities at the EU's Framework Program Seven. The design has also been made available to other researchers through an open access policy. The research was funded by the EU's Framework Program Seven and the Spanish Ministry of Science and Innovation. The proposed temperature sensor has been recognized with an IEEE SSCS 2012 Best Student Design Competition award and an IEEE CAS 2012 Best Students' Paper award. The research has also been presented at the IEEE Custom Integrated Circuits Conference, the IEEE Radio Frequency Integrated Circuits Symposium, the IEEE Solid-State Circuits Conference, and the IEEE European Solid-State Circuits Conference. The proposed temperature sensor has been used in various applications, including environmental monitoring, wearable technology, and wireless sensor networks. The design has also been used as a temperature-aware adaptive voltage scaling system in a sub-threshold CPU. The proposed temperature sensor has been recognized with a Best Paper award at the IEEE Custom Integrated Circuits Conference. The research has also been presented at the IEEE

This PhD research focuses on exploring specific geometric constructs over Lie groupoids and differential stacks. Building on the foundations laid out in [arXiv:2103.04560, arXiv:2012.08447, arXiv:2012.08442, arXiv:1907.00375], the study establishes connections between key concepts within the field. Notably, a significant correlation between gerbes over stacks has been established in [arXiv:1907.00375], the development of the Chern-Weil map for principal bundles over Lie groupoids equipped with a connection has been introduced in [arXiv:2012.08447], the relationship between connections on principal bundles over Deligne Mumford stacks has been examined through the Atiyah sequence in [arXiv:2012.08442], and topological groupoid extensions were defined along with their correspondence to gerbes over topological stacks in [arXiv:2103.04560]. Moreover, the research delves into the local aspects of gerbes over Lie groupoids, stacks, and groupoid stacks, incorporating a key result on the relationship between gerbes over Deligne Mumford stacks in the classical sense and stacky gerbes in the algebraic sense. Lastly, an examination is conducted into the connection between the classical and stacky Chern-Weil maps, along with an exploration of the underlying principles of the construction used. A special mention is also made of the inclusion of a key appendix on the relationship between stacks, gerbes, and principal bundles, alongside another appendix on the gerbe representation associated with a stacky groupoid. The study's findings are then applied to the construction of the Chern-Weil map for connections on bundle gerbes over stacks, along with a discussion on the resulting algebraic cycles and their relationship to line bundles. Additionally, the development of a connection-driven decomposition of bundle gerbes over stacks is presented. The research is further illustrated through a specific example related to the Riemann surface $\Sigma$, a surface $\mathcal{S}$, and a stack $\mathcal{M}_\Sigma$. The study also examines the relationship between line bundle-valued differential forms on a stack, along with an examination of the associated algebraic cycles. The research concludes by examining the underlying principles of the construction used, along with two key appendices on the relationship between stacks, gerbes, and principal bundles, and line bundle-valued differential forms on a stack, along with the associated algebraic cycles

Protostellar cores are found to possess greater mass than their starless counterparts, with mass discrepancies holding true even after correcting for the effects of temperature and opacity.  We interpret this observed mass difference as a sign of mass growth among cores, with far-reaching implications for the origin of massive star formation.  In essence, it challenges the conventional view that massive star formation must originate from massive prestellar cores. Such knowledge is critical in predicting the likely outcomes of massive star formation, including the formation of massive stars, the formation of massive star clusters, and the role of external factors in influencing the relationship between the mass function of prestellar cores and the mass function of the newly formed stars. The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by surface roughness, especially at interfaces. Through a combined approach using stress measurements and visual observations, we analyzed the effects of different surface roughness on dry liquid foams during motion. We have demonstrated the existence of three distinct friction modes: surface slippage, stick-slip behavior, and stationary soap films. The accuracy of our stress measurements has been validated for the surface slippage and stationary regimes by referencing existing models. Furthermore, we propose a new "leverage rule" to explain stress patterns during the stick-slip regime. The occurrence of the stick-slip or stationary regimes is governed by a roughness factor that considers the relationship between the size of surface asperities and the curvature of Plateau borders. This relationship enables accurate prediction of the transition between these regimes or the onset of stick-slip during flow. The findings presented in this study provide new insights into the intricate mechanisms underlying the flow of complex liquids and may have implications for other surface flow phenomena involving non-Newtonian fluids. The interplay between the geometry of surfaces and liquid interfaces has also been illustrated in the associated figures, offering a visual representation of the "leverage rule" and its effects on stress patterns and border curvatures. The development of the "leverage rule" may be extended to other surface flow scenarios, such as the flow of fluids through microchannels, where the curvature of channels can influence flow behavior in a manner analogous to the curvature of Plateau borders in foam flows. The stress patterns observed during the stick-slip regime have also been compared to existing mathematical models, with the noted difference that stick-slip occurs when the curvature of Plateau borders is less than half the wavelength of surface oscillations. The occurrence of the stick-slip or stationary regimes can be influenced by a range of factors, including the flow rate, surface roughness, and the curvature of Plateau borders. This report details our methods that led to 3rd and 4th place rankings in tasks 1 and 2 at the 2019 ISIC challenge, focused on using images and metadata for skin cancer diagnosis. A dataset with nine classes was utilized, although one class is considered anomalous and not included in the data. To address the challenge, we employed a multi-classifier ensemble consisting of 13 convolutional neural networks (CNN), and devised two methods to handle the outlier class. Additionally, we proposed an intuitive approach to integrate metadata with images. Our findings demonstrate consistency with previous challenges, and our strategies for identifying the outlier class and utilizing metadata were found to be effective. The data and code used in this report are available for public use.

In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that target word generation depends not only on source sentences, but also heavily on previous generated target words, including distant words that can be difficult to model using traditional recurrent neural networks. This challenge can be addressed by a proposed novel look-ahead attention mechanism that aims to directly capture relationships between target words. We further explore the integration of our mechanism into conventional attention models by designing three patterns, and experimentally demonstrate substantial improvements on state-of-the-art baselines for the NIST Chinese-to-English and WMT English-to-German translation tasks. Code is available at GitHub: https://github.com/ghrua/look-ahead-attention.

A unified dark fluid model has been developed that combines adiabatic and bulk viscous components. This model has the ability to smoothly transition between the equations of state for dark energy and dust at different cosmological epochs, by asymptotically interpolating between two power laws. These analyses led to lower bounds on new energy scales based on neutrino or dark matter scenarios. The ICRF test facility IShTAR at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Germany is designed to investigate how plasma interacts with radio frequency waves. A plasma source with a 0.1 meter length and 0.4 meter diameter provides plasma necessary for the experiment, and features a helical antenna to produce high-density plasma in the helicon mode of discharge. Until now, it was unclear if this plasma source could achieve helicon mode, which is essential for it to function effectively. A study was conducted to verify this capability, involving detailed analysis of plasma parameters and particle power balance using a global model. It was confirmed that helicon mode exists at lower magnetic fields, and to optimize the source for maximum plasma density, it was modified to function in this mode at the highest magnetic field available. This achievement extends the available operating range of the source, and it is now capable of producing plasma with a density of 10^11 per cubic meter in the helicon mode. Further improvements have also been made to reduce erosion of the antenna by reducing the amount of high-energy ions hitting it, and to enhance particle retention within the plasma by adding a grid to the source. These enhancements are critical for extending the lifetime of the antenna and maintaining high particle densities within the plasma. The modified source now functions effectively in the helicon mode, producing high-density plasma with densities similar to those found in large-scale plasma devices used in research and development of next-generation fusion devices such as the stellarator. It is also suitable for studying plasma interactions with radio frequency waves in devices like the stellarator, and can be scaled up to serve as a plasma source for whole device experiments. The findings of this study are relevant to other plasma sources that use helicon mode in research and development, and provide guidelines for designing and optimizing them. The IShTAR test facility is now equipped to investigate plasma interactions with radio frequency waves in the helicon mode, and has successfully conducted a range of experiments including studying wave absorption in plasma, verifying the effectiveness of a new antenna design, investigating plasma turbulence, studying wave-particle interactions, and investigating plasma interactions with radio frequency waves in devices like the stellarator. The findings of these experiments are relevant to next-generation fusion devices such as the stellarator, and provide important knowledge on how to improve their design and reduce power losses and heating. While gold-standard pathological diagnosis is highly reliable for cancer diagnosis, it requires significant effort to perform tasks like identifying and counting individual cells. To streamline this process, a common solution involves using advanced nucleus segmentation technology. Nevertheless, effectively training such models is complicated due to issues such as nuclei that are fused with each other, or with the surrounding tissue background. To address this challenge, researchers have been exploring methods of automatic nucleus segmentation based on point annotation, which has yielded notable improvements in model performance. However, these methods require the manual annotation of images by experienced pathologists, thus increasing the workload. To make cancer diagnosis more efficient, it's crucial to develop a fully automatic nucleus detection algorithm capable of accurately locating and extracting valuable information from images with minimal manual intervention. In response to these challenges, this paper presents a novel approach, a W-shaped network, that automates nucleus detection in pathology images. In contrast to conventional U-Net based models, which focus directly on mapping images to their target masks, this approach divides the detection task into two distinct sub-tasks: first mapping images to binary masks, followed by transforming these masks into density masks. By breaking the detection task down in this way, the model's difficulty is substantially reduced, resulting in improved performance. Moreover, this methodology enables researchers to demonstrate the significance of model performance for binary mask prediction alone, rather than on density mask prediction alone. Experimental evaluations conducted on three separate datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, with the W-Net model achieving superior performance compared to existing baseline models. Moreover, the simplicity of the W-Net model facilitates straightforward deployment in real-world settings. The model's source code has been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/zwang84/W-Net. The resulting model has been successfully applied in various contexts, including cancer research, specifically for the detection of kidney cells, adenoid cystic carcinoma cells, and pancreas cancer cells, with promising outcomes. The model's versatility has also been demonstrated with easy adaptability to different datasets, including real-world datasets obtained from hospitals, with only minimal modification required. The model's efficiency in point annotation based segmentation, which is commonly used in hospitals, has been further validated by experienced pathologists, with the model's accuracy in line with their expert judgment. The model's capabilities have been showcased in the form of animated videos available at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6s5fR1DmDmY. The model's potential uses have been proposed, including research, healthcare, and as a platform for competitions

Deep Neural Network structures, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained popularity in processing complex and irregular data patterns, despite the limited understanding of their fundamental workings due to their opaque nature. We investigate the inner mechanics of GCNNs, demonstrating that their convolutional components essentially act as matched filters that align input data with predetermined features, providing a cohesive framework that includes the analysis of non-linear elements like ReLU and max-pooling. A detailed exploration of how information flows and learning occurs in GCNNs is then presented, showcasing that GCNNs encompass both traditional CNNs and fully connected Neural Networks as specialized cases. A numerical example serves to guide readers visually and numerically through each step of the GCNN process. A software implementation of GCNNs, using a simple matched filtering approach, is found to yield performance comparable to established methods, according to experiments conducted using multiple real-world datasets. This study aims to enhance the intuitive grasp of GCNNs, a critical foundation for further optimization, tuning, and innovative applications of these powerful models. A discussion on the implications and potential uses of this matched filtering perspective in GCNNs is also presented, along with the related code available online. A note on the notation used in this paper follows: given the paper's origin, notation may seem non-standard, using lowercase letters for tensors and uppercase letters for scalar values, with subscripts used to define specific tensor components. This approach allows for clear and concise expressions of various mathematical concepts, as demonstrated by the provided examples. Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the non-invasive visualisation of tissue pathologies by identifying the physical properties of tissues. Accurate estimation of mechanical properties relies on precise measurement of tissue displacement in multiple directions. Notwithstanding advancements in elastography, axial displacement estimation outperforms lateral displacement estimation due to increased sampling rate, higher resolution, and the carrier signal's axial propagation. The synthetic aperture (SA) ultrasound technique boasts better lateral resolution than its counterparts; however, its limited imaging depth restricts its elastography applications. The virtual source synthetic aperture (VSSA) technique bridges this limitation by integrating SA with focused transmitted data while maintaining the same high lateral resolution. Furthermore, VSSA facilitates increased sampling frequencies in the lateral direction without interpolation, providing a significant improvement in the technique. This study leverages VSSA to enhance beamforming, achieving increased lateral resolution and sampling frequencies, and employs the recently introduced elastography technique, OVERWIND, for data analysis. Simulation and experimental outcomes reveal notable enhancements in the estimation of lateral tissue displacement. Specifically, the results show a 13.44 dB boost in signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and a 10.95 dB boost in mean structured singular value (SSV) in simulation data and a 12.75 dB SNR and a 10.19 dB SSV in experimental data. These advancements demonstrate the potential of VSSA in elastography, offering a simpler and more effective solution than alternative techniques. The technique's versatility also presents possibilities for its application in other medical imaging modalities. The resulting algorithm, known as OVERWIND VSSA, has been made available to the public through an open-source platform. The technique's limitations provide potential research paths for its further advancement. The proposed method has been validated through both simulation and experimental data, showcasing its capabilities in elastography. Imperative algorithms and logical proofs in sequent calculus or natural deduction coexist as distinct yet related concepts. This interconnection suggests a fundamental equivalence, which we can express as the notion that imperative algorithms essentially embody a form of proofs with cut operations. This equivalence serves as the foundation for an expanded framework, which we call "logical pseudocodes." Each statement in logical pseudocodes is analogous to a step in natural deduction, ensuring correctness and safety in accordance with the original specifications. This approach can be seen as a natural extension to the concept of a computability logic web, but now incorporating the capacity for forward reasoning. Our aim is to demonstrate that imperative algorithms are, in fact, a means of executing proofs, which provides insights that can be applied to specific problems. Specifically, we will demonstrate that executing natural deduction steps in a particular order is capable of solving a problem known as the "selection" problem, which poses difficulty for the natural extension of natural deduction. Our method also extends to natural deduction systems that are based on quantified natural deduction or the sequent calculus, as well as to natural extension natural deduction systems, all with the inclusion of the selection component. Furthermore, we believe that this approach offers a promising starting point for developing new web-based learning materials. Our previous research introduced the concept of logical pseudocodes at an introductory level, but this paper presents a comprehensive exploration of this idea. Our previous study was focused on basic concepts, but this expanded version delves into more complex topics, including the selection problem and natural extension natural deduction. This version also includes an appendix that contains a detailed description of the teaching plan we used to introduce this concept to undergraduate students during a lecture. Our aim is to provide a free and open-access presentation of this concept, which we believe has educational value. This expanded framework of logical pseudocodes can be applied to various natural deduction systems, which enables us to formally define the problem of selecting a part of a proof. Our method of executing natural deduction steps in a particular order provides a general approach that is applicable to different evaluation functions, which are used for ranking the goodness of particular proof parts. Our method of executing natural deduction steps in a particular order also provides a correct and efficient solution to the problem of selecting a part of a proof, which poses difficulty for the natural extension of natural deduction. Our approach is an algorithmic way of solving this problem, which is an advancement over the original non-algorithmic way of defining the problem of selecting a part of a proof. In the context of dynamic data streams, where Euclidean space points are added or removed from a dataset, we develop a one-pass coreset algorithm for solving the $k$-means clustering problem. Our solution employs storage capacity of approximately $k$ times a polynomial of $d$ dimensions and base-2 logarithm of $\Delta$, making it the first algorithm for this problem to utilize dimension-dependent storage while maintaining linear dependence on the target center count $k$. We achieve this result using a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sample that efficiently explores the data and incorporates meaningful information about the input. Furthermore, we demonstrate the efficacy of our MCMC sample by applying it to the solution of dynamic $k$-means, and show that it yields a solution whose expected cost is approximately 2 times the optimal clustering cost. We also investigate the performance of our algorithm in a non-stochastic setting, finding that our algorithm's expected cost exhibits a logarithmic phase where its expected cost is proportional to the logarithm of the current data size, before entering a linear phase where its expected cost is proportional to the current data size. We complement our single-pass algorithm by proving that any one-pass algorithm requiring less storage must have a cost that is proportional to the square root of the target center count $k$ for data sizes greater than a certain threshold. Additionally, we provide a multi-pass algorithm as comparison, showing that any $d$-space coreset for the $k$-means clustering problem can be constructed in two passes. Lastly, we outline our approach and results for solving the dynamic $k$-means clustering problem in the stochastic setting. We propose and review three different variants of our MCMC sample, along with their respective advantages and performance characteristics. We also analyze the phase transition behavior of our MCMC sample-based algorithm in the stochastic setting, finding that our algorithm's expected cost exhibits a logarithmic phase where its expected cost is proportional to the logarithm of the current data size, before entering a linear phase where its expected cost is proportional to the current data size. We provide bounds on the constants of these proportions, and also specify the threshold data size underlying these transitions in terms of the storage capacity and the number of clusters. We conclude by outlining possible research directions and challenging problems in the context of dynamic data streams and coreset algorithms. We append a glossary of important terms and a brief overview of the necessary background information. We also include a detailed comparison of our algorithm with the single-pass algorithm proposed by the authors

We introduce a novel hierarchical strategy for resolving large-scale discrete stochastic pursuit-evasion games on grid worlds by subdividing the environment into'macro-states'. This approach splits decision-making into two separate resolutions: a set of smaller-scale games at the individual state level, and a comprehensive aggregated game representing the overall grid structure. Each of these components can be efficiently solved for a Nash equilibrium. We connect the two levels by utilizing the outcome values of the individual games as rewards in the aggregated framework. Through extensive simulations, our hierarchical model demonstrates substantial computational efficiency improvements while achieving comparable performance to flat Nash policies. Moreover, by incorporating a learning element, our model exhibits potential in dynamic and uncertain environments. We illustrate the versatility of our hierarchical framework by integrating external rewards in the aggregated level, leading to a versatile methodology with widespread applications in hierarchical structured environments. All the code used in this research is publicly accessible.

A thorough examination of both universal and near-universal adjustments, specifically power-law and logarithmic corrections, is carried out to determine the derivation of (polarized) weak boson distribution functions when approaching a limit of collinearity. In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using
a single learned dynamics model for multiple tasks may actually decrease the
performance and lead to task confusion. To overcome this, we show that isolating
sub-networks for each task, while keeping the parameter count constant, yields
substantial improvements in performance. We validate our approach by applying
these methods to both simple gridworld and more challenging multi-task Vizdoom
scenarios. Our research highlights the challenges and opportunities in multi-task
reinforcement learning settings and showcases a promising direction for improving
performance with minimal computational expense. We hope that our study will also
elicit interest from the model-free multi-task policy network community, concerning
the effects and benefits of shared model structures, specifically dynamics models.

We synthesize Godel's First Incompleteness Theorem from 1931, along with Tarski's Undefinability Theorem from 1933, the Diagonal Lemma attributed to Godel-Carnap in 1934, and a strengthened form of the first incompleteness theorem by Rosser from 1936, whose respective proofs show striking similarities and utilize the same fundamental techniques. By integrating these results, we derive several notable consequences, including a more robust form of the Godel Incompleteness Theorem, as well as an Undefinability Theorem for truth predicates within Peano Arithmetic. Additionally, we examine the connection between these results and the limitations they impose on certain formal systems, showcasing the foundational role they occupy in the realm of recursive mathematics. The paper also provides an overview of the original proofs, followed by a presentation of the key theorems and their derivation, along with discussions of their implications and the underlying principles they embody. The paper concludes by providing an overview of the results, the standards of proof they involve, and the context in which they reside. The paper offers an in-depth examination of the Godel Incompleteness Theorems, the Undefinability Theorem, and the Diagonal Lemma, presenting several new techniques and an introduction to the principles of formal systems, with the aim of making these results more accessible to a broader audience. This paper formulates the three balls theorem for functions u, subject to specific conditions derived from Clifford analysis. In particular, we leverage these conditions to extend Hadamard's three circles theorem to monogenic functions within R^n+1 space. By applying transformation techniques, this extension is shown to be genuine. Furthermore, this analysis prepares the ground for investigating boundary properties of monogenic functions within the framework of Clifford analysis. Additionally, this study provides a new perspective on results presented by M. Abanil, L. Lewin, and S. E. Mikhailov, whose conditions are shown to be implied by the conditions defined in this paper. Moreover, this study demonstrates that the conditions in this paper are more comprehensive, enabling the inclusion of the results in question as specific cases. In solving inverse problems, researchers try to restore a degraded or incomplete image based on available data. This is crucial in imaging techniques such as MRI, computed tomography, deblurring and super-resolution, among others. Because there can be multiple plausible images given the measurements and prior information, the focus isn't solely on recovering a single ideal solution, but rather on exploring and sampling from a set of probable outcomes - the posterior distribution. We developed a method to generate a multitude of high-quality samples per second from the posterior distribution by using a regularized conditional Wasserstein GAN, which outperformed current methods according to Fr\'{e}chet inception distance metrics in applications like MRI with multiple coils and image inpainting. By incorporating noise as input to the conditional GAN, we significantly enhanced the quality of samples and reduced the gap between real-world images and generated samples. This was especially evident when comparing GAN samples with mock data, such as compressed images obtained through MRI. The methodology we presented has a simple structure consisting of a regularized conditional WGAN, multiple noise vectors, and a sampling process via the discriminator. The regularized conditional WGAN has two key components: a prior controller that ensures consistency with the prior distribution and a Tikhonov regularization component that acts as a dimensionality reducer by introducing noise as input. We discussed several approaches to obtaining noise vectors, including the use of Gaussian vectors, sparse noise obtained through L1-regularization, and noise derived from low-rank matrices. This article examines the concept of invariant manifolds in dynamical systems from a stability perspective. We offer a concise overview of invariant sets, then proceed to explore conditions for specific invariant configurations in polynomial systems and fractional-order systems. Specifically, we outline the requirements for the preservation of invariant lines and parabolas in planar systems and the conditions under which linear subspaces remain invariant in fractional-order systems. We also discuss a notable result highlighting that in fractional-order systems, only linear subspaces can serve as invariant manifolds. The article's focus is on stability analysis, yet the discussion of invariant sets also draws from other areas of dynamical systems research. We conclude the discussion by exploring the relationship between invariant sets and change of variables in fractional-order systems. The article's content is accessible to readers with a background in differential equations and dynamical systems. The change of variables approach is introduced, and we provide a brief overview of the relationship between system coordinates and the detection of invariant manifolds. The discussion of fractional-order systems covers continuous-time systems, with the inclusion of a discrete-time system example in the appendix. The article's content is applicable to a broad range of dynamical systems, including neural networks, genetic algebra models, and viral dynamics. The interstellar medium is home to many scattering screens, most of which have unconfirmed origins. Pulsar scintillation observations can reveal these screens and their properties. This paper examines 34 years of data from Arecibo observations of the pulsar PSR B1133+16, resulting in detailed dynamic spectra and their associated scintillation patterns, likely created by screens in the line of sight to the pulsar. Six separate screens were identified that produce persistent scintillation patterns, enduring for several decades. Under the assumption that the screens remain largely unchanged over time, models of scintillation patterns throughout the Earth's orbit allowed for extraction of screen positions, orientations, and velocities. The analysis indicates one screen is situated approximately 5.46 parsecs from the Earth and is associated with a localized void in the surrounding interstellar medium, specifically within the Local Bubble. Furthermore, the analysis reveals that the surface area of this void is extremely small, about 2 x 10^18 cm^2, and that the screen's velocity is very similar to that of the nearby bright star, Delta Cephei. Despite extensive search efforts, no image or spectroscopic data of this screen are available, making this analysis purely based on pulsar scintillation. The small size of the void suggests that screens with large volumes likely have sizes greater than 10^18 cm^2, a crucial insight for future investigations of the interstellar medium using similar techniques. Additionally, the similarity in velocity between the screen and Delta Cephei indicates that the screen's distance from the star is nearly equal to their radial velocity, implying that the screen's distance from the Sun is likely within a few parsecs. This discovery demonstrates the capability of pulsar scintillation analysis to probe the properties of individual screens and the surrounding interstellar medium with a high degree of precision. The similar velocity between the screen and the nearby star Delta Cephei also highlights the complexity of the Local Bubble's velocity structure. Moreover, the presence of this screen in relation to the surrounding interstellar medium in the line of sight to PSR B1133+16 has significant implications for future investigations of the pulsar's surrounding environment. The extensive data set for this pulsar includes numerous unexplored dimensions, offering a rich foundation for future analyses and investigations, such as the study of scatter broadband and the velocity distribution of the screen. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for inputs outside the training frequency range. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with two innovations. Firstly, the network adapts to given auxiliary frequency features via dynamic PDCNN architecture changes. Secondly, a cascaded network design is used to model long- and short-term signal dependencies in speech and other quasi-periodic signals. Experimental evaluations of QPNet demonstrate the benefits of PDCNNs for unseen frequency inputs and the cascaded structure's performance in speech synthesis. Human evaluator ratings reveal that the proposed method's quality and naturalness compared to WN are statistically significant. The proposed QPNet architecture also achieves a lower TR for the TIMIT dataset compared to WN. The source codes for QPNet are publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/EsraGulsen/Quasi-Periodic_WaveNet. The proposed model has promising applications in speech synthesis and other quasi-periodic signal generation tasks. The results are further validated through the demonstration of Wavenet's difficulty in modeling periodic components, the effectiveness of the proposed PDCNN structure, and the proposed method's performance in speech synthesis objective assessment. The proposed model's performance in speech synthesis is compared to the state-of-the-art text-to-speech model FairSeq-TTS. The results show that the proposed QPNet's quality and naturalness ratings are lower than FairSeq-TTT's ratings, which is expected given the limited pitch control of PDCNNs. The proposed method's performance can be further improved using the integration of PDCNNs and neural melody generation models. The integration of PDCNNs and neural melody generation models could enable the model to learn the melodic components of input signals and thus enhance its pitch control capabilities. The proposed model's performance in speech synthesis can be evaluated using the integrated system in the future. Our primary goal in this research is to pinpoint sound sources within video frames without relying on manually labeled data. Our core innovation involves training the network to distinguish between difficult image elements, including those that include the object generating the sound, to significantly enhance sound source localization performance. To accomplish this efficiently, we develop a method that automatically extracts challenging samples and incorporates them into a contrastive learning framework. Our algorithm achieves superior results on the Flickr SoundNet dataset, a prominent benchmark. Moreover, we introduce a new dataset called VGG-Sound Source, a comprehensive set of annotated video clips featuring sound sources with explicit bounding box markings. VGG-Sound Source surpasses existing datasets in scale, size, and category diversity, consisting of 5,000 videos spanning over 200 categories. Notably, it differs from Flickr SoundNet in that it is based on video data. Our algorithm also demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on this new dataset when compared to several baseline methods. Our code is available for public use at https://github.com/zhoukui, along with the VGG-Sound Source dataset accessible at https://www.robots.ox.ac.uk/~vgg/data/vggsound_source.html.

Recent advancements in graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have been primarily based on Euclidean geometry, but such methods may suffer from significant distortions when dealing with scale-free or hierarchical graphs. Researchers have proposed GCNs in non-Euclidean geometry, specifically in hyperbolic space, and have achieved notable performance improvements. However, existing hyperbolic graph operations fail to accurately follow the principles of hyperbolic geometry, potentially hindering the efficacy of these networks. This paper presents a novel hyperbolic GCN called Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN) that ensures learned node features adhere to hyperbolic geometry. LGCN redefines graph operations using the Lorentzian version and introduces a neighbourhood aggregation method based on Lorentzian distances, and it is mathematically proven that its operations are consistent across various hyperbolic geometries. Experimental evaluations on six datasets demonstrate LGCN's superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, and it is particularly effective at representing tree-likeness graphs with reduced distortion. LGCN's simplicity and flexibility also enable it to be highly versatile, allowing it to be used in various settings, from classification to generation, by adjusting its formulation of graph operations. This paper's contributions are further illustrated through a hypertext graph classification example, and it is hypothesized that LGCN's performance can be linked to its efficient dimensionality reduction capability. The code for LGCN is available at https://github.com/JinHePro/LGCN.

This research focuses on resolving an inverse problem where we aim to determine a source term within a structural acoustic partial differential equation (PDE) model, consisting of an acoustic wave equation and a Kirchhoff plate equation linked through a boundary interface. Uniqueness and a stability estimate for the source term can be established using a single measurement of the structure's boundary values. This uniqueness proof relies on the Carleman estimate, and subsequent stability results stem from observability inequality and a compactness-uniqueness argument. An operator theoretical approach provides the regularity needed for initial conditions, thereby obtaining the desired stability estimate. This inverse problem is ill-posed, and therefore, we develop a quasi-optimality cost functional to tackle it, yielding the existence of a minimal point from which we extract the unique source term, to which we apply a stability result. Numerical implementation is achieved through a gradient type algorithm, and we demonstrate this approach with a test example. This research is an extension of the previous work [J. Sprekeler, ArXiv 2017] where the source term was assumed to be random, and we now prove the uniqueness of the source term using a stability estimate in a more general setting. Furthermore, we introduce a new operator, modify the cost functional, and provide a numerical scheme in a deterministic setting. Additionally, we include a discussion on the hyper-inverse problem and the related identification problem. Lastly, we conclude with some future research directions. This study arose from the research project "Mathematical Methods for Subsurface Reservoirs and Cavities" funded by the Norwegian Research Council, and we extracted a single chapter from the related report, which is attached as an appendix. This chapter can be read as a standalone document. This research was presented at the International Conference on Inverse Problems and Applications, Moscow, held from 18 to 24 June 2018, and we included the related conference abstract in the appendix. This project was continued under the research project " Imaging and Parameter Estimation in Inverse Problems" funded by the Norwegian Research Council, and we introduced a new approach to solve the hyper-inverse problem and developed a numerical scheme for the related identification problem. We also discussed the uniqueness and stability of the source term, and provided a numerical implementation for the hyper-inverse problem and the related identification problem. This research was presented at the International Conference on Inverse Problems and Applications, Moscow, held from 18 to 24 June 2018, and we included the related conference abstract in the appendix.

Additionally, a thorough examination is performed of four distinct types of Hamiltonian dynamics: parabolic, elliptic, hyperbolic, and loxodromic dynamics. Semiclassical and high-temperature approximations are both determined and contrasted to their respective classical or quadratic behaviors. A distinguished subset of Hamiltonians is identified, for which the associated metaplectic operators can be explicitly defined, resulting in a straightforward calculation of the complex symplectic structure and thereby the thermal properties. A specialized form of these Hamiltonians, related to harmonic oscillators, is well known and constitutes a fundamental example of a Weyl-Wigner context. A related operator-theoretical approach, utilizing the Kuhn-Thamhauser theorem, is also developed and shown to yield the same complex symplectic structure, as well as a direct relation between the Weyl-Wigner and operator-based thermal state definitions. The notion of negative absolute temperature has been substantiated, no longer being merely a theoretical concept. Within this report, statistical mechanics and thermodynamics formalism are combined to illustrate negative temperature through both mathematical and graphical means, specifically in the context of a two-level system. We contend that the simplicity of these calculations can offer undergraduates a clear, tangible understanding of the concept of negative absolute temperature. Additionally, this approach may provide a richer learning experience compared to traditional, purely analytical explanations. A previous study by one of the authors demonstrated the utility of this approach in an educational setting, showing that it can help students overcome difficulties in grasping the concept of negative absolute temperature. The method presented here can be applied beyond the specific example of a two-level system, offering a more general framework for exploring statistical mechanics and thermodynamics. The report also addresses common misconceptions regarding negative absolute temperature, including the idea that it's related to negative kinetic energy or that it signifies a system's instability. Instead, it's demonstrated that negative absolute temperature is purely a relative term, with a system at a negative temperature being more energetic than a system at a positive temperature when compared to the same energy levels. The method used here can be applied to any system where the energy levels are well defined, and it may be particularly useful for illustrating the concept of negative temperature in educational settings that involve quantum systems, such as atomic or nuclear systems, where the concept of negative temperature is particularly relevant. The approach used here is not without limitations, requiring as it does the use of a specific energy basis in order to demonstrate negative absolute temperature. The report also addresses the question of how negative absolute temperature relates to the direction of time, a topic that is indirectly related to the second law of thermodynamics. The breakdown of thermal equilibrium due to the beating of two overlapping spectral lines is presented as a specific example of negative absolute temperature, along with the associated increase in decay rate of one of the atomic states. The example used here has been tested experimentally, and it may be useful for educating students about both negative absolute temperature and the related physics of open quantum systems. The report concludes by highlighting the utility of this method for exploring more complex open quantum systems, along with discussing some of the possible educational mistakes that students may make when learning about negative absolute temperature, along with some general advice on how to avoid these mistakes. We employ exact diagonalization to examine the effects of spin-orbit coupling and electron-electron interactions on the mixing of $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ $d$-orbital states in a cubic crystal structure, characteristic of transition metal oxides. By directly comparing with $t_{2g}$ only or $e_g$ only models based on electron filling, we investigate the magnetic properties of all possible $d$-shell configurations, incorporating calculations of the total magnetic moment, orbital occupation, and effective spin-orbit coupling. The resulting parameters are expressed in terms of interaction strength, spin-orbit coupling, and crystal field splitting within relevant 4d and 5d transition metal oxide ranges. Through various limits, our perturbative and numerical results converge, highlighting that $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing can be significant, with up to 20% orbital occupation outside nominal ranges. These findings hold important implications for experimental interpretation and can influence the theoretical models used to analyze magnetic properties and phases in these materials, where intermediate electron-electron coupling commonly prevails. The general approach employed here can be applied to other orbital triplets in crystal structures. The associated Python code is publicly available online. The transition from $S=1$ to $S=2$ ground state configurations is found to differ essentially, with $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing reducing to 10% or less when driving the former scenario, in contrast to over 20% for the latter. Using generative adversarial networks, a novel application in disease-aware image editing has emerged, which could revolutionize AI usage in the healthcare field. In this research, a concept for GAN-based medical imaging enhancement is demonstrated. Though GAN-based techniques excel at natural image creation and manipulation, their potential in medicine remains largely unexplored. Our research utilized the CheXpert dataset to train a StyleGAN that effectively produces authentic chest X-rays. By incorporating an encoder from the Cyclic Reverse Generator framework, we successfully developed an inverse mapping system to recreate synthetic X-rays accurately and reconstruct organs on real X-rays. By fine-tuning latent codes, we successfully transplanted a cardiac enlargement condition onto normal chest X-rays. Our research was showcased at the Medical Imaging meets NeurIPS Workshop 2020, a satellite event of the 34th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems held in Vancouver, Canada. Our dataset is available for public use at https://drive.google.

ViDaExpert is an application for multidimensional data visualization and
advanced analysis. It is capable of handling object-feature tables that include
numerical values and text-based labels for objects and features. The tool
encompasses several statistical techniques such as weighted PCA, elastic maps,
linear discriminant analysis, and decision tree construction, in addition to
K-Means clustering and multilinear regression. With customizable visualizations
and an interactive 3D viewer, ViDaExpert enables the creation of 3D scenes
from data and facilitates rapid, in-depth analysis of data, encompassing
elementary to complex methodologies. The application includes a user-friendly
graphical interface that simplifies data import, methodology selection, and
visualization customization. ViDaExpert is a Java-based tool that runs on
multiple platforms and allows users to edit 3D scenes and data visualizations
using its built-in editor or manually with the ViDaExpert Scene File Format. The
application, toolsets, and reference materials are available at the ViDaExpert
website. The development of ViDaExpert was supported by the Australian Government
Department of Education, Science and Technology. The application is suitable
for general, educational, and commercial use. The source code is available under
the GNU General Public License. The development of ViDaExpert was facilitated by
the open source nature of JMonkeyEngine and Weka. The application includes a
plugin architecture that enables users to create and integrate custom tools. The
ViDaExpert website hosts user-generated content, including plugins, tools, and
3D scenes. The application is available for download at the ViDaExpert website. The
